description.system_overview: This specification models Lamport's bakery algorithm, a mutual exclusion protocol that allows N concurrent processes to coordinate access to a critical section without relying on atomic hardware operations. The algorithm is named after the analogy of customers taking numbered tickets at a bakery and waiting for their turn to be served. It was originally published by Leslie Lamport in 1974 as 'A New Solution of Dijkstra's Concurrent Programming Problem'.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes (numbered 1 through N) that repeatedly cycle between a non-critical section, a doorway (entry protocol), a critical section, and an exit protocol. Each process independently competes for exclusive access to the critical section.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two shared arrays indexed by process identifier: (1) a ticket number for each process, representing its position in the queue (zero means the process is not competing), and (2) a boolean flag for each process indicating whether it is currently in the doorway choosing its ticket number. Each process also maintains local state for iterating over other processes during the entry protocol, tracking the maximum ticket number seen so far, and identifying which process is currently being checked in the waiting loop.
description.initial_state: All ticket numbers are zero (no process is competing). All choosing flags are false (no process is in the doorway). Each process starts in its non-critical section.
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in phases for each process: (1) Entry/doorway: The process sets its choosing flag to true, scans all other processes' ticket numbers to find the current maximum, selects a ticket number strictly greater than that maximum, then sets its choosing flag to false. (2) Waiting: The process iterates over every other process and, for each one, first waits until that process is not currently choosing a ticket number, then waits until either that process has a ticket number of zero (not competing) or the current process has higher priority. Priority is determined by lexicographic comparison of (ticket number, process identifier) pairs — a lower ticket number wins, and ties are broken by lower process identifier. (3) Critical section: The process executes its critical section. (4) Exit: The process resets its ticket number to zero and returns to the non-critical section. Nondeterminism is present in the entry and exit steps — the flag and ticket number may be written multiple times (with arbitrary intermediate values) before settling on their intended values, modeling the fact that these writes are not assumed to be atomic.
description.safety_properties: Mutual exclusion: no two distinct processes may be in the critical section at the same time.
description.liveness_properties: Deadlock freedom: if any process is trying to enter the critical section, then eventually some process enters the critical section. Starvation freedom: every process that begins trying to enter the critical section will eventually enter it.
description.model_bounds: The number of processes N is declared as a constant natural number. For model checking, N must be instantiated with a specific finite value (commonly 2 or 3).
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process when it is not in its non-critical section — that is, if a process is trying to make progress (it is past the non-critical section), it will eventually take a step. The algorithm models non-atomic reads and writes by allowing nondeterministic stuttering at the entry and exit points, where variables may be assigned intermediate arbitrary values before reaching their intended values. A formal machine-checked proof of mutual exclusion is included in the specification.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Boulangerie algorithm, a variant of Lamport's bakery algorithm for mutual exclusion, published by Yoram Moses and Katia Patkin at SIROCCO 2015. The Boulangerie algorithm improves on the bakery algorithm by eliminating unnecessary blocking: it analyzes how processes establish and detect priority, and allows a process to proceed when it can determine that another process has re-entered the doorway (and thus will choose a new, higher ticket number) or when it holds the lowest possible ticket number and only needs to check lower-numbered processes.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N concurrent processes (numbered 1 through N) that repeatedly cycle between a non-critical section, an entry protocol (doorway), a critical section, and an exit protocol. Each process independently competes for exclusive access to a shared critical section.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two shared arrays indexed by process identifier: (1) a ticket number for each process (zero means not competing), and (2) a boolean flag indicating whether the process is currently choosing its ticket number in the doorway. Each process also maintains local state for: a set of processes still to be checked during the waiting phase, the maximum ticket number observed during scanning, the identifier of the process currently being waited on, and the previously observed ticket number of the process being waited on (used to detect re-entry into the doorway).
description.initial_state: All ticket numbers are zero. All choosing flags are false. Each process starts in its non-critical section. The previously-observed-ticket variable for each process is initialized to a sentinel value indicating no previous observation.
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in phases: (1) Entry/doorway: The process sets its choosing flag to true, scans all other processes to find the maximum ticket number, selects a ticket number equal to one plus that maximum, then sets its choosing flag to false. When clearing the flag, the set of processes to check during waiting is determined: if the chosen ticket number is 1 (the lowest possible non-zero value), only processes with lower identifiers need to be checked; otherwise, all other processes are checked. (2) Waiting: For each process in the set to be checked, the process first waits until the other process is not choosing. It then resets its record of the other process's previously observed ticket number. The process checks whether the other process can be skipped: it can be skipped if the other process's ticket number is zero, or if the current process has higher priority (lower lexicographic pair of ticket number and identifier), or if the other process's ticket number has changed since the last observation (indicating it re-entered the doorway and will choose a higher number). If the other process cannot yet be skipped, the current process records the other's ticket number and re-checks. (3) Critical section: The process executes its critical section. (4) Exit: The process resets its ticket number to zero. Nondeterminism is present in the entry and exit steps — flag and ticket number may be written multiple times with arbitrary intermediate values before settling, modeling non-atomic (safe register) writes.
description.safety_properties: Mutual exclusion: no two distinct processes may be in the critical section at the same time.
description.liveness_properties: Deadlock freedom: if any process is trying to enter the critical section, eventually some process enters. Starvation freedom: every process that begins trying to enter the critical section will eventually enter it.
description.model_bounds: The number of processes N is a constant natural number. For model checking, N must be instantiated with a specific finite value.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process when it is not in its non-critical section. The specification models safe registers (non-atomic reads and writes) through nondeterministic stuttering at entry and exit points. A formal machine-checked proof of mutual exclusion is included.

description.system_overview: A concurrency game modeling symmetrical cooperation among creatures called chameneos. Creatures meet pairwise at a central meeting place. When two creatures meet, they both change color according to a complementation rule. After a fixed total number of meetings has occurred, the meeting place closes and creatures that try to enter it fade out. The system terminates when all creatures have faded.
actors_and_components: Creatures (chameneos): Entities that each have a color and a count of meetings participated in. They repeatedly attempt to enter the meeting place to meet another creature.
Meeting place (also called the Mall): A shared location that can hold at most one waiting creature at a time. Creatures enter the meeting place to find a partner for a meeting.
Global meeting counter: Tracks the total number of completed meetings system-wide.
state_variables: A mapping from each creature identifier to a pair consisting of the creature's current color (one of blue, red, yellow, or faded) and the number of meetings that creature has participated in.
The current occupant of the meeting place, which is either empty or holds one creature's identifier.
A global counter recording the total number of meetings that have occurred so far.
description.initial_state: Each creature is assigned some color from the set {blue, red, yellow} (nondeterministically), with a meeting count of zero. The meeting place is empty. The total meeting counter is zero.
actions: Enter empty meeting place: If the meeting place is empty and the total number of meetings has not yet reached the limit, a non-faded creature enters and waits in the meeting place.

Fade out: If the meeting place is empty and the total number of meetings has reached the limit, a non-faded creature that tries to enter becomes faded (its color changes to faded, retaining its meeting count).

Meet and mutate: If the meeting place is occupied by a different creature, the arriving creature and the waiting creature both adopt a new color determined by the complement rule. Both creatures' individual meeting counts are incremented by one, the global meeting counter is incremented by one, and the meeting place becomes empty.
safety_properties: When the global meeting counter reaches the maximum, the sum of all individual creature meeting counts equals twice the maximum number of meetings. This reflects that each meeting involves exactly two participants.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED

model_bounds.total_meetings_limit: A positive natural number specifying when the meeting place closes.
model_bounds.number_of_creatures: A positive natural number specifying how many creatures participate.

additional_assumptions: The color complement rule: if two creatures have the same color, both keep that color; if they have different colors, both adopt the third color not held by either.
A creature cannot meet itself (the arriving creature must be different from the one waiting in the meeting place).
It is not guaranteed that all creatures participate in at least one meeting before the system terminates.

description.system_overview: This specification models a checkpoint coordination protocol for a replicated state machine cluster, designed for the Azure DNS RingMaster system. The cluster consists of one primary and several secondary replicas. Secondaries must periodically take checkpoints (snapshots) of their local state and upload them to cloud storage, but only one secondary may checkpoint at a time to preserve read availability on the other secondaries. The primary coordinates which secondary takes a checkpoint using a lease-based mechanism replicated through the underlying Paxos consensus layer.
description.actors_and_components: The participants are a set of replica nodes forming a cluster. At any time, one node may be elected as the primary (leader), and the remaining nodes act as secondaries. The primary is responsible for selecting a secondary to take a checkpoint and issuing a checkpoint lease via the replicated log. Secondaries receive and execute replicated requests, and if designated by a lease, they schedule and perform a checkpoint. The environment includes node failures and recoveries, as well as network link failures and recoveries between any pair of nodes.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) whether each node is currently up or down, (2) whether a network path exists between each ordered pair of nodes, (3) which node is currently the elected leader (or none), (4) a replicated log of commands on each node recording which node has been assigned checkpoint duty at each log index, (5) an execution counter per node indicating which log entry the node will execute next, (6) a payload field per node used to piggyback checkpoint completion status back to the primary via vote responses, (7) the current checkpoint lease recorded at each node (including the designated node and the log index at which the lease was issued, or a sentinel indicating no lease), (8) a boolean per node indicating whether the node believes it is eligible to take a checkpoint, (9) a boolean per node indicating whether the node is currently in the process of taking a checkpoint, (10) a global timeout counter tracking which lease index has timed out, and (11) the latest completed checkpoint record containing a saved log and the log index up to which it applies.
description.initial_state: All nodes start in the up state. All network paths between nodes are available. No leader is elected. Each node has an empty replicated log. Each node's execution counter starts at the first log index. Each node's vote payload starts at the first log index. No node has a checkpoint lease. No node believes it can take a checkpoint. No node is taking a checkpoint. The timeout counter starts at the first log index. The latest checkpoint is empty (blank log at the first log index).
description.actions: The system has the following transitions: (1) Node failure: a node goes down, losing all volatile state including its execution counter, vote payload, lease knowledge, and checkpoint status; the leader is cleared if the failing node was leader. (2) Node recovery: a down node comes back up and rehydrates its log from the latest checkpoint, filling gaps with its locally persisted log; its execution counter advances to the checkpoint boundary. (3) Network failure: a directional network link between two nodes fails. (4) Network recovery: a directional network link is restored. (5) Leader election: when no leader exists, an up node that is not currently taking a checkpoint, has quorum (a majority of connected nodes), and is fully caught up (its execution counter equals the first unused log index) may be elected leader; upon election, the node's checkpoint eligibility is revoked. (6) Send replicated request: the leader selects a connected secondary node and writes a checkpoint lease assignment into the replicated log at the first open index, distributing it to all reachable nodes; the leader updates its own lease record; a new lease may only be sent if no current lease exists or the current lease should be replaced (because it timed out or the designated node reported completion). (7) Propagate replicated request: a node that has a log entry propagates it to another connected node whose log is missing that entry (log merge). (8) Process replicated request: an up node that is not taking a checkpoint reads the next entry from its log and advances its execution counter; if the entry designates this node and the node is not the leader and the entry has not timed out, the node marks itself eligible to checkpoint; otherwise eligibility is revoked; non-leader nodes also update their local lease record. (9) Start checkpoint: a node that believes it is eligible begins taking a checkpoint. (10) Finish checkpoint: a node that is taking a checkpoint completes it, recording the checkpoint (its log up to the current execution point), updating its vote payload to signal completion, clearing its lease and eligibility, and marking itself as no longer taking a checkpoint. (11) Trigger timeout: the global timeout counter advances (if at least one node has a log entry at that index), revoking checkpoint eligibility and stopping any active checkpoint for nodes whose lease index is no longer current.
description.safety_properties: The following must hold in every reachable state: (1) The leader never believes it can take a checkpoint and is never taking a checkpoint. (2) If the leader has no knowledge of a lease, then no node anywhere believes it can take or is taking a checkpoint. (3) If the leader knows of a lease, only the designated node in that lease can be eligible or taking a checkpoint. (4) At most one node believes it can take a checkpoint at any time, and at most one node is taking a checkpoint at any time. (5) A node can only be taking a checkpoint if it also believes it is eligible. (6) A node can only believe it is eligible if it holds a lease designating itself, and that lease has not timed out. (7) Replicated logs across nodes never contain conflicting values at the same index.
description.liveness_properties: Under fairness assumptions: (1) Eventually some node becomes eligible to take a checkpoint. (2) If a node is eligible, it eventually either starts a checkpoint, goes down, or its lease times out. (3) If a node is taking a checkpoint, it eventually either completes (signaling via its vote payload), goes down, or its lease times out. (4) Eventually a checkpoint is completed (the stored checkpoint record becomes non-empty).
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED in the base specification. The set of nodes and the majority threshold are declared as constants. Model-checking bounds are defined in a separate configuration module.
description.additional_assumptions: Fairness assumptions ensure progress: weak fairness on node recovery and network recovery (if a node or link can recover, it eventually does), and strong fairness on leader election, sending replicated requests, propagating requests, processing requests, starting checkpoints, and finishing checkpoints. The timeout mechanism is modeled as a global counter rather than real-time clocks; the underlying consensus system (Paxos/RSL) is assumed to ensure that time dilation between replicas stays within a bounded margin, so that a secondary's local timeout expires before the primary's.

description.system_overview: A model of the cigarette smokers problem, originally described by Suhas Patil in 1971. A dealer places a combination of ingredients on a table, and smokers who each have an infinite supply of one ingredient check whether the offered ingredients, combined with their own, allow them to smoke. At most one smoker smokes at any time. The dealer waits for the current smoker to finish before placing a new offer.
actors_and_components: Smokers: Each smoker possesses an infinite supply of exactly one ingredient. A smoker can smoke when the dealer's offer, combined with the smoker's own ingredient, provides a complete set of all ingredients. Each smoker has a boolean state indicating whether they are currently smoking.
Dealer: An agent that places a subset of ingredients on the table. The offered subset is always missing exactly one ingredient. After a smoker finishes, the dealer places a new offer.
state_variables: A mapping from each ingredient to the smoking status (true or false) of the smoker who holds an infinite supply of that ingredient.
The current offer on the table: either a subset of ingredients missing exactly one ingredient, or empty (indicating a smoker is currently smoking).
description.initial_state: No smoker is smoking (all smoking flags are false). The dealer has placed an initial offer on the table, chosen nondeterministically from the set of valid offers.
actions: Start smoking: When the dealer's offer is non-empty, exactly one smoker whose ingredient completes the full set begins smoking. The offer is then cleared (set to empty).

Stop smoking: When the offer is empty (meaning someone is smoking), the single currently-smoking smoker stops smoking and the dealer places a new offer chosen nondeterministically from the set of valid offers.
safety_properties: At most one smoker is smoking at any given moment.
description.liveness_properties: The specification includes a weak fairness condition on the next-state relation, ensuring the system continues to make progress (smokers eventually smoke and stop).

model_bounds.ingredients: A set of ingredients, originally {matches, paper, tobacco}.
model_bounds.offers: A set of subsets of ingredients, each containing all but one ingredient.

additional_assumptions: Each valid offer is missing exactly one ingredient from the complete set.
The set of offers is a subset of all subsets of ingredients.
Every smoker has an infinite supply of exactly one distinct ingredient.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Coffee Can problem, a mathematical puzzle attributed to Edsger W. Dijkstra (who credited his colleague Carel S. Scholten) and popularized by David Gries in his 1987 book 'The Science of Programming'. A coffee can contains some black beans and white beans. Two beans are repeatedly drawn at random: if they match in color, both are discarded and a new black bean is added from an external supply; if they differ, the black one is discarded and the white one is returned. The process reduces the bean count by one each iteration and terminates when exactly one bean remains. The puzzle asks what can be determined about the color of the final bean based on the initial bean counts.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a single coffee can containing a population of black and white beans, plus an unlimited external supply of black beans. There are no concurrent actors; the system proceeds by a single sequential process of repeatedly drawing and replacing beans.
description.state_variables: The system tracks the number of black beans and the number of white beans currently in the can. These two counts together fully determine the state of the system at any point.
description.initial_state: The can starts with some combination of black and white beans such that the total number of beans is between one and a configurable upper bound. All combinations of black and white bean counts within this range are considered as possible starting states.
description.actions: Three possible actions exist, each requiring at least two beans in the can: (1) Draw two black beans -- both are removed and one black bean is added back, reducing the total by one and the black count by one. (2) Draw two white beans -- both are removed and one black bean is added, reducing the total by one, increasing the black count by one, and decreasing the white count by two. (3) Draw one black and one white bean -- the black bean is discarded and the white bean is returned, reducing the total by one and the black count by one. A fourth action handles termination: when only one bean remains, the system holds steady with no further changes.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: the bean counts always remain within the valid range. Monotonic decrease: each non-stuttering step reduces the total number of beans in the can. Loop invariant: the parity (odd or even) of the white bean count is preserved by every step -- if the white count starts even it stays even, and if it starts odd it stays odd.
description.liveness_properties: Eventual termination: the system eventually reaches a state where exactly one bean remains in the can. Termination hypothesis: if the initial white bean count is even, the system eventually reaches a state with one black bean and no white beans; if the initial white bean count is odd, the system eventually reaches a state with one white bean and no black beans.
description.model_bounds: A constant upper bound on the maximum number of beans of each color constrains the state space. For model checking, this bound must be set to a specific finite value.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for the overall next-state action, ensuring the system cannot stutter indefinitely and must eventually draw beans when more than one remains. The system is fully specified with an initial-state predicate, a next-state relation, and a fairness condition.

description.system_overview: Models the Die Hard 3 water jug puzzle where heroes must measure exactly 4 gallons of water using a 5-gallon jug, a 3-gallon jug, and a water faucet. The goal is to find a sequence of pouring actions that results in exactly 4 gallons in the larger jug. A model checker is used to find the shortest solution via breadth-first search by treating the goal state as an invariant violation.
actors_and_components: A 5-gallon jug that can be filled from the faucet, emptied onto the ground, or used to pour water to/from the other jug
A 3-gallon jug with the same capabilities
A water faucet that provides unlimited water
state_variables: The current water level of the large (5-gallon) jug, represented as an integer from 0 to 5
The current water level of the small (3-gallon) jug, represented as an integer from 0 to 3
description.initial_state: Both jugs start completely empty (each containing 0 gallons of water).
actions: Fill the small jug: sets the small jug to its full capacity (3 gallons) while the large jug remains unchanged.
Fill the large jug: sets the large jug to its full capacity (5 gallons) while the small jug remains unchanged.
Empty the small jug: dumps the small jug to 0 gallons while the large jug remains unchanged.
Empty the large jug: dumps the large jug to 0 gallons while the small jug remains unchanged.

Pour from the small jug to the large jug: transfers water from the small jug into the large jug. The large jug receives the lesser of (a) the combined water in both jugs and (b) 5 gallons (its capacity). The small jug loses whatever the large jug gained.

Pour from the large jug to the small jug: transfers water from the large jug into the small jug. The small jug receives the lesser of (a) the combined water in both jugs and (b) 3 gallons (its capacity). The large jug loses whatever the small jug gained.
safety_properties: Type correctness: the water level in the small jug is always between 0 and 3 inclusive, and the water level in the large jug is always between 0 and 5 inclusive.

Not-solved invariant: the large jug never contains exactly 4 gallons. This is intentionally expected to be violated; the counterexample trace produced by the model checker is the solution to the puzzle.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The state space is fully enumerable: the small jug ranges over 4 values (0 through 3) and the large jug ranges over 6 values (0 through 5), giving at most 24 reachable states.
expected_output_files: DieHard.cfg - configuration file specifying the specification formula and invariants to check
description.additional_assumptions: The jugs are not calibrated, so partial filling or partial emptying is not meaningful. Only completely filling a jug from the faucet, completely emptying a jug, or pouring from one jug to another (until one is full or the other is empty) are valid actions.

description.system_overview: A generalized version of the Die Hard water jug puzzle that supports an arbitrary number of jugs, each with a specified positive integer capacity, and an arbitrary goal quantity of water to measure. The model checker finds a solution by searching for a state where any jug contains the goal amount, treating this as an invariant violation to produce a counterexample trace.
actors_and_components: A configurable set of jugs, each with a specified positive integer capacity
A water faucet that provides unlimited water for filling any jug
state_variables: A mapping from each jug to its current water level, represented as a non-negative integer
description.initial_state: All jugs start completely empty (each containing 0 units of water).
actions: Fill a jug: sets a chosen jug to its full capacity while all other jugs remain unchanged.
Empty a jug: dumps a chosen jug to 0 while all other jugs remain unchanged.

Pour from one jug to another: transfers water from a source jug to a destination jug. The amount poured is the lesser of (a) the water in the source jug and (b) the remaining capacity of the destination jug. The source jug loses the poured amount, and the destination jug gains it.
safety_properties: Type correctness: the water level in each jug is always a non-negative integer.

Not-solved invariant: no jug ever contains exactly the goal amount of water. This is intentionally expected to be violated; the counterexample trace produced by the model checker is the solution to the puzzle.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The state space depends on the number of jugs and their capacities. Each jug can hold values from 0 to its capacity, so the total state space is the product of (capacity + 1) for each jug.
description.additional_assumptions: Each jug capacity must be a positive integer, and the goal must be a non-negative integer. The jugs are not calibrated, so only completely filling, completely emptying, or pouring between jugs (until one is full or the other is empty) are valid actions. The specification requires a separate model-checking module to supply concrete values for the jug set, capacities, and goal.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Dining Philosophers problem using the Chandy-Misra solution. The classic problem, originally formulated by Edsger Dijkstra in 1965, involves multiple philosophers seated around a circular table who alternate between thinking and eating. Each philosopher requires two shared forks (one on each side) to eat. The Chandy-Misra variant (1984) extends the original formulation by allowing philosophers to communicate directly and pass forks to each other, using a clean/dirty fork mechanism to prevent both deadlock and starvation.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a configurable number of philosopher processes arranged in a ring topology, and a set of shared forks equal in number to the philosophers. Each fork is positioned between two adjacent philosophers. Philosophers cycle through thinking, waiting for forks, and eating. Forks are the shared resources that mediate exclusive access to eating.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) For each fork: which philosopher currently holds it and whether it is in a clean or dirty state. (2) For each philosopher: whether the philosopher is currently hungry (wanting to eat) or sated (wanting to think). (3) For each philosopher: the current phase of activity (looping through fork management, eating, or thinking).
description.initial_state: Each fork begins in a dirty state. Forks are distributed asymmetrically: each fork is initially held by the lower-numbered of the two adjacent philosophers (with a specific assignment rule for the second fork to break symmetry). All philosophers start in a hungry state, ready to attempt acquiring forks to eat. Each philosopher begins at the start of its main processing loop.
description.actions: Each philosopher repeatedly executes the following cycle: (1) Fork surrender: If the philosopher holds a dirty fork on either side, it cleans the fork and passes it to the neighboring philosopher on that side. The left side is checked first, then the right. (2) Eating attempt: If the philosopher is hungry and holds both adjacent forks in a clean state, it eats. Eating causes both held forks to become dirty and transitions the philosopher to a sated state. (3) Thinking: If the philosopher is not hungry (having just eaten), it thinks, which makes it hungry again, and the cycle repeats.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: all fork assignments remain valid philosopher identifiers, fork cleanliness flags remain boolean, hunger states remain boolean, and philosopher phases remain within the expected set. Exclusive access: no two philosophers who share a fork may eat at the same time.
description.liveness_properties: Starvation freedom: every philosopher eventually gets to eat again. This is guaranteed by the combination of fair scheduling and the clean/dirty fork mechanism, which gives priority to philosophers who have not eaten recently.
description.model_bounds: The number of philosophers is declared as a positive integer constant. For model checking, this is typically set to a small finite value such as 5.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each philosopher process, ensuring that no philosopher is indefinitely prevented from taking steps when it is able to do so. The specification uses PlusCal (an algorithmic language that compiles to TLA+) and includes the compiled translation.

description.system_overview: This specification models a Multi Producer, Multi Consumer (MPMC) Disruptor, a high-performance inter-thread communication data structure based on the LMAX Exchange Disruptor pattern. Multiple producer threads publish events into a shared ring buffer, and multiple consumer threads read all published events in a multicast fashion (every consumer reads every event). The primary purpose of the model is to verify the absence of data races between producers and consumers and to check that all consumers eventually read all published values.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of two types of participants: writers (producer threads) and readers (consumer threads). Writers compete to claim sequence numbers and publish events into slots of a fixed-size ring buffer. Readers independently track their progress and consume events from the ring buffer. The ring buffer itself is a shared circular data structure that tracks which slots are being read, which are being written, and the values stored in each slot.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) the ring buffer contents, including the value stored in each slot, which readers are currently accessing each slot, and which writers are currently accessing each slot; (2) a shared counter representing the next sequence number available for a writer to claim; (3) the sequence number each writer has currently claimed; (4) for each slot in the ring buffer, whether it has been published in the current round (using an even/odd round encoding to distinguish successive writes to the same slot); (5) a read cursor per consumer indicating the last sequence number it has consumed; (6) a program counter per thread indicating whether it is currently accessing a slot or advancing to the next; (7) a history variable per consumer recording the sequence of all values that consumer has read, used for liveness verification.
description.initial_state: All ring buffer slots contain a null value with no active readers or writers. The next available sequence number is zero. All writers have a claimed sequence of negative one (indicating no claim). All publication flags are set to indicate unpublished. All read cursors start at negative one (no events consumed). All threads (both writers and readers) start in the advancing state. All consumer read histories are empty sequences.
description.actions: The system has four transitions: (1) Begin write: a writer claims the next available sequence number if the slowest consumer is far enough ahead that the writer will not overwrite unconsumed data (the consumer must be at most one full ring buffer cycle behind); the writer atomically increments the shared sequence counter, records its claimed sequence, writes its value into the corresponding ring buffer slot, marks itself as accessing that slot, and transitions to the accessing state. (2) End write: a writer that is currently accessing a slot finishes the write by removing itself from the slot's writer set, flipping the publication flag for that slot to indicate the new value is published, and transitioning back to the advancing state. (3) Begin read: a reader checks whether the next sequence number it needs to read has been published (using the even/odd round encoding); if so, it marks itself as accessing the corresponding slot, records the value read into its history, and transitions to the accessing state. (4) End read: a reader that is currently accessing a slot finishes the read by removing itself from the slot's reader set, advancing its read cursor, and transitioning back to the advancing state.
description.safety_properties: Two invariants must hold: (1) Type correctness: all variables remain within their expected domains. (2) No data races: for every slot in the ring buffer, no slot is simultaneously being read and written (the sets of active readers and active writers for each slot must not both be non-empty), and at most one writer accesses any given slot at a time.
description.liveness_properties: Eventually and permanently, every consumer must have read all published values in order. Specifically, for each consumer and each sequence number from zero up to the maximum, once that sequence number has been published it will eventually be the case that the consumer has read it and recorded the correct value.
description.model_bounds: The maximum number of published events bounds the model. The ring buffer has a fixed size. The sets of writers and readers are finite and specified as constants. A state constraint limits exploration to states where the next sequence number has not exceeded the maximum.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for consumer read actions (both beginning and ending reads), ensuring consumers make progress when enabled. No fairness is assumed for producers, meaning the model allows producers to stop publishing at any point. The publication mechanism uses an even/odd round encoding per slot: a producer flips the flag each time it publishes to a slot, and consumers check whether the flag matches the expected parity for the sequence number they want to read. The available published sequence for consumers is computed conservatively to handle the case where a slower producer has not yet published its slot even though a faster producer has published a later slot.

description.system_overview: This specification models a Single Producer, Multi Consumer (SPMC) Disruptor, a high-performance inter-thread communication pattern based on the LMAX Exchange Disruptor. A single producer thread publishes events into a fixed-size ring buffer, and multiple consumer threads each independently read all published events in multicast fashion. The model verifies the absence of data races between the producer and consumers and ensures all consumers eventually read all published values.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of two types of participants: a single writer (producer thread) and multiple readers (consumer threads). The writer publishes events sequentially into a ring buffer. Each reader independently consumes all events from the ring buffer. The ring buffer is a shared circular data structure that tracks slot contents and which threads are actively accessing each slot.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) the ring buffer contents, including the value in each slot, which readers are currently accessing each slot, and which writers are currently accessing each slot; (2) a write cursor indicating the sequence number of the last published event; (3) a read cursor per consumer indicating the last sequence number consumed by that consumer; (4) a program counter per thread indicating whether it is currently accessing a slot or advancing to the next; (5) a history variable per consumer recording the sequence of all values read, used for liveness verification.
description.initial_state: All ring buffer slots contain a null value with no active readers or writers. The write cursor starts at negative one (nothing published). All read cursors start at negative one (nothing consumed). All threads start in the advancing state. All consumer read histories are empty.
description.actions: The system has four transitions: (1) Begin write: the producer checks that the slowest consumer is far enough ahead that writing the next slot will not overwrite unconsumed data (the consumer must be at most one ring buffer cycle behind); the producer then writes its sequence number as the value into the corresponding slot, marks itself as accessing that slot, and transitions to the accessing state. (2) End write: the producer finishes writing by removing itself from the slot's writer set, advancing the write cursor to make the event visible to consumers, and transitioning back to the advancing state. (3) Begin read: a consumer checks whether the next sequence it needs to read has been published (the write cursor is at or past that sequence); if so, it marks itself as accessing the slot, records the value into its read history, and transitions to the accessing state. (4) End read: a consumer finishes reading by removing itself from the slot's reader set, advancing its read cursor, and transitioning back to the advancing state.
description.safety_properties: Two invariants must hold: (1) Type correctness: all variables remain within their expected domains. (2) No data races: for every slot in the ring buffer, a slot is never simultaneously being read and written (the reader and writer sets for each slot cannot both be non-empty), and at most one writer accesses any slot at a time.
description.liveness_properties: Eventually and permanently, every consumer must have read all published values in order. For each consumer and each sequence number up to the maximum, once the write cursor has reached or passed that sequence, the consumer will eventually have read it and recorded the correct value.
description.model_bounds: The maximum number of published events bounds the model. The ring buffer has a fixed size. The writer and reader sets are finite constants. A state constraint limits exploration to states where the write cursor has not reached the maximum.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for consumer read actions (both beginning and ending reads), ensuring consumers make progress when enabled. No fairness is assumed for the producer. Because there is only a single producer, the publication mechanism is simpler than the multi-producer case: the write cursor directly indicates which sequence numbers are available for reading, without needing an additional per-slot publication tracking mechanism.

description.system_overview: This specification models a generic ring buffer (circular buffer) data structure used as the foundation for the Disruptor inter-thread communication pattern. The ring buffer has a fixed number of slots, each of which can hold a value. It provides read and write operations with tracking of which threads are currently accessing each slot, enabling detection of data races between producer and consumer threads.
description.actors_and_components: The ring buffer is parameterized by a set of reader threads, a set of writer threads, a fixed size, a set of permissible values, and a null sentinel value. Readers perform multi-step read operations (begin read, read value, end read) and writers perform multi-step write operations (write value, end write). The ring buffer itself does not define a complete system specification; it is a reusable component intended to be instantiated by higher-level specifications.
description.state_variables: The ring buffer tracks three things for each slot (indexed from zero to one less than the buffer size): (1) the value currently stored in the slot (initially null), (2) the set of readers currently accessing the slot, and (3) the set of writers currently accessing the slot.
description.initial_state: All slots contain the null value. No readers are accessing any slot. No writers are accessing any slot.
description.actions: The ring buffer provides the following operations: (1) Write: a writer writes a value to a slot at a given index, simultaneously adding itself to that slot's writer set and updating the slot's stored value. (2) End write: a writer removes itself from a slot's writer set, indicating it has finished writing. (3) Begin read: a reader adds itself to a slot's reader set, indicating it is beginning to read. (4) Read: returns the value currently stored at a given index (a pure query with no state change). (5) End read: a reader removes itself from a slot's reader set, indicating it has finished reading. An index-of operator maps a sequence number to a slot index using modular arithmetic (sequence number modulo buffer size).
description.safety_properties: The no-data-races invariant requires that for every slot: (a) the set of active readers and the set of active writers are never both non-empty at the same time (no simultaneous read and write to the same slot), and (b) at most one writer is accessing any given slot at a time. A type invariant ensures that slot values are either null or a member of the value set, reader sets are subsets of the reader set parameter, and writer sets are subsets of the writer set parameter.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED. The ring buffer module defines no temporal properties; liveness requirements are specified by the higher-level modules that instantiate it.
description.model_bounds: The buffer size, reader set, writer set, value set, and null value are all declared as constants to be supplied by the instantiating module. The buffer size must be a positive natural number. The writer and reader sets must be non-empty. The null value must not be a member of the value set.
description.additional_assumptions: This module is designed as a reusable library component, not a standalone specification. It uses local imports (not exported to instantiating modules). The data race invariant is expected to be asserted by any specification that uses this ring buffer. The module does not define an initial state, next-state relation, or specification formula on its own; those are provided by the higher-level Disruptor specifications that instantiate it.

description.system_overview: This specification models Einstein's Riddle (also known as the Zebra Puzzle), a classic constraint satisfaction logic puzzle. The puzzle involves five houses in a row, each with a unique color, occupied by a person of a unique nationality, who drinks a unique beverage, smokes a unique brand of cigar, and keeps a unique pet. Fifteen clues constrain the relationships between these attributes. The goal is to find the unique assignment of all attributes to houses that satisfies every clue simultaneously. The specification encodes the puzzle as an initial-state constraint satisfaction problem and searches for a solution by checking all valid permutations against the clue constraints.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of five houses arranged in a linear order (first through fifth). Each house is characterized by five attributes: the nationality of its occupant, the color of the house, the pet kept by the occupant, the brand of cigar smoked by the occupant, and the beverage consumed by the occupant. There are no dynamic actors; the specification models a single static assignment problem.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five ordered sequences, one for each attribute category: (1) a sequence mapping each house position to a nationality, (2) a sequence mapping each house position to a house color, (3) a sequence mapping each house position to a pet, (4) a sequence mapping each house position to a cigar brand, and (5) a sequence mapping each house position to a beverage. Each sequence is a permutation of five distinct values for that category.
description.initial_state: The initial state assigns a permutation of values to each attribute category, subject to three constraints that are applied immediately to prune the search space: the middle house (position three) has milk as its beverage, the first house is occupied by the Norwegian, and the second house is blue. All valid permutations of the remaining attribute categories are considered.
description.actions: The system has no meaningful transitions. Once an initial assignment is chosen, the state does not change. The specification is structured to find a solution entirely within the initial state by exploring all valid permutation combinations.
description.safety_properties: The solution-finding property is expressed as an invariant: the negation of the conjunction of all fifteen puzzle clues. These clues encode constraints such as: the Brit lives in the red house, the Swede keeps dogs, the Dane drinks tea, the green house is immediately left of the white house, the green house owner drinks coffee, the person who smokes a particular brand rears birds, the yellow house owner smokes a particular brand, the center house occupant drinks milk, the Norwegian lives in the first house, certain smokers live next to certain pet owners, certain smokers drink certain beverages, the German smokes a particular brand, the Norwegian lives next to the blue house, and a certain smoker has a neighbor who drinks water. When the model checker finds a counterexample to this negated invariant, that counterexample is the puzzle's solution.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The puzzle has a fixed size: exactly five houses and five values per attribute category. No configurable bounds are needed. The total search space is the product of all valid permutations across the five attribute categories, subject to the initial-state pruning constraints.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses a helper module for sequence manipulation functions. The puzzle is also designed to be solvable by SMT-based model checkers which can find the solution much faster than explicit-state enumeration, due to the purely combinatorial constraint satisfaction nature of the problem.

description.system_overview: This specification models a basic grow-only counter Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Each node in a distributed system maintains a vector of counters, one per node. Nodes can increment their own counter and propagate state to other nodes through gossip. The specification is part of a collection illustrating how ordinarily-infinite monotonic systems can be made finite for model checking.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of distributed nodes, each maintaining a local view of every node's counter value. Nodes act both as writers (incrementing their own counter) and as gossip participants (sending and receiving state updates to synchronize their views).
description.state_variables: The system tracks a two-dimensional mapping from each node to its view of every node's counter value. Each node maintains a vector indexed by all nodes, where each entry is a natural number representing that node's current counter value as known to the viewing node.
description.initial_state: All counter values in all nodes' views are initialized to zero. Every node's view of every other node's counter starts at zero.
description.actions: There are two types of transitions: (1) Increment: a node increments its own entry in its local counter vector by one. Only a node's own counter entry in its own view is modified. (2) Gossip: one node sends its entire counter vector to another node. The receiving node updates each entry in its view to the maximum of its current value and the sender's value for that entry. This merge operation ensures values only increase.
description.safety_properties: Each node's own view of its own counter must always be at least as large as any other node's view of that counter. In other words, a node always has the most up-to-date value of its own counter. Additionally, all counter values must remain non-negative natural numbers conforming to the expected type structure.
description.liveness_properties: Convergence: the system must repeatedly reach states where all nodes have identical counter vectors. That is, infinitely often, all nodes agree on every counter value. Monotonicity: counter values as observed by any node must never decrease across transitions.
description.model_bounds: The set of nodes is declared as a constant. For model checking, this is typically instantiated as a small finite set (for example, three nodes). The finite monotonic technique bounds counter values by limiting the maximum divergence between the lowest and highest counter values across the system.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on all gossip actions between every pair of nodes, ensuring that gossip will eventually occur whenever it is enabled. Additionally, the specification assumes that from some point onwards, only gossip actions are performed (increments happen only finitely often). This combination ensures eventual convergence. The overall specification with these fairness conditions is machine closed despite the second condition not being a standard fairness assumption.

description.system_overview: This specification models a distributed replicated log system inspired by the Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF). Multiple servers each maintain their own copy of an append-only log. Servers can extend their logs with new values and copy missing entries from other servers. The specification demonstrates how the finite monotonic technique can be used to find violations of liveness properties, specifically showing that full synchronization (all logs identical) is not guaranteed even under fairness.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of servers, each maintaining its own log, and a finite set of possible values that can be appended to logs. A constant parameter controls the maximum allowed divergence (lag) between any two servers' log lengths.
description.state_variables: The system tracks a mapping from each server to its own local log, represented as an ordered sequence of values. Each server's log grows independently but is bounded in how far it can diverge from other servers' logs.
description.initial_state: All servers start with an empty log (a sequence of length zero).
description.actions: There are two types of transitions: (1) Copy: a server whose log is shorter than another server's log copies a suffix of entries from the longer log to its own. The number of entries copied is close to (but may be slightly less than) the full difference in log lengths, specifically between one less than the difference and the full difference. This means a copy operation may not fully catch up the lagging server. (2) Extend: a server whose log is at least as long as every other server's log appends new values to its log. The number of new entries appended is bounded so that the resulting lag between the extending server and the shortest-logged server does not exceed the lag parameter. This action is only enabled for servers that currently have the longest (or tied for longest) log.
description.safety_properties: Bounded lag: the absolute difference in log lengths between any two servers must never exceed the lag parameter. Type correctness: all logs remain sequences of valid values.
description.liveness_properties: All extending: every server must always eventually strictly extend its log (make progress). This property is verified to hold. In-sync: all servers should always eventually have identical logs. This property is demonstrated to NOT hold -- the model checker correctly finds a counterexample because copy operations are allowed to transfer only a partial suffix, so a follower may never fully catch up.
description.model_bounds: The lag parameter, server set, and value set are declared as constants. The lag must be a natural number and the server set must be finite. For model checking, typical values are three servers, one value, and a lag of three.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for both the extend and copy actions for every server. Unlike the CRDT and replicated log examples, this specification has a machine-closed fairness constraint. However, it makes the unrealistic assumption that a server can consistently read the state of all other servers, which would not hold in a real distributed system where messaging protocols would be needed to determine lag between servers. The specification relies on community library modules for sequence and finite set extensions.

description.system_overview: This specification models a basic append-only replicated log system. Multiple nodes share a single global log of transactions. Nodes can append new transactions to the log and independently execute (consume) transactions from it. The specification is part of a collection illustrating how ordinarily-infinite monotonic systems can be made finite for model checking.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of nodes and a set of possible transactions. The shared global log grows as nodes append transactions. Each node independently tracks how many transactions it has executed from the log. Nodes act both as writers (appending transactions) and as executors (processing transactions from the log).
description.state_variables: The system tracks two pieces of state: (1) a global ordered sequence of transactions representing the replicated log, and (2) a mapping from each node to a natural number indicating how many log entries that node has executed so far.
description.initial_state: The global log starts as an empty sequence. Each node's execution counter starts at zero, meaning no transactions have been executed.
description.actions: There are two types of transitions: (1) Write transaction: a node that has executed all current log entries (its execution count equals the log length) appends a new transaction to the end of the log and increments its own execution counter. This means only a fully caught-up node can write. (2) Execute transaction: a node that has not yet executed all log entries (its execution count is less than the log length) increments its execution counter by one, representing processing the next pending entry. The log itself is not modified during execution.
description.safety_properties: Each node's execution counter must never exceed the length of the log. In other words, no node can claim to have executed more transactions than currently exist in the log. Additionally, type correctness is maintained: the log remains a sequence of transactions and all execution counters remain natural numbers.
description.liveness_properties: Convergence: the system must repeatedly reach states where all nodes have executed every transaction in the log (all execution counters equal the log length).
description.model_bounds: The set of nodes and the set of possible transaction values are declared as constants. For model checking, these are instantiated as small finite sets (for example, three nodes and two transaction values).
description.additional_assumptions: Two alternative fairness specifications are provided, each sufficient to guarantee convergence: (1) Execute-fair: weak fairness on each node's execute action, combined with the assumption that eventually only execute actions occur (each node eventually stops writing). (2) Write-fair: weak fairness on each node's write action for each transaction, combined with the assumption that eventually only write actions occur. Both work because infinite suffixes of either action type imply convergence via the write action's enablement condition (a node must be caught up to write). The specification also defines several insufficiently fair and effectively false variants for illustration. The specification notes that with a single node, the execute action is never enabled because the writing node immediately increments its own counter.

description.system_overview: A specification of Conway's Game of Life, a cellular automaton played on a square grid. Each cell is either alive or dead. At each step, the entire grid updates simultaneously according to rules based on the number of live neighbors each cell has. The grid has fixed boundaries (cells outside the grid are treated as dead).
actors_and_components: Cells: Each position on the grid holds a cell that is either alive (true) or dead (false).
Grid: An N-by-N square grid of cells. Positions outside the grid boundaries are considered dead for neighbor-counting purposes.
state_variables: A mapping from each grid position (row, column pair within the N-by-N grid) to a boolean value indicating whether the cell at that position is alive or dead.
description.initial_state: Each cell on the grid is nondeterministically assigned to be alive or dead. Any valid configuration of the grid is a possible initial state.
actions: Tick (simultaneous update): Every cell on the grid is updated simultaneously based on its current neighbor count. A live cell with exactly two or three live neighbors survives; a dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes alive; all other cells become dead.
description.safety_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED

model_bounds.grid_size: A natural number specifying the dimension of the square grid (N-by-N).

additional_assumptions: Each cell has up to eight neighbors (the cells directly adjacent horizontally, vertically, and diagonally).
Cells outside the grid boundaries are treated as dead (value zero) when counting neighbors.
The update is fully deterministic given the current grid state: once an initial configuration is chosen, each subsequent generation is uniquely determined.

description.system_overview: This specification models Huang's termination detection algorithm for distributed systems, proposed by Shing-Tsaan Huang in 1989. The algorithm solves the problem of determining when a distributed computation has completed -- that is, when all processes have become idle and no computational messages remain in transit. It uses a weight-splitting mechanism where the total weight across all processes and in-transit messages is conserved, allowing a designated controlling agent to detect global termination by observing that its own weight has returned to the initial total.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of processes interconnected in a fully meshed network, with one distinguished process designated as the leader (controlling agent). Each process can be in either an active or idle state. The leader initiates the computation and monitors for termination. Non-leader processes participate in the computation by sending and receiving messages, and report their weight back to the leader when they become idle.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three categories of state: (1) an activity flag for each process indicating whether it is currently active or idle, (2) a weight value for each process represented as a dyadic rational number (a fraction whose denominator is a power of two), and (3) a message queue for each process containing the weights of messages in transit to that process.
description.initial_state: The leader process starts in the active state with a weight of one. All other processes start in the idle state with a weight of zero. All message queues are initially empty.
description.actions: The system supports the following transitions: (1) Send message: An active process sends a computational message to any other process. It halves its current weight and attaches the halved weight to the message, which is appended to the recipient's message queue. (2) Receive message (non-leader): A non-leader process receives a message from its queue, becomes active, and adds the message's weight to its own weight. Messages may be received in any order. (3) Go idle (non-leader): An active non-leader process becomes idle. It sends its entire weight to the leader's message queue and resets its own weight to zero. (4) Leader goes idle: The active leader becomes idle without transferring any weight. (5) Leader receives message: The leader receives a weight message from its queue and adds the weight to its own, without changing its activity status.
description.safety_properties: The detection is safe: whenever the leader detects termination (it is idle and its weight equals one), actual termination has occurred -- meaning all processes are idle and all message queues are empty. Detection never produces a false positive. Additionally, a type correctness invariant ensures that the sum of all process weights and all in-transit message weights always equals one.
description.liveness_properties: The detection is live: if actual termination occurs (all processes are idle and all message queues are empty), the leader will eventually detect termination. The converse of detection leading to confirmed terminated state is also guaranteed.
description.model_bounds: The set of processes and the leader are declared as constants. For model checking, the denominator of weight fractions is constrained to not exceed 8, preventing the weight values from halving toward infinitely small values. A typical configuration uses 5 processes including the leader.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for the leader receiving messages, the leader going idle, and for each non-leader process receiving messages and going idle. The specification uses dyadic rationals (fractions with power-of-two denominators) to represent weights, ensuring exact arithmetic without rounding errors. The network is fully meshed, meaning any process can send a message to any other process. Messages may be received in any order (not necessarily FIFO). The algorithm assumes reliable message delivery -- it cannot detect termination if a message is lost in transit or if a process fails.

description.system_overview: This specification formalizes client-centric database isolation levels based on the framework introduced by Crooks et al. in 'Seeing is Believing: A Client-Centric Specification of Database Isolation' (PODC 2017), with TLA+ formalization by Tim Soethout et al. It provides reusable definitions for checking whether a set of transactions satisfies various isolation guarantees (serializability, snapshot isolation, strict serializability, read committed, read uncommitted) by examining the states observable by clients rather than implementation-specific mechanisms.
description.actors_and_components: The system models database transactions operating on a key-value store. The key abstractions are: transactions (ordered sequences of read and write operations on keys), executions (totally ordered sequences of transactions applied to an initial state, producing intermediate states), and commit tests (predicates that each isolation level defines to determine whether a transaction's observations are consistent with the isolation guarantee).
description.state_variables: The system tracks: a database state mapping keys to values, a set of transactions where each transaction is a sequence of read and write operations, and for strict serializability, a timestamp mapping from transactions to their start and commit times. An execution pairs each transaction with its parent state (the state from which it reads and writes).
description.initial_state: The database starts in a state where all keys map to an initial value. The set of transactions and their ordering are inputs to the isolation-level checking predicates rather than evolving state.
description.actions: This is primarily a library of definitions rather than a state-machine specification. The key operations are: (1) Computing all possible executions (permutations) of a set of transactions from an initial state, applying each transaction's write effects sequentially. (2) Determining read states for each operation -- the set of execution states from which the operation could have read its observed value. (3) Checking completeness -- whether all operations in a transaction can read from the same state. (4) Checking no-conflict -- whether the keys modified between a transaction's complete state and its parent state are disjoint from the transaction's write set. (5) Applying commit tests for each isolation level to determine satisfaction.
description.safety_properties: Each isolation level defines what must hold: Serializability requires that all operations in every transaction read from the transaction's parent state (the state must be complete at the parent state). Snapshot isolation requires that there exists some state from which all operations can read and that the transaction's writes do not conflict with changes between that state and the parent state. Strict serializability adds real-time ordering constraints to serializability. Read committed requires only that each operation has at least one valid read state. Read uncommitted imposes no constraints.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The key set and value set are declared as variables that must be instantiated by the importing specification. No specific bounds are defined in this module; bounds come from the instantiating model-checking configuration.
description.additional_assumptions: The framework assumes that each transaction writes each key at most once. Read states for write operations include all states up to and including the parent state by convention. The module provides helper operators for computing set permutations, applying transaction effects to states via sequential reduction, finding element indices in sequences, converting sequences to sets, computing set intersections, and other utilities. The module is designed to be instantiated by concrete specifications that supply specific keys, values, and transactions for checking.

description.system_overview: This specification models a simple key-value store with snapshot isolation semantics, written in PlusCal (an algorithmic language that compiles to TLA+). Transactions operate on local snapshots of the store and use a write-conflict detection mechanism to ensure snapshot isolation. The specification instantiates a client-centric isolation framework to formally verify that the system satisfies snapshot isolation but not full serializability (it can exhibit write-skew anomalies).
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a shared key-value store, a set of concurrent transaction processes (each identified by a unique transaction ID), and tracking state for conflict detection. Each transaction process independently takes a snapshot, performs reads and writes on its local copy, and attempts to commit. The specification also integrates a client-centric isolation checking module to verify isolation guarantees.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) the shared data store mapping keys to values, (2) the set of currently open (active) transactions, (3) a per-transaction record of keys whose writes were missed (occurred after the transaction took its snapshot), (4) each transaction's local snapshot of the store, (5) each transaction's selected read key set, (6) each transaction's selected write key set, (7) each transaction's log of read and write operations (used for isolation verification), and (8) each transaction's current program phase.
description.initial_state: The store maps all keys to a designated no-value sentinel. No transactions are open. All missed-write sets are empty. All local snapshots map all keys to the no-value sentinel. Read and write key sets are empty. Operation logs are empty. All transaction processes start at their initial phase.
description.actions: Each transaction process goes through four sequential phases: (1) Start: the transaction registers itself as active, takes a snapshot of the current store, and non-deterministically selects a non-empty set of keys to read and a non-empty set of keys to write. (2) Read: the transaction reads the values of its selected keys from its local snapshot and logs these as read operations. (3) Update: the transaction writes its own transaction ID as the value for each key in its write set within its local snapshot. (4) Commit: the transaction checks whether any of its write keys overlap with keys written by other transactions since the snapshot was taken (the missed set). If there is no conflict, the transaction commits by removing itself from the active set, updating the missed-write tracking for all remaining active transactions, merging its written keys into the shared store, and logging write operations. If there is a conflict, the transaction aborts without modifying the store. After all transactions complete, the system stutters.
description.safety_properties: Snapshot isolation: the set of committed transactions must satisfy the snapshot isolation commit test, meaning each transaction can be explained as reading from some consistent state where no conflicting concurrent writes occurred. Type correctness: the store maps keys to valid values (transaction IDs or the no-value sentinel), the active transaction set is a subset of all transaction IDs, and the missed-write tracking maps each transaction to a subset of keys.
description.liveness_properties: Termination: all transaction processes eventually complete (reach their done state). This is guaranteed by weak fairness on each transaction process.
description.model_bounds: The key set, transaction ID set, and no-value sentinel are declared as constants. For model checking, typical configurations use two keys and three transaction IDs.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each transaction process. The specification writes the transaction's own ID as the value for all write operations, simplifying the model while still capturing conflict behavior. The specification notes that serializability is NOT satisfied due to write-skew anomalies, which can be demonstrated by enabling the serializability invariant. The specification suggests as an exercise to add more yield points (smaller atomic actions) to explore what breaks when the commit action is split further.

description.system_overview: This specification models a simple key-value store exhibiting snapshot isolation. Concurrent transactions each work on a private snapshot of the store. If two concurrent transactions write to the same key, the one that commits later is rejected (write-write conflict detection). If they write to different keys, both succeed. The specification was contributed by Andrew Helwer.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a shared key-value store and a set of concurrent transaction processes identified by unique transaction IDs. Each transaction operates on a private snapshot of the store and can perform key additions, value updates, and key removals before attempting to commit or rolling back.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five pieces of state: (1) the shared data store mapping keys to values, (2) the set of currently open transactions, (3) each transaction's private snapshot of the store, (4) a per-transaction log of which keys have been written during the transaction, and (5) a per-transaction set of keys whose writes were missed (committed by other transactions after this transaction opened).
description.initial_state: The store maps all keys to a designated absence-of-value sentinel. No transactions are open. All transaction snapshots map all keys to the no-value sentinel. All write logs are empty sets. All missed-write sets are empty.
description.actions: There are six possible transitions: (1) Open transaction: a transaction not yet in the active set joins, and its snapshot is populated with the current store state. (2) Add: an open transaction sets a key that currently has no value in its snapshot to a new value, and records the key as written. (3) Update: an open transaction changes a key's value in its snapshot (the key must already have a value, and the new value must differ), recording the key as written. (4) Remove: an open transaction sets a key that currently has a value back to the no-value sentinel, recording the key as written. (5) Rollback: an open transaction is closed without merging changes; its snapshot, write log, and missed set are all reset to their initial empty states. (6) Close (commit): an open transaction whose written keys do not overlap with its missed keys merges its snapshot writes into the shared store. The transaction is removed from the active set, all other open transactions have the committing transaction's written keys added to their missed sets, and the committing transaction's snapshot and tracking state are reset.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: the store maps keys to valid values, the transaction set is a valid subset of transaction IDs, snapshots are valid stores per transaction, write logs are sets of keys per transaction, and missed sets are sets of keys per transaction. Transaction lifecycle invariant: for any open transaction, if the store differs from the snapshot on a key that the transaction has not written, then that key must be in the missed set; for any inactive transaction, its snapshot must be all no-value sentinels and its write log and missed set must be empty.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The key set, value set, and transaction ID set are declared as constants. For model checking, typical small configurations use two to three keys, two to three values, and two to three transaction IDs.
description.additional_assumptions: The no-value sentinel is defined as a value chosen from outside the value set, ensuring it is distinguishable from any actual value. The specification does not include fairness assumptions or liveness properties; it focuses on safety verification of snapshot isolation's write-write conflict detection mechanism.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Knuth-Yao algorithm for simulating a fair six-sided die using fair coin flips. The algorithm, introduced by Knuth and Yao in 1976, constructs an optimal binary decision tree where each internal node represents a coin flip and each leaf represents one of the six die outcomes. The probability of reaching each outcome is tracked using dyadic rational arithmetic to ensure uniform distribution.
description.actors_and_components: The system has a single actor: a sequential process that repeatedly flips a fair coin and traverses a fixed binary decision tree. The tree has seven internal nodes (the initial node plus six intermediate nodes) and six leaf nodes corresponding to the six die faces. A dyadic rational arithmetic module provides exact probability tracking.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) the current probability of being in the current execution path, represented as a dyadic rational number (a fraction whose denominator is a power of two), (2) the current node in the binary decision tree (either one of seven intermediate decision nodes or one of six terminal outcome nodes), and (3) the result of the most recent coin flip (heads or tails).
description.initial_state: The system begins at the root of the binary decision tree with probability equal to one. The initial coin flip is chosen nondeterministically as either heads or tails.
description.actions: There is one main transition: if the current node is not a terminal outcome node, the system advances to the next node according to the transition table based on the current coin flip result. Specifically, from the root node, heads leads to one subtree and tails to another.
