This is stronger than simply checking the invariant holds on reachable states -- it verifies that any state satisfying the invariant will continue to satisfy it after any valid transition.
description.actors_and_components: This module extends the parent Prisoners specification and defines an inductive invariant test specification. It reuses all actors and components from the parent module: the set of prisoners, the designated counter, the two switches, and the counting mechanism.
description.state_variables: All state variables are inherited from the parent Prisoners module: the two switch positions, the per-prisoner signal counts, and the counter's running tally.
description.initial_state: Instead of using the parent module's initial predicate, this module uses the combined type-correctness and counting invariant as the initial predicate. This means model checking starts from every state satisfying the invariant, not just the true initial states, which is how inductive invariant checking works.
description.actions: All actions are inherited from the parent Prisoners module. The next-state relation is the same: each step has exactly one prisoner enter the room and flip one switch according to the counting strategy.
description.safety_properties: The combined type-correctness and counting invariant must be preserved by every transition: if the system is in a state satisfying the invariant and takes a valid step, the resulting state must also satisfy the invariant. This establishes inductiveness.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: Inherits the same constants as the parent specification: the set of prisoners and the designated counter must be instantiated with finite values for model checking.
description.additional_assumptions: The module notes that the number of states satisfying the type invariant is not much larger than the number of reachable states in the original specification, so TLC can verify the inductive invariant almost as quickly as it can check the original specification.

description.system_overview: This specification models the classic 'prisoners and switches' puzzle, originally presented on the Car Talk radio show. A group of prisoners must determine when every prisoner has visited a room containing two switches, without any communication outside the room. The prisoners agree on a strategy beforehand: they designate one prisoner as the counter, who uses one of the switches to track visits. If the counter correctly declares that all prisoners have visited, they all go free; an incorrect declaration results in execution.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of prisoners partitioned into two roles: (1) a single designated counter, and (2) all remaining non-counter prisoners. The room contains two toggle switches, labeled A and B. Switch A serves as the signaling mechanism for counting, while switch B acts as a dummy toggle that prisoners flip when they cannot meaningfully interact with switch A.
description.state_variables: The system tracks four pieces of state: (1) whether the first switch is in the up or down position (a boolean), (2) whether the second switch is in the up or down position (a boolean), (3) for each non-counter prisoner, how many times that prisoner has moved the first switch to the up position (a count from zero to two), and (4) the counter's running tally of how many times the counter has moved the first switch to the down position.
description.initial_state: The two switches may start in any position (both up, both down, or mixed -- the prisoners do not know the initial configuration). Every non-counter prisoner's signal count starts at zero. The counter's tally starts at zero.
description.actions: On each step, exactly one prisoner is brought into the room and must flip exactly one switch. A non-counter prisoner flips the first switch to the up position if it is currently down and the prisoner has not yet signaled twice; otherwise, the prisoner flips the second switch. The counter flips the first switch to the down position if it is currently up (incrementing the tally by one); otherwise, the counter flips the second switch. The counter declares success when the tally reaches twice the number of other prisoners.
description.safety_properties: If the counter declares that all prisoners have visited, then every prisoner has indeed been in the room at least once. The counter's declaration is never premature.
description.liveness_properties: The counter eventually reaches the required tally and declares that all prisoners have visited the room, guaranteeing eventual freedom.
description.model_bounds: The set of prisoners and the identity of the counter are declared as constants. For model checking, the prisoner set must be instantiated with a specific finite set (commonly 3 to 6 prisoners).
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for every prisoner's action, meaning every prisoner is brought into the room infinitely often. This models the warden's guarantee that no prisoner is permanently excluded. The reason each non-counter prisoner signals twice (rather than once) is to handle the unknown initial switch position: since the first switch might start in the up position, one phantom signal could be counted, so requiring two signals per prisoner with a threshold of twice the count of non-counter prisoners ensures correctness regardless of initial switch state.

description.system_overview: This specification models a fair solution to the readers-writers problem, a classic concurrency challenge where multiple processes compete for access to a shared resource. Some processes wish to read (and can do so concurrently with other readers) while others wish to write (requiring exclusive access). This solution uses a first-come-first-served queue to prevent starvation of either readers or writers, ensuring fair access to the shared resource.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a fixed number of actor processes, each of which can request either read or write access to a shared resource. A waiting queue maintains the order in which access requests arrive. Actors transition between four states: idle, waiting in the queue, actively reading or writing, and stopping their activity.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) the set of processes currently reading the shared resource, (2) the set of processes currently writing to the shared resource, and (3) an ordered queue of pending access requests, where each request records whether the process wants to read or write and which process made the request.
description.initial_state: No process is reading. No process is writing. The waiting queue is empty.
description.actions: Processes can perform five types of actions: (1) Request to read: a process that is not already waiting to read joins the end of the waiting queue with a read request. (2) Request to write: a process that is not already waiting to write joins the end of the waiting queue with a write request. (3) Begin reading or writing: if the queue is non-empty and no process is currently writing, the request at the front of the queue is examined. If it is a read request, the process begins reading. If it is a write request and no process is currently reading, the process begins writing. In both cases, the request is removed from the front of the queue. (4) Stop activity: any process that is currently reading or writing may voluntarily stop, removing itself from the active reader or writer set.
description.safety_properties: Two safety conditions are maintained: (1) Readers and writers are never simultaneously active -- if any process is writing, no process is reading, and vice versa. (2) At most one writer is active at any time.
description.liveness_properties: Every process eventually gets to read and eventually gets to write. Every active reader eventually stops reading and every active writer eventually stops writing. These properties together ensure no process is starved of access.
description.model_bounds: The number of actor processes is declared as a constant. For model checking, this must be instantiated with a specific finite value.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on all actions: requesting to read, requesting to write, processing the queue, and stopping activity. This ensures that every enabled action eventually occurs, preventing indefinite postponement. The queue-based design provides first-come-first-served fairness, distinguishing this solution from simpler readers-preference or writers-preference approaches that can cause starvation.

description.system_overview: This specification models a simplified version of Leslie Lamport's Fast Paxos protocol, which extends classic Paxos to allow values to be learned in fewer message delays. The specification was written by Lim Ngian Xin Terry and Gaurav Gandhi, referencing Lamport's Fast Paxos paper and Zhao Wenbing's 'Fast Paxos Made Easy'. Fast Paxos introduces fast rounds where acceptors can propose values directly without the leader choosing a value, alongside classic rounds for collision recovery.
description.actors_and_components: The system has replicas (acceptors), a unique coordinator (leader), quorums (majority subsets), and fast quorums (larger subsets, at least three-quarters of the replicas). The coordinator is assumed to be unique, so Phase 1a and 1b of classic Paxos are omitted. All agents can communicate with one another.
description.state_variables: The system tracks six pieces of state: (1) the set of all messages sent, (2) the decided value (or a sentinel if no decision), (3) per-replica highest ballot seen, (4) per-replica highest ballot in which a value was accepted, (5) per-replica the value accepted in that highest ballot, and (6) a coordinator value tracking which value the coordinator has committed to (or a sentinel if none).
description.initial_state: Same as classic Paxos for the first five variables: empty message set, decision is the sentinel, all per-replica trackers at zero/sentinel. The coordinator value is also initialized to the sentinel.
description.actions: The protocol has six actions: (1) Fast Any (Phase 2a Fast): The coordinator starts a fast round by sending an accept-request message with the special 'any' value in a fast ballot. (2) Fast Propose (Phase 2b Fast): A replica receiving a fast-round accept-request (one containing the 'any' value) may respond with an acceptance message containing its own proposed value, provided the ballot is at least as high as its highest-seen ballot, it has not already responded to this ballot, and either it has not previously accepted a value or it accepts the same value. (3) Fast Decide: If all replicas in a fast quorum have sent acceptance messages in the same fast ballot and they all proposed the same value, that value is decided. (4) Classic Accept (Phase 2a Classic): If a fast round resulted in a collision (replicas in a fast quorum proposed more than one value), the coordinator selects a value for a classic round. If a majority of the fast quorum voted for one value, the coordinator must select that value. Otherwise, the coordinator may select any value from those proposed. The coordinator sends an accept-request with this value in a classic ballot numbered higher than the fast ballot. (5) Classic Accepted (Phase 2b Classic): Same as standard Paxos Phase 2b -- replicas accept the proposal if the ballot is high enough. (6) Classic Decide: If all replicas in a (classic) quorum accepted the same classic ballot, the value is decided.
description.safety_properties: Non-triviality: if a decision has been made, the decided value must have been proposed by some replica in a fast round (there exists an acceptance message for that value in a fast ballot). Type correctness: all variables have their expected types. Consistency: at most one value is ever decided.
description.liveness_properties: The specification includes strong fairness conditions on both Fast Decide and Classic Decide, ensuring that if deciding is repeatedly enabled, a decision is eventually made.
description.model_bounds: Four replicas, three values, ballot numbers from zero through four, fast ballots are a subset (for example, ballots one and three), classic ballots are the remaining ballots. Quorums are all majority subsets. Fast quorums are all subsets of size at least three-quarters of the replicas. Symmetry is exploited over replicas and values.
description.additional_assumptions: There is a unique coordinator, so Phase 1 is omitted entirely. All agents can communicate directly. Agent failures are modeled as pauses (agents restore from stable storage on restart). Fast quorums must be at least three-quarters of the replicas. Any classic quorum must overlap with the intersection of any two fast quorums. The fast ballot set and classic ballot set partition the full ballot set. A majority-value function determines whether a single value has majority support in a set of acceptance messages. The specification extends the companion classic Paxos module.

description.system_overview: This specification models the classic Paxos consensus protocol without explicit leaders or learners. It specifies the two-phase message-passing algorithm through which a set of acceptor processes (called replicas) agree on a single value. The specification was written as a companion to a simplified Fast Paxos implementation, referencing Leslie Lamport's original Fast Paxos paper.
description.actors_and_components: The system has replicas (acceptors that participate in voting), proposers (implicit -- they initiate ballots by sending prepare messages), and quorums (majority subsets of replicas, where any two quorums overlap). Learners are not modeled. Two special sentinel constants are used: one representing the absence of a value and another representing an open (any) value for fast rounds.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five pieces of state: (1) the set of all messages sent in the system, (2) a decision variable recording the chosen value (or a sentinel if no value has been chosen), (3) for each replica, the highest ballot number it has seen, (4) for each replica, the highest ballot number in which it accepted a value, and (5) for each replica, the value it accepted in that highest ballot (or a sentinel if none).
description.initial_state: The message set is empty. The decision is the 'no value' sentinel. All replicas have their highest-seen ballot, highest-accepted ballot, and accepted value initialized to zero, zero, and the 'no value' sentinel respectively.
description.actions: The protocol has five actions: (1) Prepare (Phase 1a): A proposer sends a prepare message with a ballot number greater than zero. (2) Promise (Phase 1b): A replica receiving a prepare message with a ballot number higher than its current highest-seen ballot updates that tracker and replies with a promise message containing its current highest-accepted ballot and value. (3) Accept (Phase 2a): Once a proposer has collected promise messages from all replicas in some quorum for a given ballot, it selects a value -- either the value associated with the highest accepted ballot reported by any responder, or any value if no responder had accepted. It then sends an accept-request message. At most one accept-request per ballot. (4) Accepted (Phase 2b): A replica receiving an accept-request with a ballot at least as high as its highest-seen ballot updates all its trackers and sends an acceptance message. (5) Decide: When all replicas in some quorum have sent acceptance messages for the same ballot, the decision variable is set to the accepted value.
description.safety_properties: Non-triviality: if a value has been decided, then either no decision has been made or the decided value appeared in some accept-request message. Additionally, promise messages are consistent with acceptor state (a value is reported only if the accepted ballot is positive, and vice versa). Consistency: at most one value may be decided -- the decision variable, once set to a real value, can only be set again to the same value.
description.liveness_properties: The specification includes a strong fairness condition on the decide action, ensuring that if deciding is repeatedly enabled, a decision is eventually made. However, the specification notes that Paxos is not guaranteed to terminate by the FLP impossibility result -- it can have safety and fault tolerance but not guaranteed liveness.
description.model_bounds: Four replicas, three values, ballot numbers from a finite set (for example, zero through two), quorums as all majority subsets of the replicas. Symmetry is exploited over replicas and values.
description.additional_assumptions: The replicas form a finite set. The quorum overlap property holds. Ballot zero is always in the ballot set. Messages are accumulated and never removed. The two sentinel constants ('any' and 'none') are distinct from each other and from all values. The specification includes a forced-value function that selects the value from the promise message with the highest accepted ballot, used in the Phase 2a value selection.

description.system_overview: This specification models the single-lane bridge problem, a classic concurrency scenario where a bridge over a river is only wide enough to permit a single lane of traffic. Cars travel in two opposing directions along a road that includes the bridge. Cars moving in the same direction may be on the bridge simultaneously, but cars moving in opposite directions must never occupy the bridge at the same time. The problem explores synchronization, mutual exclusion, and fairness in resource sharing.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of two groups of cars: one group traveling in one direction (right-to-left) and another traveling in the opposite direction (left-to-right). The road is modeled as a sequence of positions, with a contiguous subset of positions forming the bridge. A waiting queue manages access to the bridge, determining which car enters next when the bridge is available.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two pieces of state: (1) the current position of each car on the road, represented as a mapping from each car to a position on the road, and (2) an ordered queue of cars waiting to enter the bridge, representing the order in which cars arrived at the bridge entrance.
description.initial_state: Cars traveling in one direction start at one end of the road, and cars traveling in the opposite direction start at the other end. The waiting queue is initialized with any cars that happen to start adjacent to the bridge entrance.
description.actions: Three types of movement are possible: (1) Move outside the bridge: a car whose next position is not on the bridge advances one position along the road. If this brings the car to the bridge entrance, it joins the end of the waiting queue. (2) Move inside the bridge: a car already on the bridge advances one position, provided no other car occupies the target position. (3) Enter the bridge: the car at the front of the waiting queue may enter the bridge if either the bridge is empty or all cars currently on the bridge are traveling in the same direction as the entering car and the target position is unoccupied. Cars travel in a circular pattern, returning to their starting position after reaching the far end of the road.
description.safety_properties: Three safety properties are maintained: (1) No two cars occupy the same bridge position simultaneously. (2) The number of cars on the bridge never exceeds the bridge capacity. (3) Cars traveling in opposite directions are never on the bridge at the same time.
description.liveness_properties: Two liveness properties hold: (1) Every car that enters the bridge eventually exits the bridge. (2) Every car eventually enters the bridge (no car is permanently denied access).
description.model_bounds: Four constants define the model: the set of cars traveling in each direction, the set of positions constituting the bridge, and the full set of road positions. For model checking, these must be instantiated with specific finite sets.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for all car movement actions, ensuring every car that can make progress eventually does so. The road is circular: a car reaching one end wraps around to the other end, modeling continuous traffic flow. The bridge must be a strict subset of the road positions, with positions before and after the bridge on each side.

description.system_overview: This specification models a sliding block puzzle, commonly known as Klotski. The puzzle consists of a rectangular board with several pieces of various shapes that can slide horizontally and vertically into empty spaces. The goal is to move a designated large piece to a target position by sliding other pieces out of the way. The model checker explores the full state space of reachable board configurations to determine whether the goal position is achievable.
description.actors_and_components: There are no concurrent actors. The system consists of a rectangular grid board and a collection of rigid pieces (blocks) of various sizes and shapes placed on the board. Each piece occupies one or more grid cells. There are also empty cells (not occupied by any piece) that allow pieces to slide. The key puzzle variant defined is the Klotski configuration, which uses a 4-wide by 5-tall grid with ten pieces: one 2-by-2 square block, several 1-by-2 and 2-by-1 rectangular blocks, and several 1-by-1 unit blocks.
description.state_variables: The system tracks the current board configuration, which is the set of all pieces currently on the board, where each piece is itself a set of grid positions it occupies. Each grid position is a coordinate pair within the bounds of the board.
description.initial_state: The board starts in the standard Klotski starting configuration. The ten pieces are placed in their traditional positions on the 4-by-5 grid, with two empty cells remaining.
description.actions: In each step, one empty cell is selected. For each direction (up, down, left, right), if there is an adjacent piece in that direction, the system considers sliding that entire piece one cell in the opposite direction (toward the empty cell). The move is valid only if the resulting position of the piece remains entirely within the board bounds and does not overlap with any other piece. The board configuration is updated by replacing the old piece position with the new one. Multiple possible moves may exist in each state (one for each combination of empty cell and valid sliding direction), creating nondeterministic branching.
description.safety_properties: The board must always be a valid set of non-overlapping pieces on the grid (type correctness). The goal invariant states that the 2-by-2 block has NOT reached its target position (bottom-center of the board). When the model checker finds a violation of this invariant, it has found a solution path from the initial configuration to the goal.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The board dimensions are fixed at width 4 and height 5. All grid positions are integer coordinate pairs within these bounds. The number and shapes of pieces are fixed by the chosen puzzle variant (Klotski uses 10 pieces). The README notes that TLC finds 25,955 distinct states for the Klotski variant.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses an invariant-violation technique for puzzle solving: the goal condition is stated as an invariant (the goal has NOT been reached), and a counterexample trace produced by the model checker represents a solution to the puzzle. The specification also supports other puzzle variants (Pennant with 1,398 states, Ma's Puzzle with 110,804 states) by changing the piece definitions, board dimensions, and goal conditions.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Slush protocol, the simplest member of the Snow family of probabilistic consensus protocols introduced in the Avalanche whitepaper (Team Rocket, 2018). Slush is a metastable consensus mechanism where nodes repeatedly sample random subsets of peers and adopt a sufficiently popular opinion, causing the network to rapidly converge on a single color (opinion). Since TLA+ has no probabilistic modeling capabilities, this spec serves primarily as executable pseudocode for the protocol.
description.actors_and_components: The system has three types of concurrent processes: (1) Loop processes, one per node, which drive the main Slush iteration loop -- each loop process samples peers, collects responses, and potentially flips its node's color. (2) Query processes, one per node, which respond to incoming query messages by replying with their node's current color (or adopting the query color if the node is uncolored). (3) A client request process that assigns initial colors to uncolored nodes, representing external transactions arriving at the network. Each node has an associated loop process and query process, linked by a host mapping.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a color assignment for each node, which is either one of two colors or uncolored; (2) a set of in-flight messages including query messages (from loop processes to query processes), query reply messages (responses back to loop processes), and termination messages (indicating a loop process has finished all iterations); (3) a program counter for each process tracking its current execution step; (4) a sample set for each loop process recording which peers were queried in the current round; (5) an iteration counter for each loop process tracking how many rounds have been completed.
description.initial_state: All nodes start uncolored. The message set is empty. Each loop process's sample set is empty with zero iterations completed. Each query process starts in its reply loop, each loop process starts waiting for a color assignment, and the client request process starts ready to assign colors.
description.actions: The protocol operates through these steps: (1) Client assigns color: the client process picks an uncolored node and assigns it a random color (one of two possible colors). This repeats until all nodes have a color. (2) Require color: each loop process waits until its host node has been assigned a color before beginning iterations. (3) Query sample set: the loop process selects a random subset of fixed size from the other nodes' query processes and sends a query message containing its current color to each member of the sample. (4) Respond to query: a query process receives a query message; if its host node is uncolored, it adopts the query's color, then replies with its current color. (5) Tally replies: the loop process waits until it has received replies from all sampled peers, then counts how many replies are of each color. If one color meets or exceeds the flip threshold, the node adopts that color. The loop process then clears its sample set, increments its iteration counter, and continues. (6) Loop termination: after completing all iterations, the loop process broadcasts a termination message. (7) Query loop exit: query processes exit when all loop processes have sent termination messages.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: the color assignment maps nodes to colors or uncolored, and all messages in the message set conform to one of the defined message types (query, query reply, or termination).
description.liveness_properties: Termination: all processes eventually reach a done state. Note that convergence to a single color is a probabilistic property that cannot be expressed in TLA+.
description.model_bounds: The number of nodes, the number of iterations per loop process, the sample set size, and the flip threshold are declared as constants. A small configuration uses 3 nodes, 1 iteration, a sample size of 2, and a flip threshold of 2. Medium configurations may increase the node count or iteration count.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification is written using PlusCal syntax which is translated to TLA+. Nodes are paired with their loop and query processes through a host mapping (a set of triples). The number of nodes must equal the number of loop processes and query processes. The spec models a fully connected network where any node can sample any other node. Because TLA+ lacks probabilistic reasoning, the specification cannot verify convergence guarantees -- it can only check structural properties like type safety and termination.

description.system_overview: This specification is a modified version of the spanning tree algorithm in which the edge set is not a declared constant but is instead defined as a randomly chosen set of edges joining the nodes. This allows the model checker to test the spanning tree algorithm on a randomly generated graph each time it runs, making it easy to check the algorithm's correctness across a variety of different graph topologies without manually specifying each one.
description.actors_and_components: The system operates on an undirected graph with a fixed set of nodes but a randomly generated edge set. There is a single designated root node. The algorithm is the same centralized spanning tree algorithm: in each step, it nondeterministically selects a node and one of its neighbors, then updates the node's distance and parent if an improvement is possible.
description.state_variables: The system maintains two mappings over all nodes: (1) a parent function that maps each node to its parent in the spanning tree (the root and unreachable nodes map to themselves), and (2) a distance function that maps each node to a natural number representing its computed distance from the root. The edge set is defined (not a variable) but is computed randomly at initialization time.
description.initial_state: Every node's parent is set to itself. The root node's distance is set to 0. All other nodes' distances are set to the maximum cardinality constant. The edge set is determined by randomly choosing, for each node, a subset of other nodes to connect to, and forming two-element edge sets from those choices.
description.actions: Same as the base spanning tree algorithm: choose a node and one of its graph neighbors such that the neighbor's distance plus one is strictly less than the node's current distance. Choose a new distance for the node that is strictly less than its current distance but at least the neighbor's distance plus one. Update the node's distance and parent accordingly.
description.safety_properties: When the algorithm terminates, the postcondition holds: for every node, one of three cases applies: (1) it is the root with distance 0 and parent equal to itself; (2) it is unreachable with maximum distance, parent equal to itself, and all neighbors also unreachable; or (3) it has a distance between 1 and the maximum minus one, its parent is a graph neighbor, and its distance equals its parent's distance plus one. The safety property asserts this postcondition always holds upon termination. Additionally, a type correctness invariant checks that the parent mapping goes from nodes to nodes, the distance mapping goes from nodes to natural numbers, and all edges are two-element subsets of nodes.
description.liveness_properties: The postcondition is eventually reached. This is ensured by weak fairness on the transition relation.
description.model_bounds: The set of nodes, the root node, and the maximum cardinality constant are declared as constants. A typical model configuration uses six nodes. The maximum cardinality must be a natural number at least as large as the number of nodes. On a few test runs with six nodes, the model checker took an average of slightly more than 30 seconds.
description.additional_assumptions: The edge generation uses a non-standard random element selection mechanism that does not obey the normal rules of mathematical equality (evaluating the same expression twice may yield different results). This is a deliberate hack for testing purposes. The root must be a member of the node set.

description.system_overview: This specification is a modified version of the spanning tree algorithm in which the edge set is not a declared constant but is instead a state variable that is initialized to any possible set of edges with nodes from the node set. This allows the model checker to exhaustively test the spanning tree algorithm on all possible undirected graphs having a particular number of nodes, verifying correctness for every graph topology.
description.actors_and_components: The system operates on an undirected graph with a fixed set of nodes. The edge set is a variable that can take on any valid graph structure. There is a single designated root node. The algorithm is the same centralized spanning tree algorithm as the base module.
description.state_variables: The system maintains three state components: (1) a parent function that maps each node to its parent in the spanning tree, (2) a distance function that maps each node to a natural number representing its computed distance from the root, and (3) an edge set variable that holds the graph structure (initialized nondeterministically and then held constant throughout execution).
description.initial_state: Every node's parent is set to itself. The root node's distance is set to 0. All other nodes' distances are set to the maximum cardinality constant. The edge set is chosen nondeterministically from all possible sets of two-element subsets of the node set, representing every possible undirected graph (without self-loops) on those nodes.
description.actions: Same as the base spanning tree algorithm: choose a node and one of its graph neighbors such that the neighbor's distance plus one is strictly less than the node's current distance. Choose a new distance for the node that is strictly less than its current distance but at least the neighbor's distance plus one. Update the node's distance and parent accordingly. The edge set remains unchanged during all transitions.
description.safety_properties: When the algorithm terminates, the postcondition holds for every possible graph: for every node, one of three cases applies: (1) it is the root with distance 0 and parent equal to itself; (2) it is unreachable with maximum distance, parent equal to itself, and all neighbors also unreachable; or (3) it has a distance between 1 and the maximum minus one, its parent is a graph neighbor, and its distance equals its parent's distance plus one. The safety property asserts this postcondition holds upon termination.
description.liveness_properties: The postcondition is eventually reached. This is ensured by weak fairness on the transition relation.
description.model_bounds: The set of nodes, the root node, and the maximum cardinality constant are declared as constants. Testing with 4 nodes takes a few seconds. Testing with 5 nodes takes about 25 minutes. Testing with 6 nodes will likely exhaust available memory, because computing the initial edge set requires enumerating all subsets of all subsets of the node set, which for N nodes contains 2 to the power of 2 to the N elements.
description.additional_assumptions: The root must be a member of the node set. The maximum cardinality must be a natural number at least as large as the number of nodes. The edge set variable is initialized nondeterministically but never changes after initialization, effectively acting as a universally quantified constant. This module uses randomization support for the nondeterministic initial state generation.

description.system_overview: This specification models an algorithm to compute a rooted spanning tree of an undirected graph. The algorithm computes the parent relation and distance from a designated root node for every node in the graph. It effectively assumes all edges have weight 1. If the graph is not connected, nodes without a path to the root remain unattached (their parent is themselves). The algorithm repeatedly finds nodes whose distance can be improved via a neighbor and updates them.
description.actors_and_components: The system operates on an undirected graph defined by a set of nodes and a set of edges. There is a single designated root node. The algorithm is centralized: in each step, it nondeterministically selects a node and one of its neighbors, then updates the selected node's distance and parent if an improvement is possible.
description.state_variables: The system maintains two mappings over all nodes: (1) a parent function that maps each node to the node considered its parent in the spanning tree (the root and unreachable nodes map to themselves), and (2) a distance function that maps each node to a natural number representing its computed distance from the root.
description.initial_state: Every node's parent is set to itself. The root node's distance is set to 0. All other nodes' distances are set to a large constant that serves as a stand-in for infinity (this constant must be at least as large as the number of nodes).
description.actions: The algorithm has one action: choose a node and one of its graph neighbors such that the neighbor's distance plus one is strictly less than the node's current distance. Then choose a new distance value for the node that is strictly less than its current distance but at least the neighbor's distance plus one. Update the node's distance to this new value and set the node's parent to the chosen neighbor. The reason the algorithm allows setting the distance to any value in this range (rather than just the neighbor's distance plus one) is to support refinement by a distributed implementation where a node may receive stale information from neighbors.
description.safety_properties: When the algorithm terminates (no further transitions are enabled), the postcondition holds: for every node, one of three cases applies: (1) it is the root, with distance 0 and parent equal to itself; (2) it is unreachable, with distance equal to the maximum constant, parent equal to itself, and all of its neighbors also unreachable; or (3) it has a distance between 1 and the maximum minus one, its parent is one of its graph neighbors, and its distance equals its parent's distance plus one. The safety property states that this postcondition always holds upon termination.
description.liveness_properties: The algorithm eventually terminates: eventually, no further transitions are enabled. This is ensured by weak fairness on the transition relation.
description.model_bounds: The graph is specified by constants: the set of nodes, the set of edges (each edge is a two-element subset of nodes), the root node (which must be in the node set), and a maximum cardinality constant (a natural number at least as large as the number of nodes, used in place of infinity).
description.additional_assumptions: No self-loops are permitted (each edge has exactly two distinct endpoints). There is at most one edge between any pair of nodes. The algorithm is designed so that it can be refined by a distributed message-passing implementation.

description.system_overview: This specification models the core algorithm of a model checker for state-based specifications, similar to the TLC model checker for TLA+. The algorithm takes a directed state graph with designated initial states and a set of violation states, then performs an exhaustive breadth-first exploration of all reachable states. If a violation state is found, the algorithm constructs a counterexample trace from an initial state to the violating state. If all states are explored without finding a violation, the algorithm reports success.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a single sequential model-checking process that explores a state graph. The inputs are: a directed graph with a set of states, a set of initial states, and a transition function mapping each state to its successor states; a set of violation states representing safety property violations; and a null value used as a placeholder.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a FIFO queue of states awaiting exploration, initialized with a permutation of the initial states; (2) a set of already-explored states ensuring each state is visited at most once; (3) the current state being examined; (4) the set of unexplored successor states of the current state; (5) a loop counter for iterating through initial states; (6) a counterexample sequence that, when populated, contains a path from an initial state to a violating state; (7) a trace-back forest recording predecessor-successor pairs used to reconstruct the counterexample path; (8) a program counter tracking the algorithm's current phase.
description.initial_state: The exploration queue is initialized with one of the possible permutations of the initial states (modeling the fact that initial states have no defined order). The explored-states set is empty. The current state is null. The successor set is empty. The loop counter starts at one. The counterexample is an empty sequence. The trace-back forest is an empty sequence.
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in four phases: (1) Initial state checking: iterate through the initial states in queue order, marking each as explored. If any initial state is a violation state, record it as the start of a counterexample and jump to trace reconstruction. (2) Post-initialization assertion: verify that all initial states have been explored. (3) Successor exploration: dequeue the next state, compute its unexplored successors. If the state has no successors at all (a deadlock), record it as a counterexample. Otherwise, for each unexplored successor: mark it as explored, enqueue it, record the predecessor-successor pair in the trace-back forest, and check whether it is a violation state. If it is, start trace reconstruction. If the queue becomes empty and no violation was found, assert that the violation set was empty and terminate successfully. (4) Trace reconstruction: starting from the violation state, repeatedly prepend the predecessor from the trace-back forest until an initial state is reached, producing the complete counterexample path.
description.safety_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.liveness_properties: If violation states exist, the model checker eventually produces a counterexample: a non-empty sequence whose last element is a violation state and whose first element is an initial state. Termination: the algorithm eventually finishes exploring all states or finding a violation. The specification also checks that the algorithm terminates via a temporal property.
description.model_bounds: The state graph, violation states, and null value are declared as constants. For model checking, specific test graphs with known structures are used (defined in a companion test module). Graph sizes range from single-node graphs to 50-node graphs with various topologies.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on the next-state relation, ensuring the algorithm makes progress. The specification is written using PlusCal syntax with a fair algorithm annotation. The exploration queue is initialized with a nondeterministic permutation of initial states because the order of initial states is undefined. The algorithm treats states with no outgoing transitions (other than self-loops) as deadlocked states. The trace-back forest stores predecessor-successor pairs as sequences of two-element sequences.

description.system_overview: This specification defines a collection of test graphs used to verify the correctness of a model-checking algorithm specification. Each test graph is a directed graph with designated initial states and violation states, designed to exercise different scenarios such as cycles, forests, deadlocks, unreachable violations, empty graphs, and larger graphs with complex connectivity. The module instantiates the model checker specification with one of these test graphs.
description.actors_and_components: This module defines no independent actors. It provides graph definitions as test fixtures and instantiates the model checker algorithm module with a selected test graph and its corresponding violation states. The model checker's behavior (a single sequential exploration process) is inherited through instantiation.
description.state_variables: All state variables are inherited from the instantiated model checker specification: the exploration queue, explored-states set, current state, successor set, loop counter, counterexample sequence, trace-back forest, and program counter. This module adds no new state variables.
description.initial_state: Inherited from the model checker specification. The exploration queue begins with a permutation of the selected test graph's initial states.
description.actions: All actions are inherited from the model checker specification: initial state checking, post-initialization assertion, successor exploration with violation detection, and trace reconstruction.
description.safety_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.liveness_properties: Inherited from the model checker specification: the algorithm terminates, and if violations exist, a valid counterexample path is eventually produced. A liveness property checks that if violation states are non-empty, eventually a counterexample is found with its last element being a violation state and its first element being an initial state.
description.model_bounds: The module defines 13 test graphs of various sizes: graphs with 1 to 50 states, with varying numbers of initial states (including zero), different violation state sets (including empty sets), and different structural properties (cycles, trees, forests, fully connected subgraphs, sink nodes, disconnected components). A null model value constant is also required. The default instantiation uses a 50-state graph.
description.additional_assumptions: The graphs are defined as records with three fields: a set of states (represented as integers), a set of initial states (a subset of the states), and a sequence of successor sets indexed by state number. The violation states for each graph are chosen to test specific scenarios: violations reachable via different path lengths, unreachable violations, no violations at all, and immediate violations in initial states.

description.system_overview: This specification is a variant of the Simple algorithm from Lamport's 'Teaching Concurrency' that generalizes the shared registers from atomic to regular registers. Regular registers, as defined in Lamport's 1986 paper 'On Interprocess Communication' (Distributed Computing 1, 2, pp. 77-101), are weaker than atomic registers: a read that overlaps a write may return either the old value or the new value being written. This specification models regular register semantics by representing each register as a set of values, and proves that the correctness property (at least one process reads 1 after all terminate) still holds under this weaker memory model.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes, numbered 0 through N-1, arranged logically in a circle. Each process has a shared regular register that it writes to and that its right neighbor reads. The generalization to regular registers was proposed by Yuri Abraham in 'On Lamport's Teaching Concurrency' (Bulletin of EATCS No. 127, February 2019).
description.state_variables: The system tracks two arrays indexed by process number (0 through N-1): (1) a shared register array where each entry is a nonempty set of values from {0, 1}, representing the possible values a read might return from that regular register, and (2) a local read-result array where each process stores the value it obtained from reading its left neighbor's register (a single value, either 0 or 1). A program counter array tracks which of four steps each process is currently at.
description.initial_state: Each shared register is initialized to the singleton set {0} (representing a register whose value is definitely 0). All local read-results are initialized to 0. Every process begins at its first step.
description.actions: Each process executes three steps in sequence, modeling a regular register write as two substeps: (1) Begin-write step: the process changes its shared register from {0} to {0, 1}, representing the intermediate state where a concurrent read might see either the old value 0 or the new value 1. (2) Complete-write step: the process changes its register from {0, 1} to {1}, representing the completion of the write -- any subsequent read will now definitely see 1. (3) Read step: the process nondeterministically selects any value from the set currently in its left neighbor's register (at position (i-1) modulo N), stores that value as its local read-result, and terminates. After all processes terminate, a stuttering step prevents deadlock reporting.
description.safety_properties: The key correctness property is identical to the Simple specification: whenever all processes have terminated, at least one process must have read the value 1. The specification also includes a type-correctness invariant ensuring the register sets are nonempty subsets of {0, 1}, the read-results are in {0, 1}, and the program counters are in the expected set. An inductive invariant ensures that any process past the write-completion step has its register equal to {1}.
description.liveness_properties: Termination: eventually all processes reach the terminated state.
description.model_bounds: N (the number of processes) is a constant positive natural number. For model checking, N is set to a specific finite value.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification includes a complete formal machine-checked proof of the correctness property. The proof follows the same structure as the Simple proof but requires an additional decomposition step for the read action to handle the nondeterministic choice from the register set. Each local read-result variable is accessible only to its own process (it is local, not shared). The regular register model assumes single-writer registers -- each register is written by exactly one process.

description.system_overview: This specification models a simple concurrent algorithm from Lamport's 'Teaching Concurrency' article (ACM SIGACT News, Volume 40, Issue 1, March 2009). The algorithm demonstrates a fundamental property of concurrent systems: N processes are arranged in a logical circle, each process writes a value to its own shared register and then reads its left neighbor's register, and the specification proves that after all processes terminate, at least one process must have observed the value written by its neighbor.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes, numbered 0 through N-1, arranged logically in a circle. Each process has a shared register that it writes to and that its right neighbor reads. Process i's left neighbor is the process at position (i-1) modulo N, and its right neighbor is at position (i+1) modulo N.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two arrays, each indexed by process number (0 through N-1): (1) a shared write-register array where each process stores a value of either 0 or 1, and (2) a local read-result array where each process stores the value it read from its left neighbor's register (also 0 or 1). Additionally, a program counter array tracks which step each process is currently at.
description.initial_state: Both arrays are initialized to all zeros. Every process begins at its first step (the write step).
description.actions: Each process executes two steps in sequence: (1) Write step: the process sets its own entry in the shared register array to 1. (2) Read step: the process reads the value in its left neighbor's shared register (the neighbor at position (i-1) modulo N) and stores the result in its own local read-result entry, then terminates. After all processes have terminated, a stuttering step allows the system to remain in its final state indefinitely (to prevent the model checker from reporting deadlock).
description.safety_properties: The key correctness property is: whenever all processes have terminated, at least one process must have read the value 1 from its left neighbor. Informally, since all processes write 1 to their registers and then read their left neighbor, it is impossible for all reads to return 0 -- at least one process must see the write from its neighbor. The specification also includes a type-correctness invariant ensuring the arrays and program counters remain within their expected ranges, and an inductive invariant that strengthens the correctness property to be provable by induction.
description.liveness_properties: Termination: eventually all processes reach the terminated state.
description.model_bounds: N (the number of processes) is a constant positive natural number. For model checking, N is set to a specific finite value.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification includes a complete formal machine-checked proof that the correctness property is an invariant. The proof uses an inductive invariant that combines type correctness with two conditions: (1) any process that has completed its write step has value 1 in its register, and (2) either some process has not yet terminated, or some process read the value 1. The shared registers are assumed to be atomic (each read or write is an instantaneous action). The specification is also discussed in Section 7.2 of Lamport's 'Proving Safety Properties' document.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm without pruning. It instantiates the main algorithm specification with a concrete five-node graph and specific edge set, enabling exhaustive verification of the algorithm's properties using a model checker.
description.actors_and_components: The module defines five nodes (identified by integers one through five) connected by a specific set of five undirected edges forming a connected graph. It instantiates the main Yo-Yo algorithm without pruning, inheriting all node roles and message-passing behavior.
description.state_variables: All state variables are inherited from the main specification: each node's phase (downward or upward), incoming and outgoing neighbor sets, and mailbox of pending messages.
description.initial_state: Inherited from the main specification with the concrete graph: edges orient from smaller to larger identity among the five nodes. All nodes start in the downward phase with empty mailboxes.
description.actions: All actions are inherited from the main Yo-Yo specification without pruning: downward broadcasting by sources, forwarding of minimum values by internal and sink nodes, upward yes/no replies, and edge reversal on 'no' responses.
description.safety_properties: The configuration checks type correctness and a neighbor consistency invariant as invariants. A temporal property verifies that no new source nodes are created during execution.
description.liveness_properties: The configuration checks a stabilization liveness property: the algorithm eventually reaches a state where there is a single source (the minimum-identity node), all downward messages carry its identity, and all upward messages say 'yes'.
description.model_bounds: Five nodes (integers one through five) with edges connecting: nodes one and two, nodes one and five, nodes three and four, nodes three and five, and nodes four and five. An alternative larger graph with eleven nodes is included as a comment.
description.additional_assumptions: The module declares the four state variables from the main specification and uses module instantiation to import all definitions, actions, and properties. The chosen graph topology is connected and undirected as required by the algorithm.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm with pruning. It instantiates the pruning variant of the algorithm with a concrete five-node graph, enabling exhaustive verification of termination and correctness properties.
description.actors_and_components: The module defines five nodes (integers one through five) connected by the same edge set as the non-pruning model-checking module. It instantiates the Yo-Yo algorithm with pruning, which includes node activation tracking and edge pruning during the upward phase.
description.state_variables: All state variables are inherited from the pruning specification: each node's activation flag, phase, incoming and outgoing neighbor sets, and mailbox.
description.initial_state: Inherited from the pruning specification with the concrete five-node graph.
description.actions: All actions are inherited from the pruning specification: downward broadcasting, minimum forwarding, upward replies with prune flags, edge reversal, edge pruning, and node deactivation.
description.safety_properties: The configuration checks type correctness, a neighbor consistency invariant, and a property that deadlock occurs if and only if the termination condition is met. The no-new-source property is commented out because it fails for the small example graph due to pruning effects.
description.liveness_properties: The configuration checks that the algorithm eventually terminates: the minimum-identity node becomes the leader, all other nodes become inactive, and all mailboxes are empty.
description.model_bounds: Five nodes (integers one through five) with edges connecting: nodes one and two, nodes one and five, nodes three and four, nodes three and five, and nodes four and five. Deadlock checking is disabled. An alternative larger graph with eleven nodes is included as a comment.
description.additional_assumptions: The module declares the five state variables from the pruning specification (including the activation variable) and uses module instantiation to import all definitions. The chosen graph ensures the pruning algorithm can be tested for termination.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm with pruning, parameterized to verify correctness across all connected undirected graphs over a fixed number of nodes. Unlike the basic pruning specification that operates on a single fixed graph, this version nondeterministically selects the graph's edge set during initialization, enabling verification of the algorithm for every possible connected graph topology of the given size.
description.actors_and_components: The participants are nodes numbered from one to a parameter specifying the total number of nodes. The edge set is drawn from all possible undirected edges (without self-loops) over these nodes, constrained to form a connected graph. Node roles (leader, source, sink, internal) are determined dynamically based on edge orientations, and nodes communicate via directed messages along oriented edges.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five pieces of state per node: (1) an activation flag, (2) the current phase (downward or upward), (3) the set of incoming neighbors, (4) the set of outgoing neighbors, and (5) a mailbox of pending messages. Messages in the downward phase carry a sender and a value; messages in the upward phase carry a sender, a yes/no reply, and a boolean prune flag.
description.initial_state: All nodes start active and in the downward phase with empty mailboxes. A subset of all possible edges is chosen nondeterministically, subject to the constraint that the resulting graph is connected. Edges are then oriented from smaller to larger node number, establishing initial incoming and outgoing neighbor sets for each node.
description.actions: The actions are identical to the pruning variant of the Yo-Yo algorithm. Downward phase: sources broadcast their identity; other nodes forward the minimum received value. Upward phase: nodes send yes/no replies with prune flags. Pruning removes redundant edges and deactivates lone sink nodes. Edge reversal occurs for 'no' responses. The graph is progressively simplified until only one leader remains.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A neighbor consistency invariant accounts for edges being reversed or pruned. The specification checks that the system reaches deadlock if and only if the termination condition holds (the minimum node is the leader, all others are inactive, and all mailboxes are empty).
description.liveness_properties: The algorithm eventually terminates with the minimum-identity node as the isolated leader and all other nodes inactive, for every connected graph topology of the given size.
description.model_bounds: The number of nodes is provided as a single constant parameter. The model-checking configuration sets this to five nodes. Deadlock checking is disabled. The set of all possible edges is computed as all two-element subsets of the node set.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification assumes the number of nodes is a positive natural number. It relies on an external community module for checking graph connectivity. Weak fairness is assumed on the next-state action. The nondeterministic edge selection in the initial state allows the model checker to explore all connected graph topologies, at the cost of a much larger state space compared to checking a single fixed graph.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm for connected undirected graphs without pruning, as introduced by Nicola Santoro. The algorithm elects the node with the smallest identity as leader by orienting edges and iteratively eliminating candidate source nodes through alternating downward and upward message-passing phases. Without pruning, the algorithm stabilizes but does not terminate, as no node can detect that stabilization has occurred.
description.actors_and_components: The participants are nodes in a connected undirected graph, each identified by a unique integer. Nodes communicate by sending messages to neighbors along directed edges. Nodes are classified dynamically as sources (only outgoing edges), sinks (only incoming edges), or internal nodes (both incoming and outgoing edges). Sources are candidates for leadership.
description.state_variables: The system tracks four pieces of state per node: (1) the current phase of the node (downward or upward), (2) the set of incoming neighbors (nodes from which edges point toward this node), (3) the set of outgoing neighbors (nodes toward which edges point away from this node), and (4) a mailbox containing pending messages. Messages are of two types: downward-phase messages carrying a sender identifier and a value (the minimum identity seen), and upward-phase messages carrying a sender identifier and a yes-or-no reply.
description.initial_state: All nodes start in the downward phase. Edges are oriented from smaller to larger node identity: each node's incoming neighbors are those neighbors with smaller identities, and outgoing neighbors are those with larger identities. All mailboxes are empty. This initial orientation ensures that the node with the globally smallest identity is a source.
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in rounds of two phases. In the downward phase: source nodes broadcast their own identity to all outgoing neighbors and switch to the upward phase. Non-source nodes wait until they have received a downward message from every incoming neighbor, then forward the minimum received value to all outgoing neighbors and switch to the upward phase. In the upward phase: sink nodes (which have no outgoing edges and thus receive no upward replies) examine the downward messages received, reply 'yes' to all incoming neighbors that sent the minimum value and 'no' to all others, then switch to the downward phase. Internal nodes wait until they have received an upward reply from every outgoing neighbor. If any reply is 'no', they send 'no' to all incoming neighbors. Otherwise, they send 'yes' to incoming neighbors that sent the smallest value during the downward phase and 'no' to all others. Source nodes wait for upward replies from all outgoing neighbors; neighbors that sent 'no' become incoming neighbors (edge reversal). After the upward phase, edges along which 'no' was sent reverse their direction, potentially changing node classifications.
description.safety_properties: A neighbor consistency invariant holds: a node has another as an outgoing neighbor if and only if the other has the first as an incoming neighbor, except when an edge is being reversed (indicated by a pending 'no' message in one of their mailboxes). No new source nodes are created during execution: if a node becomes a source, it was already a source. Type correctness ensures all variables remain in their expected domains.
description.liveness_properties: The system eventually stabilizes to a state where there is exactly one source node (the one with the smallest identity), all downward messages carry that node's identity, and all upward messages say 'yes'. However, the algorithm does not terminate because no node can detect this stabilization.
description.model_bounds: The graph topology (nodes and edges) is provided as constants. The model-checking configuration uses a five-node graph with specific edges.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification assumes the graph is connected and undirected with no self-loops, and all node identities are distinct integers. Weak fairness is assumed on the next-state action. The algorithm uses asynchronous message passing where each node can take a step independently when its preconditions are met.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm with pruning for connected undirected graphs. It extends the base algorithm by adding graph pruning during the upward phase to remove redundant edges and nodes, ensuring the algorithm terminates when the sole remaining source becomes isolated and declares itself leader. All other nodes become inactive.
description.actors_and_components: The participants are nodes in a connected undirected graph, each with a unique integer identity. Nodes are dynamically classified as leaders (isolated source with no neighbors), sources (only outgoing edges), sinks (only incoming edges), or internal nodes (both). Nodes communicate via directed edges carrying two types of messages: downward messages with a value and upward messages with a yes/no reply and a prune flag.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five pieces of state per node: (1) an activation flag indicating whether the node is still participating, (2) the current phase (downward or upward), (3) the set of incoming neighbors, (4) the set of outgoing neighbors, and (5) a mailbox of pending messages. Messages in the upward phase carry an additional boolean flag indicating whether the receiving node should prune the corresponding edge.
description.initial_state: All nodes start active and in the downward phase. Edges are oriented from smaller to larger identity. All mailboxes are empty.
description.actions: The algorithm operates in rounds of downward and upward phases, as in the base version, but the upward phase includes pruning. During the downward phase, active source nodes broadcast their identity to outgoing neighbors; active non-source nodes wait for all incoming downward messages, then forward the minimum value to outgoing neighbors. During the upward phase, pruning rules apply: (1) A sink node with only a single incoming neighbor becomes inactive and is removed from the graph, since it contributes no useful information. (2) When a node receives the same value from multiple incoming neighbors (indicating redundant paths from the same source), it non-deterministically keeps one sender per distinct value and marks the others for pruning. Upward messages include a prune flag that tells the receiver to drop the corresponding edge. Source nodes process upward replies by reversing edges for 'no' responses and removing edges marked for pruning. The combined effect of edge reversal and pruning progressively simplifies the graph until only the minimum-identity node remains as an isolated leader.
description.safety_properties: A neighbor consistency invariant accounts for edges being reversed ('no' messages pending) or pruned (prune-flagged messages pending). Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A property checks that deadlock occurs if and only if the termination condition holds.
description.liveness_properties: The algorithm eventually terminates: the minimum-identity node becomes the leader (isolated with no neighbors), all other nodes become inactive, and all mailboxes are empty.
description.model_bounds: The graph topology is provided as constants. The model-checking configuration uses a five-node graph with specific edges. Deadlock checking is disabled since the algorithm terminates by reaching a deadlock state.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification assumes the graph is connected and undirected with no self-loops, and all node identities are distinct integers. Weak fairness is assumed on the next-state action. The pruning variant may create new source nodes (unlike the base algorithm), which is expected behavior as the graph is simplified.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Atomic Commitment Protocol with Simple Broadcast (ACP-SB), a distributed transaction commitment protocol from Babaoglu and Toueg's work on non-blocking atomic commitment. The protocol coordinates a group of participants and a coordinator to agree on committing or aborting a distributed transaction. The simple broadcast variant sends messages sequentially, which means a coordinator failure during broadcast can leave some participants without a decision, making it a blocking protocol that does not guarantee termination under failures.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of two types of actors: (1) A single coordinator that collects votes from participants, makes a commit or abort decision, and broadcasts the decision. (2) A set of participants, each of which votes yes or no on the transaction, can detect failures, and ultimately reaches a commit or abort decision. Both the coordinator and participants can crash (die) at any time.
description.state_variables: The system tracks the following state: For each participant: their vote (yes or no), whether they are alive, their final decision (undecided, commit, or abort), whether they are faulty (have crashed), and whether they have sent their vote to the coordinator. For the coordinator: whether it has sent a vote request to each participant, the vote received from each participant (or a waiting indicator if not yet received), whether it has broadcast its decision to each participant (or a not-sent indicator), its own decision (commit, abort, or undecided), whether it is alive, and whether it is faulty.
description.initial_state: All participants start alive and non-faulty, each with a nondeterministically chosen vote of yes or no, undecided about the final outcome, and having not yet sent their vote. The coordinator starts alive and non-faulty, has not sent vote requests to any participant, has not received any votes (all waiting), has not broadcast any decision (all not-sent), and is undecided.
description.actions: The coordinator actions are: (1) Send a vote request to a participant (if the coordinator is alive and has not already requested from that participant). (2) Receive a vote from a participant (if the coordinator is alive, undecided, has requested all votes, is waiting on that participant, and the participant has sent its vote). (3) Detect a participant fault (if the coordinator is alive, undecided, has requested all votes, is waiting on that participant, and the participant has died without sending its vote -- the coordinator then decides to abort). (4) Make a decision (if the coordinator is alive, undecided, and has received all votes -- if all votes are yes, decide commit; otherwise, decide abort). (5) Broadcast the decision to a participant using simple broadcast (if the coordinator is alive, has made a decision, and has not yet sent it to that participant). (6) Die (the coordinator crashes and becomes faulty). The participant actions are: (1) Send vote (if the participant is alive and has received a vote request). (2) Abort on vote (if the participant is alive, undecided, has sent its vote, and its vote is no -- it decides unilaterally to abort). (3) Abort on timeout for vote request (if the participant is alive, undecided, and the coordinator has died without sending a vote request). (4) Decide based on coordinator broadcast (if the participant is alive, undecided, and the coordinator has sent a decision to it -- the participant adopts that decision). (5) Die (the participant crashes and becomes faulty).
description.safety_properties: AC1 (Agreement/Consistency): No two participants can decide differently -- it is impossible for one participant to have committed while another has aborted. AC2 (Commit validity): If any participant decides commit, then all participants must have voted yes. AC3 (Abort validity): If any participant decides abort, then either at least one participant voted no, or at least one participant is faulty, or the coordinator is faulty. AC4 (Irrevocability): Each participant decides at most once -- once a participant decides commit, it remains committed forever; once it decides abort, it remains aborted forever.
description.liveness_properties: AC3 liveness component: Eventually either all participants reach a decision (commit or abort), or at least one participant is faulty, or the coordinator is faulty. Note: The simple broadcast variant does NOT satisfy the non-blocking termination property AC5 (which would require that every non-faulty participant eventually decides). This is because a coordinator crash during broadcast can leave some participants permanently undecided.
description.model_bounds: The set of participants is declared as a constant. For model checking, safety was checked with up to 4 participants (without symmetries) and 6 participants (with symmetries). Liveness was checked for up to 4 participants.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on participant progress actions and coordinator progress actions, excluding death transitions -- that is, if a participant or the coordinator is able to make progress (send votes, make decisions, etc.), it eventually does. Death transitions are not subject to fairness and can occur at any time. The specification uses asynchronous communication rather than synchronous communication, and failure detection is modeled as immediate (magical) rather than timeout-based.

description.system_overview: A distributed implementation of the scheduling resource allocator that introduces explicit message-passing communication between client processes and the allocator. Where the scheduling allocator uses shared state, this implementation models a realistic distributed system where clients and the allocator run on separate machines and coordinate through asynchronous messages. The module claims to be a refinement of the scheduling allocator specification.
description.actors_and_components: Three types of actors: (1) client processes that maintain local state about their pending requests and held resources, (2) the allocator process that maintains the authoritative record of outstanding requests, allocated resources, and the client schedule, and (3) an asynchronous communication network modeled as a set of messages in transit.
description.state_variables: Six state variables organized in three groups. Allocator-side: outstanding requests per client, allocated resources per client, and the client schedule (inherited from the scheduling allocator). Client-side: each client's locally tracked pending requests and locally held resources. Network: a set of messages currently in transit, where messages carry a type (request, allocate, or return), a client identifier, and a set of resources.
description.initial_state: The allocator-side state starts as in the scheduling allocator (no requests, no allocations, empty schedule). Each client starts with no pending requests and no held resources. The network starts empty.
description.actions: Seven actions model the distributed protocol. Client-initiated: (1) a client sends a resource request message to the network, (2) a client receives an allocation message and updates its local holdings, (3) a client sends a return message for held resources. Allocator-initiated: (4) the allocator receives and processes a request message (with a guard preventing premature handling), (5) the allocator decides to allocate resources and sends an allocation message, (6) the allocator receives a return message and updates its allocation records. Shared: (7) the schedule action extends the schedule with unscheduled clients.
description.safety_properties: Resource mutual exclusion: no two clients hold the same resource simultaneously. The type correctness invariant covers both the inherited scheduling allocator types and the new client and network state. A cross-component invariant relates allocator-side and client-side variables through messages in transit, ensuring consistency despite asynchronous communication: at most one request per client is in transit, and client-local state plus in-transit messages equals the allocator's view.
description.liveness_properties: All liveness properties from the scheduling allocator are preserved: clients eventually return resources after their requests are satisfied, the allocator eventually allocates resources when possible, the scheduler eventually schedules pending clients. Additionally, weak fairness is required for all message reception actions, ensuring messages are eventually delivered.
description.model_bounds: For model checking: 3 clients and 2 resources. The network is modeled as an unordered set of messages, allowing arbitrary delays, reordering, and duplication.
description.additional_assumptions: The implementation assumes an asynchronous reliable network where messages may be delayed and reordered but are eventually delivered (ensured by fairness conditions on message reception). A race condition exists where request messages can arrive at the allocator before earlier return messages, leading to refinement violations. The allocator guards against this by requiring that the client's allocation record is empty before processing a request message. The specification asserts refinement of the scheduling allocator as a theorem.

description.system_overview: A refined specification of the resource allocator that adds a scheduling mechanism to prevent deadlocks. The simple allocator can paint itself into a corner by allocating resources in an order that prevents any client from obtaining its full request. This scheduling allocator maintains an ordered schedule of clients with outstanding requests and allocates resources respecting that order, ensuring that prioritized clients can eventually obtain all their requested resources.
description.actors_and_components: Three kinds of actors: client processes that request and return resources, the resource allocator that grants resources according to the schedule, and a scheduler component that determines the order in which clients with pending requests are served.
