description.state_variables: Three state variables: (1) a mapping from clients to their sets of outstanding resource requests, (2) a mapping from clients to their sets of currently allocated resources, and (3) a sequence of clients representing the current schedule order. The schedule determines allocation priority.
description.initial_state: No resources have been requested or allocated, and the schedule is empty.
description.actions: Four actions exist. (1) A client requests a non-empty set of resources when it has no pending requests and holds nothing. (2) The allocator grants available resources to a scheduled client, provided no earlier-scheduled client has requested any of those resources; if the grant fully satisfies the client's request, the client is removed from the schedule. (3) A client returns a non-empty subset of held resources. (4) The scheduler appends clients with unsatisfied requests (not yet in the schedule) to the schedule in an arbitrary permutation order.
description.safety_properties: Resource mutual exclusion: no resource is simultaneously allocated to two different clients. A type correctness invariant constrains all state variables to proper types. A lower-level allocator invariant ensures: all scheduled clients have outstanding requests, no client holds resources requested by an earlier-scheduled client, and each scheduled client's request can be satisfied from currently available resources plus resources held by higher-priority clients.
description.liveness_properties: Three liveness properties hold: (1) clients will eventually return resources once their requests are fully satisfied, (2) every requested resource will eventually be allocated, and (3) each client's outstanding request set is infinitely often empty. Fairness conditions include weak fairness on returns (after request satisfaction), weak fairness on allocation, and weak fairness on scheduling.
description.model_bounds: For model checking: 3 clients and 2 resources. Symmetry reduction applies only to resources (not clients, because the schedule sequence breaks client symmetry).
description.additional_assumptions: The set of resources is assumed finite. The scheduling strategy is nondeterministic: clients are added to the schedule in any permutation order. This generality allows verification that correctness holds regardless of scheduling policy. The specification uses helper operators for computing permutation sequences of finite sets, removing elements from sequences, and computing the range of functions.

description.system_overview: A high-level specification of a resource allocator managing a finite set of resources shared among a set of client processes. Clients request sets of resources, the allocator grants available resources (possibly partially), and clients return resources after use. The specification is deliberately abstract, omitting implementation details such as communication mechanisms and scheduling strategies.
description.actors_and_components: Two kinds of actors: client processes and the resource allocator. Clients issue resource requests, receive allocations, and return resources. The allocator tracks outstanding requests and granted allocations, ensuring exclusive access to resources.
description.state_variables: Two mappings from clients to sets of resources: one tracking each client's outstanding (unsatisfied) resource requests, and one tracking the resources currently allocated to each client. A derived constant computes the set of currently available (unallocated) resources.
description.initial_state: No resources have been requested or allocated. Every client has an empty set of outstanding requests and an empty set of allocated resources.
description.actions: Three actions exist. (1) A client issues a request for a non-empty set of resources, but only if it has no pending requests and holds no resources. (2) The allocator grants a non-empty subset of available resources that the client has requested; partial fulfillment is allowed. (3) A client returns a non-empty subset of the resources it currently holds, even before its full request has been satisfied.
description.safety_properties: Resource mutual exclusion: no resource is ever allocated to two different clients simultaneously. A type correctness invariant ensures outstanding requests and allocations are functions from clients to subsets of resources.
description.liveness_properties: Three liveness properties are specified. (1) Clients will eventually return all resources once their requests are fully satisfied (weak fairness on the return action). (2) Every requested resource will eventually be allocated to the requesting client (strong fairness on allocation). (3) Each client's set of outstanding requests is infinitely often empty, meaning every request is eventually fully satisfied.
description.model_bounds: For model checking, the specification uses 3 clients and 2 resources as symbolic constants. Symmetry reduction over permutations of clients and resources is defined but noted as incompatible with liveness checking.
description.additional_assumptions: The set of resources is assumed to be finite. The set of clients need not be finite since only finitely many will have issued requests at any point. A client cannot extend a pending request once it has been issued. Two alternative system specifications are provided with different fairness conditions: the original requires clients to always eventually return held resources, while a weaker variant only requires returns after the full request is satisfied. The weaker variant does not guarantee all liveness properties.

description.system_overview: This specification models a buffered random access file, which is a caching layer used to speed up interaction with the filesystem. It corresponds to the BufferedRandomAccessFile class in the TLC model checker's Java source code. The specification covers the core fields and the seek, read, write, flush, and set-length operations. Correctness is established by showing that the buffered implementation refines the behavior of a general random access file abstraction.
description.actors_and_components: The system has two layers: (1) the buffered random access file, which maintains an in-memory buffer, position tracking, and dirty flag, and (2) the underlying file, which represents the persistent storage with its own content and pointer. A separate abstract specification of a general random access file serves as the refinement target. A common definitions module provides shared constants and helper operators for array manipulation.
description.state_variables: The system tracks eight pieces of state: (1) a dirty flag indicating whether the buffer has been modified but not yet written to disk, (2) the logical length of the file, (3) the current read/write position (cursor), (4) the buffer's starting offset within the file, (5) the buffer contents (a fixed-size array), (6) the disk position tracking where the underlying file pointer is, (7) the underlying file's content, and (8) the underlying file's pointer position.
description.initial_state: The dirty flag is false. The file length, current position, buffer start offset, disk position, and file pointer are all zero. The buffer is filled with a special arbitrary symbol. The underlying file content is empty.
description.actions: The specification defines several actions: (1) Flush buffer: if the buffer is dirty, write its relevant contents to the underlying file at the buffer's starting offset, then clear the dirty flag. (2) Seek: move the cursor to a new position; if the new position is outside the current buffer window and the buffer is clean, load a new buffer window from the underlying file aligned to the buffer size. (3) Set length: resize the file to a new length, adjusting the cursor if it exceeds the new length and updating buffer contents accordingly. (4) Single-byte read: read one byte from the buffer at the current cursor position and advance the cursor. (5) Single-byte write: write one byte to the buffer at the current cursor position, mark dirty, advance cursor, and update length if needed. (6) Bulk read: read multiple bytes from the buffer. (7) Write-at-most: write as many bytes as fit in the current buffer window.
description.safety_properties: The specification checks five internal invariants: (1) the logical length equals the length of the logical file content and the disk position equals the file pointer, (2) the cursor is within the buffer window (buffer start offset to buffer start offset plus buffer size), (3) buffered content matches the logical file content at the corresponding offsets, (4) non-buffered content matches the raw disk content, and (5) if any buffered byte differs from the disk, the dirty flag must be set. The specification also verifies refinement: the buffered implementation refines the general random access file specification, and each operation refines its abstract counterpart (flush is silent, seek refines abstract seek, set-length refines abstract set-length, reads refine abstract reads, writes refine abstract writes).
description.liveness_properties: The specification checks that it is always possible to restore the buffer-window invariant: when dirty, a flush is always enabled; flushing clears the dirty flag; when not dirty, seeking to the current position is enabled; and seeking to the current position restores the buffer-window invariant.
description.model_bounds: The model checking configuration uses a symbol set of two symbols, a maximum file offset of three, and a buffer size of two. A symmetry reduction is applied over the symbol set.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses zero-indexed arrays (unlike standard one-indexed sequences in the language) to match Java conventions and help prevent off-by-one errors. Undefined or uninitialized bytes are represented by a special arbitrary symbol rather than nondeterministic choice, which simplifies definitions and reduces state space. The specification includes the general random access file and common definitions as inner modules.

description.system_overview: This specification models the voucher cancellation operation, implemented using the Two-Phase Commit protocol. A Voucher Transaction Provider coordinates voucher holders and voucher issuers to atomically cancel previously issued vouchers. This operation is an addendum to RFC 3506 and is not described in the original RFC.
description.actors_and_components: Four types of participants interact: (1) A Voucher Transaction Provider (the coordinator) managing the commit/abort decision. (2) Voucher Holders who currently hold the vouchers. (3) Voucher Issuers who originally issued the vouchers. (4) The vouchers themselves, which transition from valid to cancelled. Communication uses a shared message pool where messages accumulate and are never removed.
description.state_variables: The system tracks seven pieces of state: (1) each voucher's current status (valid or cancelled), (2) each voucher's lifecycle phase (working or done), (3) each holder's participation state (holding, prepared, cancelled, or aborted), (4) each issuer's participation state (waiting, prepared, cancelled, or aborted), (5) the coordinator's state (initial or done), (6) the set of participants from which the coordinator has received cancellation preparation confirmations, and (7) the pool of all messages sent.
description.initial_state: All vouchers are in the valid state with lifecycle in the working phase (since cancellation presupposes a previously issued voucher). All holders are in the holding state. All issuers are in the waiting state. The coordinator is in the initial state with empty preparation confirmations and empty message pool.
description.actions: The coordinator can: receive preparation confirmations from a holder and an issuer, cancel a voucher (transitioning it to cancelled and lifecycle to done, enabled only when all participants have prepared), or spontaneously abort. Each holder can: prepare for cancellation (sending a preparation message), spontaneously abort, receive a cancellation message (transitioning to cancelled state), or receive an abort message (transitioning to aborted state). Each issuer can: prepare, spontaneously abort, receive a cancellation message (transitioning to cancelled), or receive an abort message (transitioning to aborted).
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A consistency invariant ensures no holder and issuer reach conflicting decisions: a holder must not be cancelled while an issuer is aborted, and a holder must not be aborted while an issuer is cancelled.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The model-checking configuration uses three vouchers, three holders, and three issuers. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification imports and claims to implement the voucher lifecycle specification as a refinement. Messages are modeled as a growing set that is never consumed. Preparation messages from the coordinator are not explicitly modeled. The cancellation operation requires the voucher to be in the valid/working state, meaning it must have been previously issued.

description.system_overview: This specification models the voucher issuance operation from RFC 3506, implemented using the Two-Phase Commit protocol. A Voucher Transaction Provider coordinates voucher holders and voucher issuers to atomically issue vouchers, ensuring that all parties either agree to the issuance or the transaction is aborted.
description.actors_and_components: Four types of participants interact: (1) A Voucher Transaction Provider (the coordinator) that manages the commit/abort decision. (2) Voucher Holders who will receive the issued vouchers. (3) Voucher Issuers who create the vouchers. (4) The vouchers themselves, which transition from a pre-issuance state to a valid state. Communication occurs through a shared message pool; messages are never removed, allowing multiple receipt.
description.state_variables: The system tracks seven pieces of state: (1) each voucher's current status (pre-issuance or valid), (2) each voucher's lifecycle phase (initial or working), (3) each holder's participation state (waiting, prepared, holding, or aborted), (4) each issuer's participation state (waiting, prepared, issued, or aborted), (5) the coordinator's state (initial or done), (6) the set of participants from which the coordinator has received preparation confirmations, and (7) the pool of all messages sent so far.
description.initial_state: All vouchers are in the pre-issuance state with lifecycle in the initial phase. All holders and issuers are in the waiting state. The coordinator is in the initial state with an empty set of preparation confirmations and an empty message pool.
description.actions: The coordinator can: receive preparation confirmations from a holder and an issuer (adding them to its confirmed set), issue a voucher (transitioning it to valid and the lifecycle to working, enabled only when all participants have confirmed preparation), or spontaneously abort (broadcasting an abort message). Each holder can: prepare (sending a preparation confirmation message), spontaneously choose to abort, receive an issuance message (transitioning to the holding state), or receive an abort message (transitioning to the aborted state). Each issuer can: prepare (sending a preparation confirmation), spontaneously choose to abort, receive an issuance message (transitioning to the issued state), or receive an abort message.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A consistency invariant ensures that no holder and issuer reach conflicting decisions: it must never be the case that a holder is in the holding state while an issuer is aborted, or that a holder is aborted while an issuer is in the issued state. The specification also claims to implement the voucher lifecycle specification as a refinement.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The model-checking configuration uses three vouchers, three holders, and three issuers. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: Messages are modeled as a set that only grows (messages are never consumed). This simplification allows any message to be received multiple times, which does not cause problems in this protocol. Preparation messages from the coordinator to participants are not explicitly modeled; participants spontaneously decide to prepare. Abort messages from participants to the coordinator are also eliminated; instead, the coordinator can spontaneously decide to abort.

description.system_overview: This specification models the lifecycle of a voucher as defined in RFC 3506 (Requirements and Design for Voucher Trading System). A voucher is a digital representation of the right to claim goods or services. The specification captures the state transitions a voucher undergoes from creation through to final disposition (redemption or cancellation).
description.actors_and_components: The system manages a set of vouchers. Each voucher is an independent entity that progresses through its lifecycle. There are no explicit participant roles in this module; it captures only the voucher state machine itself, abstracting away the parties involved in transactions.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two pieces of state per voucher: (1) the voucher's current status, which can be phantom (not yet issued), valid (issued and active), redeemed (used to claim goods/services), or cancelled (voided), and (2) the lifecycle machine state, which tracks whether the voucher's lifecycle process is in its initial phase, working phase, or completed.
description.initial_state: All vouchers begin in the phantom status (not yet issued) with their lifecycle machines in the initial phase.
description.actions: Four operations can be performed on a voucher: (1) Issue: transitions a phantom voucher to valid status and moves the lifecycle to the working phase; this is a one-way transition that cannot be reversed. (2) Transfer: can only occur when a voucher is valid; it represents changing the voucher's holder but does not alter the voucher's status or lifecycle state. (3) Redeem: transitions a valid voucher in the working phase to redeemed status and completes the lifecycle. (4) Cancel: transitions a valid voucher in the working phase to cancelled status and completes the lifecycle.
description.safety_properties: A type correctness invariant ensures voucher statuses and lifecycle states remain in their expected domains. A consistency invariant ensures that the voucher status and lifecycle state are always compatible: a completed lifecycle must correspond to either redeemed or cancelled status, an initial lifecycle must correspond to phantom status, and a working lifecycle must correspond to valid status.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The set of vouchers is provided as a constant parameter. The model-checking configuration uses three vouchers. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification does not include fairness assumptions. The transfer operation is a no-op in terms of voucher state (it leaves both the status and lifecycle unchanged), capturing the fact that ownership transfer does not affect the voucher's lifecycle position.

description.system_overview: This specification models the voucher redemption operation from RFC 3506, implemented using the Two-Phase Commit protocol. A Voucher Transaction Provider coordinates voucher holders and voucher collectors to atomically redeem vouchers, transitioning them from valid to redeemed status. Redemption represents the holder claiming the goods or services promised by the voucher.
description.actors_and_components: Four types of participants interact: (1) A Voucher Transaction Provider (the coordinator) managing the commit/abort decision. (2) Voucher Holders who present vouchers for redemption. (3) Voucher Collectors who fulfill the voucher's promise. (4) The vouchers themselves, transitioning from valid to redeemed. Communication uses a shared message pool.
description.state_variables: The system tracks seven pieces of state: (1) each voucher's current status (valid or redeemed), (2) each voucher's lifecycle phase (working or done), (3) each holder's participation state (holding, prepared, redeemed, or aborted), (4) each collector's participation state (waiting, prepared, redeemed, or aborted), (5) the coordinator's state (initial or done), (6) the set of participants from which the coordinator has received redemption preparation confirmations, and (7) the pool of all messages sent.
description.initial_state: All vouchers are in the valid state with lifecycle in the working phase (since redemption presupposes issuance). All holders are in the holding state. All collectors are in the waiting state. The coordinator is in the initial state with empty preparation confirmations and empty message pool.
description.actions: The coordinator can: receive preparation confirmations from a holder and a collector, redeem a voucher (transitioning it to redeemed and lifecycle to done, enabled only when all participants have prepared), or spontaneously abort. Each holder can: prepare for redemption (sending a preparation message), spontaneously abort, receive a redemption message (transitioning to redeemed state), or receive an abort message. Each collector can: prepare, spontaneously abort, receive a redemption message (transitioning to redeemed), or receive an abort message.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A consistency invariant ensures no holder and collector reach conflicting decisions: a holder must not be redeemed while a collector is aborted, and a holder must not be aborted while a collector is redeemed.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The model-checking configuration uses three vouchers, three holders, and three collectors. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification imports and claims to implement the voucher lifecycle specification as a refinement. Messages accumulate in a set and are never consumed. Preparation messages from the coordinator are not explicitly modeled. The redemption operation requires the voucher to be in the valid/working state.

description.system_overview: This specification models the voucher transfer operation from RFC 3506, implemented using the Two-Phase Commit protocol. A Voucher Transaction Provider coordinates the transfer of vouchers between two types of holders: source holders (current owners) and destination holders (future owners). The transfer operation changes voucher ownership without altering the voucher's lifecycle state.
description.actors_and_components: Four types of participants interact: (1) A Voucher Transaction Provider (the coordinator) managing the commit/abort decision. (2) Source Voucher Holders who currently own the vouchers and wish to transfer them. (3) Destination Voucher Holders who are waiting to receive the vouchers. (4) The vouchers themselves, which remain in the valid state throughout the transfer. Communication uses a shared message pool.
description.state_variables: The system tracks seven pieces of state: (1) each voucher's current status (always valid during a transfer), (2) each voucher's lifecycle phase (always working during a transfer), (3) each source holder's participation state (holding, prepared, transferred, or aborted), (4) each destination holder's participation state (waiting, prepared, holding, or aborted), (5) the coordinator's state (initial or done), (6) the set of participants from which the coordinator has received transfer preparation confirmations, and (7) the pool of all messages sent.
description.initial_state: All vouchers are in the valid state with lifecycle in the working phase. All source holders are in the holding state. All destination holders are in the waiting state. The coordinator is in the initial state with empty preparation confirmations and empty message pool.
description.actions: The coordinator can: receive preparation confirmations from a source holder and a destination holder, execute a transfer (broadcasting a transfer message, enabled only when all participants have prepared), or spontaneously abort. Each source holder can: prepare for transfer (sending a preparation message), spontaneously abort, receive a transfer message (transitioning to the transferred state), or receive an abort message. Each destination holder can: prepare, spontaneously abort, receive a transfer message (transitioning to the holding state, indicating they now own the voucher), or receive an abort message.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures all variables remain in expected domains. A consistency invariant ensures no source holder and destination holder reach conflicting decisions: a source holder must not be in the transferred state while a destination holder is aborted, and a source holder must not be aborted while a destination holder is in the holding state.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The model-checking configuration uses three vouchers, three source holders, and three destination holders. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification imports and claims to implement the voucher lifecycle specification as a refinement. The RFC does not distinguish between source and destination holders, but the specification introduces this distinction for clarity. Unlike other voucher operations, transfer does not change the voucher's status or lifecycle state; it only changes the holder identity, which is not explicitly tracked in this specification. Messages accumulate in a set and are never consumed.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Chang-Roberts algorithm for leader election in a unidirectional ring network. The algorithm was published by Ernest Chang and Rosemary Roberts in 1979 as 'An improved algorithm for decentralized extrema-finding in circular configurations of processes' (CACM 22(5): 281-283). In this algorithm, processes arranged in a ring each have a unique identifier, and the goal is to elect the process with the smallest identifier among the initiators as the leader.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes arranged in a unidirectional ring. Each process has a unique numeric identifier. Each process has a successor (the next process clockwise in the ring); the last process's successor wraps around to the first. Some processes are initiators that begin the election, while others start passively. Processes communicate by passing messages (identifiers) along the ring to their successor.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a set of pending messages at each process, representing identifiers that have arrived but not yet been processed; (2) a program counter for each process indicating its current execution phase; (3) whether each process is an initiator (determined nondeterministically at startup); (4) the election state of each process, which can be candidate (still in the running), lost (eliminated from contention), or won (elected as leader).
description.initial_state: All message sets are empty. Each process nondeterministically decides whether it is an initiator. Initiators begin in the candidate state; non-initiators begin in the lost state. All processes start at the first phase of execution (before sending their initial message).
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in two phases per process: (1) Initial send: if the process is an initiator, it sends its own identifier to its successor by adding it to the successor's message set. All processes then move to the main loop phase. (2) Main loop (repeated): the process picks one message (an identifier) from its pending message set and processes it according to its current state: (a) If the process has already lost, it forwards the identifier to its successor unchanged. (b) If the process is still a candidate and the received identifier is smaller than its own identifier, the process marks itself as lost and forwards the received identifier to its successor. (c) If the process is still a candidate and the received identifier is greater than or equal to its own, the message is not forwarded (it is consumed). If the received identifier equals the process's own identifier, the process has won the election and marks itself as the winner.
description.safety_properties: When any process declares itself the winner: (1) that process must be an initiator, (2) all other processes must be in the lost state, and (3) every other initiator must have a strictly larger identifier than the winner. In other words, the winner is the initiator with the smallest identifier, and the election result is unique and consistent.
description.liveness_properties: If at least one process is a candidate (i.e., at least one initiator exists), then eventually some process wins the election.
description.model_bounds: N (the number of processes) is a constant positive natural number. The identifiers are provided as a sequence of N distinct natural numbers. For model checking, typical instantiation uses N equal to 6 with a specific sequence of distinct identifiers.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process, ensuring every process eventually takes a step when it is enabled. The algorithm is written in PlusCal and translated to TLA+. The ring is unidirectional: messages can only travel from a process to its successor. The algorithm allows infinite stuttering (self-loops) after all processes have terminated to prevent spurious deadlock detection.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the Chang-Roberts leader election algorithm. It instantiates the base Chang-Roberts specification with a specific number of processes and a deterministic identity assignment (sequential identifiers from 1 to N), making the state space finite for exhaustive verification.
description.actors_and_components: Same as the Chang-Roberts specification: N processes arranged in a unidirectional ring, each with a unique identifier. This module fixes the identifiers to be sequential integers starting from 1.
description.state_variables: Inherits all state variables from the Chang-Roberts specification: message sets per process, program counters, initiator flags, and election states. No additional state variables are introduced.
description.initial_state: Same as the Chang-Roberts specification, with identifiers assigned as the sequence 1, 2, 3, ..., N.
description.actions: Inherits all actions from the Chang-Roberts specification without modification.
description.safety_properties: Checks two invariants from the base specification: (1) type correctness ensuring all variables are within expected domains, and (2) correctness of the election outcome (the winner is the initiator with the smallest identifier and all others have lost).
description.liveness_properties: Checks the liveness property from the base specification: if any process is a candidate, eventually some process wins the election.
description.model_bounds: N is set to 3 processes. Identifiers are the sequence 1, 2, 3. Deadlock checking is disabled (to allow stuttering after termination).
description.additional_assumptions: By using sequential identifiers (1, 2, ..., N), the identity assignment is deterministic. The base specification allows arbitrary distinct identifiers, but this configuration uses the simplest possible assignment for efficient model checking.

description.system_overview: This specification models an age-tracking communication channel for a partially synchronous distributed system, based on the failure detector framework of Chandra and Toueg (1996). Messages in transit are wrapped in boxes that track how long each message has been traveling. The channel supports picking up new messages, delivering messages to recipients, and aging all in-transit messages at each tick of an environmental clock.
description.actors_and_components: The communication channel itself is the primary component. It interacts with processes that send and receive messages. Messages are wrapped in boxes that carry both the message content and an age counter indicating how many environmental clock ticks the message has been in transit. The channel is parameterized by a set of all possible messages and a set of possible boxes.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two pieces of state: (1) The set of all message boxes currently in transit, where each box contains a message and an age counter. (2) The set of messages being delivered to a process in the current transition (these are the unpacked message contents, without age information).
description.initial_state: No boxes are in transit (empty set). No messages are being delivered (empty set).
description.actions: Three operations are defined: (1) Pickup: Given a set of messages to send, each message is packaged into a box with age zero and added to the set of in-transit boxes. The delivery set is cleared. (2) Deliver: A subset of in-transit boxes destined for a given receiver is nondeterministically chosen. The messages from those boxes are unpacked and placed in the delivery set, and the delivered boxes are removed from the in-transit set. (3) Attain age: At each tick of the environmental clock, every box still in transit has its age incremented by one. The delivery set is cleared.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: The set of in-transit items must be a subset of the valid box type (containing message content and integer age). The set of delivered items must be a subset of the valid message type.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.additional_assumptions: This module is designed to be instantiated by a controller module that defines the concrete message and box types and orchestrates the interactions between processes and the channel. The age tracking enables enforcement of message delay bounds in a partial synchrony model.

description.system_overview: This specification models the behavior of correct processes in an eventually perfect failure detector, based on the framework of Chandra and Toueg (1996) for unreliable failure detectors in reliable distributed systems. Each process periodically sends alive messages to all other processes, periodically makes predictions about which processes have crashed, and receives messages from others. Predictions are based on whether a process has heard from another process within an adaptive timeout interval.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of processes, each of which acts as both a sender and a receiver. Each process has a local clock, maintains a suspicion list of processes it believes have crashed, tracks adaptive timeout intervals for each other process, and records how long it has been since it last heard from each other process. Processes periodically send alive messages and periodically evaluate their suspicion lists.
description.state_variables: For each process, the system tracks: (1) A suspicion set -- which other processes it currently suspects of having crashed. (2) A timeout interval for each other process -- the duration it waits before suspecting that process. (3) A counter for each other process tracking how many ticks since last hearing from that process. (4) A local clock value (integer). (5) A set of outgoing messages that the process wants to send in the current transition. The sending and predicting operations are separated by local clock timing: a process sends alive messages at every multiple of a send interval, and makes predictions at every multiple of a predict interval, with these two intervals constrained to never coincide.
description.initial_state: No process suspects any other process of having crashed. All timeout intervals are set to a default value. All last-heard counters are zero (all processes are considered recently heard from). All local clocks start at zero. No outgoing messages exist.
description.actions: Three main process actions, determined by the local clock: (1) Send alive: When the local clock is at a multiple of the send interval (but not the predict interval), the process creates alive messages addressed to every other process, places them in its outgoing message set, increments its local clock, and increments last-heard counters for processes it has not yet timed out on. (2) Predict: When the local clock is at a multiple of the predict interval (but not the send interval), the process adds to its suspicion set any process from which it has not heard for longer than the corresponding timeout interval. It increments last-heard counters and its local clock. (3) Receive: At all other clock values, the process receives incoming messages. For each process from which it receives an alive message, it resets the corresponding last-heard counter to zero and removes that process from its suspicion set. If a suspected process sends a message that is received, the timeout interval for that process is increased by one (adaptive timeout). The local clock is reset to zero when it exceeds all relevant thresholds (send interval, predict interval, and all timeout intervals), creating a finite clock domain.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: Last-heard counters are integers. Timeout intervals are integers. Suspicion sets are subsets of the process set. Outgoing messages are subsets of the message type.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.additional_assumptions: The send interval and predict interval must both be positive and must not be multiples of each other, ensuring that send and predict operations never happen simultaneously. This module is designed to be instantiated by a controller that manages the communication channel and environmental clock. The adaptive timeout mechanism ensures that correct processes are eventually no longer suspected.

description.system_overview: This specification models a parameterized, partially synchronous system implementing an eventually perfect failure detector, based on Chandra and Toueg (1996). It serves as an environment controller that composes two sub-specifications: an age-tracking communication channel and the per-process failure detector logic. The controller manages a global environmental clock, process crashes, message delivery, and enforces the partial synchrony constraints on message delay and relative process speeds.
description.actors_and_components: The system has three layers: (1) An environment controller managing a global clock, crash tracking, and partial synchrony constraints. (2) A communication channel that wraps messages in age-tracked boxes and supports pickup, delivery, and aging operations. (3) A set of N processes (numbered 1 through N), each running a failure detector that sends alive messages, receives messages, and makes failure predictions. Up to T processes may crash. The environment controller orchestrates interactions between these layers.
description.state_variables: The system tracks state across three layers. Communication layer: the set of age-tracked message boxes in transit, and the set of messages being delivered in the current transition. Process layer: for each process, a suspicion set, adaptive timeout intervals for each other process, last-heard counters, a local clock, and outgoing messages. Environment layer: for each process, a pause counter tracking how long since its last transition; a movement indicator recording what action the process last took (none, initialized, send, receive, predict, or crash); a crash flag indicating whether the process has crashed; and a global count of total failures so far.
description.initial_state: No messages are in transit or being delivered. No process suspects any other. All timeout intervals are set to a default value. All last-heard counters are zero. All local clocks are zero. No outgoing messages exist. All process pause counters are zero. All movement indicators show initialized. No process has crashed. The failure count is zero.
description.actions: Three top-level actions: (1) Crash: A non-crashed process crashes if the total failure count is below the maximum allowed. The process is marked as crashed, the failure count increases, its movement is recorded as crash, and its pause counter is set to a sentinel value. No channel or process-layer state changes. (2) Environmental tick: If at least one correct process took a transition in the previous tick, the global clock advances. All in-transit message ages increase by one. All movement indicators reset to none. All non-crashed process pause counters increase by one. (3) Process tick: A non-crashed process that has not yet moved in the current tick takes one action. Its pause counter resets to zero. It either (a) predicts which processes have crashed based on its timeout intervals, (b) sends alive messages to all processes and the channel picks up the messages destined for non-crashed processes, or (c) receives messages delivered by the channel and updates its suspicion list and timeout intervals accordingly. Crashed processes may also have messages delivered from the channel (to prevent unbounded message aging), but these messages are not processed. All three top-level actions are constrained by partial synchrony: the relative speed constraint requires that no correct process pauses for more than a bound on relative speed, and the message delay constraint requires that no message destined for a receiving process has an age exceeding the delay bound when that process performs a receive.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: All process-layer and channel-layer variables conform to their types. Pause counters for correct processes are bounded. Crash flags and pause counters are consistent (crashed processes have sentinel pause values). The failure count is between zero and the maximum. Timeout intervals and message ages are bounded by computed upper limits derived from the timing parameters. Last-heard counters are bounded.
description.liveness_properties: Strong Completeness: Eventually, every crashed process is permanently suspected by every correct process. Eventually Strong Accuracy: There is a point in time after which no correct process is suspected by any other correct process. Together these define an eventually perfect failure detector.
description.model_bounds: N = 3 processes, T = 1 maximum failures, default timeout d0 = 2, send interval = 2, predict interval = 3, message delay bound = 1, relative speed bound = 1. With these parameters, TLC verification takes approximately 2 hours.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on the combined environmental tick and process tick actions, subject to both the message delay and relative speed constraints. The send and predict intervals must be positive and must not be multiples of each other. The specification uses a finite encoding of local clocks (resetting when exceeding all thresholds) and bounded counters to make the state space finite for model checking. Upper bounds on message ages and timeout intervals are computed from the timing parameters.

description.system_overview: This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, which appeared in 'Solution of a Problem in Concurrent Programming Control' in Communications of the ACM, September 1965. This was the first algorithm to solve the mutual exclusion problem for N concurrent processes using only shared variables, founding the study of concurrent algorithms. The algorithm uses two boolean arrays and a shared integer to coordinate access to a critical section.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of concurrent processes. Each process repeatedly cycles through four phases: non-critical section, entry protocol, critical section, and exit protocol. All processes compete for mutually exclusive access to a single shared critical section.
description.state_variables: The system maintains: (1) a boolean array with one entry per process, initially all true, which a process sets to false when it begins the entry protocol and resets to true when it exits the critical section; (2) a second boolean array with one entry per process, initially all true, used during the entry protocol to signal readiness -- a process sets it to true when yielding priority and to false when asserting priority; (3) a single shared integer identifying one distinguished process, initially set to an arbitrary process. Each process also has a local temporary variable used to iterate over other processes during the entry protocol.
description.initial_state: Both boolean arrays have all entries set to true. The shared integer is set to an arbitrary process from the process set. All processes begin at the start of their non-critical section. Each process's local temporary variable is uninitialized.
description.actions: Each process cycles through these steps: (1) The process sets its first boolean flag to false, signaling it wants to enter the critical section. (2) The process checks whether it is the currently distinguished process (the shared integer). If not, it yields by setting its second boolean flag to true, then reads the distinguished process's first boolean flag: if that flag is true (the distinguished process is idle), the process claims the distinguished role by writing its own identity to the shared integer. It then loops back to recheck. (3) If the process is the distinguished process, it sets its second boolean flag to false, asserting priority. It then iterates over all other processes, checking each one's second boolean flag. If any other process also has its second flag set to false (also asserting priority), the process goes back to step 2. (4) If no other process is asserting priority, the process enters the critical section. (5) Upon exiting, the process resets its second boolean flag to true and its first boolean flag to true, then returns to the non-critical section.
description.safety_properties: Mutual exclusion: at most one process is in the critical section at any time.
description.liveness_properties: Deadlock freedom: if some process is trying to enter the critical section, then eventually some process (not necessarily the same one) enters the critical section. The algorithm is NOT starvation-free: it is possible for a process to wait indefinitely while other processes repeatedly enter the critical section.
description.model_bounds: The set of processes is declared as a constant. For model checking, it must be instantiated with a specific finite set (a 3-process model has about 90,000 reachable states; a 4-process model has about 33 million).
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process's next-state action, ensuring that no process halts permanently if it can always take a step. A stronger specification variant restricts fairness to apply only when the process is not in its non-critical section, allowing processes to remain in their non-critical sections indefinitely (modeling voluntary idleness). Under this stronger variant, a correspondingly stronger deadlock-freedom property is required that accounts for processes anywhere in the entry protocol, not just at the initial step.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Disk Synod (Disk Paxos) algorithm by Gafni and Lamport (2003), which implements distributed consensus using shared disks instead of separate acceptor processes. Processes communicate by reading and writing blocks on a set of shared disks. The algorithm operates in phases: a recovery phase (phase 0), a preparation phase (phase 1, analogous to Paxos phase 1), and an acceptance phase (phase 2, analogous to Paxos phase 2). Progress requires a majority of disks to be accessible, and the algorithm tolerates arbitrary process crashes.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of: (1) A set of N processes, each identified by a number, that propose values and attempt to reach consensus. Each process owns a unique set of ballot numbers. (2) A set of shared disks, where each disk stores a block for each process. Blocks contain a master ballot number, a ballot number, and an input value. (3) A majority quorum requirement on the disk set: any two sets of disks that each constitute a majority must overlap.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) Input mapping: each process's current proposed input value. (2) Output mapping: each process's output (either a chosen value or a no-output indicator). (3) Disk state: for each disk and each process, a block containing a master ballot number, a ballot number, and an input value (or a no-input indicator). (4) Phase: each process is in phase 0 (recovery), 1 (preparation), 2 (acceptance), or 3 (output produced). (5) A local disk block for each process, containing the same three fields as a disk block. (6) A set of disks written: which disks each process has written to in the current phase. (7) Blocks read: for each process and each disk, the set of blocks read from other processes on that disk.
description.initial_state: Each process starts with a nondeterministically chosen input value. All outputs are set to the no-output indicator. All disk blocks are initialized with zero ballot numbers and the no-input indicator. All processes start in phase 0. Each process's local disk block is initialized to zeroes and no-input. No disks have been written to. No blocks have been read.
description.actions: The protocol actions are: (1) Start ballot: A process in phase 1 or 2 begins a new ballot by selecting a ballot number higher than its current master ballot, resetting to phase 1, and clearing its written/read tracking. (2) Phase 1 or 2 write: A process writes its local disk block to a disk, recording the disk as written. (3) Phase 1 or 2 read: A process reads another process's block from a disk it has already written to. If the read block has a master ballot at least as high as the process's own, the process must start a new ballot. Otherwise, the block is recorded. (4) End phase 1: When a process has written to and read from a majority of disks, it sets its ballot equal to its master ballot and selects an input value -- either its own input (if no block with a non-initial input was read) or the input from the block with the highest ballot among those read. Then it advances to phase 2. (5) End phase 2: When the same majority condition is met, the process outputs its input value and advances to phase 3. (6) Fail: A process crashes, resets to phase 0 with a fresh input, clears its local block to the initial state, clears its output, and resets tracking state. Its data on the disks persists. (7) Phase 0 read: A recovering process reads its own block from a disk. (8) End phase 0: When the process has read its own block from a majority of disks, it selects a new ballot number higher than any master ballot it saw, restores the block with the highest ballot, sets the master ballot to the new one, and enters phase 1.
description.safety_properties: Consensus: The specification implements the abstract Synod specification, guaranteeing that at most one value is chosen, and all processes that output must output the same value. Any chosen value was originally proposed by some process.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: N processes, a finite set of valid inputs, a finite set of disks, and a majority predicate must be supplied as constants. Ballot numbers for each process must be disjoint positive natural numbers.
description.additional_assumptions: Each process has a unique set of ballot numbers, and these sets are pairwise disjoint. The majority quorum property is assumed: the full disk set is a majority, and any two majority subsets intersect. The specification extends the abstract Synod module and is proven to implement the Synod specification (DiskSynodSpec implies SynodSpec).

description.system_overview: This specification extends the Disk Synod (Disk Paxos) algorithm with a set of hierarchical invariants (HInv1 through HInv6) used for proving that the Disk Synod algorithm correctly implements the abstract Synod consensus specification. It adds auxiliary history variables to track the globally chosen value and the set of all inputs ever proposed, enabling the statement and checking of detailed inductive invariants.
description.actors_and_components: The same actors as DiskSynod: N processes communicating through shared disks. This module adds two auxiliary tracking variables for verification purposes: a record of the globally chosen consensus value and the accumulated set of all input values ever proposed by any process.
description.state_variables: All state variables from the DiskSynod specification (input, output, disk blocks, phase, local disk block, disks written, blocks read), plus: (1) A chosen value: initially a no-output indicator, set to the first value any process outputs and never changed afterward. (2) A set of all inputs: accumulates every input value any process has ever had, including after restarts.
description.initial_state: Same as DiskSynod, plus: the chosen value starts as the no-output indicator. The all-inputs set is initialized to the set of initial inputs across all processes.
description.actions: The next-state relation wraps the DiskSynod next-state relation, additionally updating: (1) The chosen value: if no value is chosen yet and some process produces output, the output of that process becomes the chosen value; otherwise the chosen value is unchanged. (2) The all-inputs set: augmented with any new input values from all processes.
description.safety_properties: Six hierarchical invariants are defined: HInv1 (type invariant): All variables have correct types. HInv2 (block invariants): All blocks associated with a process have ballots from that process's ballot set, ballot consistency (zero ballot if and only if no-input indicator), master ballot is at least as large as ballot, inputs come from the accumulated input set, and phase-specific constraints on disks written, blocks read, and block values. HInv3 (read consistency): If two processes in phases 1 or 2 have each read the other's block from the same disk, then at least one of them has the current version. HInv4 (ballot dominance): A non-phase-0 process's master ballot dominates all its blocks' ballots, and every majority set of disks contains a disk where the process's stored block has been superseded. HInv5 (value agreement): A phase-2 process either has the unique value at its ballot (no higher-ballot block disagrees) or has been superseded on a majority of disks. HInv6 (chosen value safety): If a value has been chosen, it satisfies the value-chosen predicate (a majority of disks lock it in), and all process outputs are either that value or the no-output indicator.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: Same constants as DiskSynod must be instantiated. For model checking, the invariants are checked as state predicates.
description.additional_assumptions: This module extends DiskSynod and inherits all its assumptions. The hierarchical invariants are intended to be proven inductively: each invariant depends on the previous ones. A majority set type is defined for use in the invariants.

description.system_overview: This specification models the abstract Synod consensus protocol, originally described by Lamport as the foundation for Paxos-family algorithms. The Synod protocol allows N processes to agree on a single chosen value from a set of possible inputs, even in the presence of process failures. A process can propose a value and may later output a chosen value, or it can fail and restart with a new input. The protocol guarantees that at most one value is ever chosen.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes (numbered 1 through N). Each process has an input value and can produce an output. An inner specification module tracks a global chosen value and the set of all input values ever proposed. Processes can choose (output a value) or fail (reset and start with a new input).
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) An input mapping from each process to its current proposed input value. (2) An output mapping from each process to either a chosen value or a special indicator meaning no output yet. Internally, the specification also tracks: (3) A chosen value (initially a special no-output indicator). (4) The set of all input values that any process has ever proposed (accumulated across failures and restarts).
description.initial_state: Each process starts with a nondeterministically chosen input from the set of valid inputs. All outputs are set to the no-output indicator. No value has been chosen yet. The set of all inputs is initialized to the set of initial inputs across all processes.
description.actions: Two actions per process: (1) Choose: A process that has not yet produced output selects a value to output. If no value has been globally chosen yet, the process nondeterministically selects any value from the set of all inputs ever proposed, sets that as the globally chosen value, and outputs it. If a value has already been chosen, the process outputs that value. (2) Fail: A process resets its output to the no-output indicator, nondeterministically selects a new input value from the valid inputs, and adds it to the accumulated set of all inputs. The chosen value is not affected by failures.
description.safety_properties: Consensus safety: At most one value is ever chosen. Any process that produces output must output the same chosen value. A chosen value must have been proposed by some process at some point.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: N is declared as a constant positive natural number. The set of valid inputs is a constant. For model checking, these must be instantiated with finite values.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses existential quantification over internal variables (the chosen value and accumulated input set) to hide implementation details. The Synod specification serves as an abstract specification that concrete algorithms (like DiskSynod) are proven to implement.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Echo algorithm for constructing a spanning tree in an undirected connected graph starting from a single initiator node. The Echo algorithm is a classical distributed algorithm where the initiator broadcasts explorer messages to all its neighbors, and each non-initiator node, upon receiving the first explorer message, designates the sender as its parent and forwards explorer messages to all remaining neighbors. Once a node has received responses from all its neighbors, it sends an acknowledgment back to its parent. When the initiator has collected responses from all neighbors, a spanning tree has been constructed. The algorithm was introduced in the context of distributed termination detection and network traversal.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of nodes arranged in an undirected, connected, irreflexive (no self-loops), symmetric graph. One distinguished node acts as the initiator and becomes the root of the spanning tree. All other nodes are non-initiator participants. Nodes communicate by sending and receiving messages through their graph edges. There are two types of messages: explorer messages (used to propagate the tree construction wave outward) and acknowledgment messages (used to confirm child relationships back toward the root).
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a message inbox for each node, holding the set of unprocessed messages (each tagged with a message type and sender identity); (2) a parent pointer for each node, indicating which neighbor is this node's parent in the spanning tree (initially a sentinel value meaning no parent); (3) a set of children for each node, recording which neighbors have acknowledged a child relationship; (4) a count of received messages for each node; (5) the set of neighbors for each node, derived from the graph topology; (6) a program counter for each node tracking its current execution phase.
description.initial_state: All message inboxes are empty. Every node's parent pointer is set to a sentinel value (no parent). Every node's children set is empty. Every node's received-message count is zero. Each node's neighbor set is computed from the graph structure. All nodes begin at the first phase of execution.
description.actions: The algorithm proceeds in three phases per node: (Phase 1) If the node is the initiator, it sends explorer messages to all its neighbors. Non-initiator nodes skip this step. (Phase 2) Each node loops, receiving one message at a time from its inbox. For a non-initiator receiving its very first message, that message must be an explorer; the sender is recorded as the node's parent, and the node sends explorer messages to all neighbors except the parent. For subsequent messages, the node simply consumes the message. If an acknowledgment message is received, the sender is added to the node's children set. The loop continues until the node has received a message from every neighbor. (Phase 3) After the loop, each non-initiator sends an acknowledgment message to its parent. The initiator does nothing in this phase. The algorithm terminates when all nodes have completed all three phases.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: parent pointers are always either a valid node or the sentinel value; children sets contain only valid nodes; received counts do not exceed the number of neighbors; messages are well-formed with valid types and senders that are neighbors. The initiator never acquires a parent. Every node's parent is one of its neighbors (or the sentinel). A node appears in another node's children set only if the latter is the first node's parent. At termination, the initiator is an ancestor of every other node and the ancestor relation is acyclic, confirming a valid spanning tree.
description.liveness_properties: Termination: eventually all nodes complete their execution.
description.model_bounds: The set of nodes, the identity of the initiator, and the graph adjacency relation are declared as constants. For model checking, these must be instantiated with a specific finite graph.
description.additional_assumptions: The graph must be connected (there is a path between any two nodes), symmetric (edges are undirected), and irreflexive (no node has an edge to itself). The connectivity assumption guarantees that a spanning tree including all nodes can be constructed. Communication is modeled as shared sets of messages (not ordered channels). Stuttering is allowed after termination to prevent spurious deadlock reports.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the Echo spanning tree algorithm. It extends the Echo specification and instantiates the constants with a small fully-connected graph of three nodes to enable exhaustive state-space exploration by a model checker.
description.actors_and_components: Same as the Echo specification: a set of nodes in an undirected connected graph with a single initiator. This module defines a concrete three-node graph and picks one node as the initiator.
description.state_variables: Inherits all state variables from the Echo specification. No additional state variables are introduced.
description.initial_state: Same as the Echo specification, instantiated with a three-node fully-meshed graph where every pair of distinct nodes is connected. One node is chosen deterministically as the initiator.
description.actions: Inherits all actions from the Echo specification without modification. A test variant of the specification is also provided that prints the graph adjacency relation to standard output at startup.
description.safety_properties: Inherits from the Echo specification: type correctness and the spanning tree ancestor properties (at termination, the initiator is an ancestor of all other nodes and the ancestor relation is acyclic).
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The node set consists of three string-valued nodes. The graph is fully meshed (every distinct pair of nodes is connected). The initiator is chosen deterministically from the node set. An alternative graph definition uses a nondeterministic choice of any connected, symmetric, irreflexive graph over the node set.
description.additional_assumptions: This module is designed for model checking only. The fully-meshed graph ensures all assumptions of the Echo specification (connectivity, symmetry, irreflexivity) are satisfied. A sentinel constant for the no-parent value is declared as a model value distinct from all nodes.

description.system_overview: This specification models Dijkstra's self-stabilizing token ring algorithm, published as EWD426. The algorithm arranges N nodes in a ring and ensures that, regardless of the initial configuration, the system eventually stabilizes to a state where exactly one token circulates. A token is implicitly defined by the relationship between the integer values held by neighboring nodes. This algorithm is historically significant as the first self-stabilizing algorithm, founding the field of self-stabilization in distributed computing. Dijkstra received the 2002 ACM PODC Influential Paper Award for this work.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N nodes numbered 0 through N-1 arranged in a unidirectional ring. Node 0 plays a special role as the token generator. All other nodes (1 through N-1) act as token passers that copy values from their predecessor.
description.state_variables: Each node maintains a single integer counter with values in the range 0 through M-1, where M is a system parameter. The presence of a token is not stored explicitly but is derived from the relationship between adjacent counters: for node 0, a token is present when its counter equals its predecessor's (node N-1) counter; for any other node i, a token is present when its counter differs from its predecessor's (node i-1) counter.
description.initial_state: Each node's counter is initialized to an arbitrary value in the range 0 through M-1. This models the self-stabilizing property: the algorithm must converge to a legitimate state from any arbitrary starting configuration.
description.actions: Node 0 (token creation): When node 0's counter equals node N-1's counter, node 0 increments its counter by one modulo M. This effectively creates a new token. Other nodes (token passing): When node i's counter differs from node i-1's counter, node i copies node i-1's counter value. This effectively passes the token forward along the ring. Only one node acts at a time (interleaving semantics).
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: all counters remain in the range 0 through M-1.
description.liveness_properties: Stabilization: the system eventually reaches and remains in a state where exactly one token exists in the ring. This is expressed as an eventually-always property on the unique token predicate. The unique token state means there exists a position in the ring such that all counters before that position equal the first node's counter and all counters from that position onward equal one less than the first node's counter (modulo M).
description.model_bounds: N (number of nodes) and M (counter value range) are declared as constants. Both must be positive integers, and M must be at least N (the relationship N is at most M+1 is required for stabilization to be guaranteed). For model checking, typical values are N=6, M=6.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on the combined next-state relation, ensuring that if any node can act, eventually some node will act. The constraint M >= N is essential: if M < N, cyclic configurations can persist indefinitely and the system may never stabilize.

description.system_overview: This specification models the basic thermocycling process of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), a biochemical technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA. PCR works by repeatedly cycling through three temperature-dependent phases: denaturation (high heat separates double-stranded DNA into single-stranded templates), annealing (cooling allows short primer sequences to bind to complementary sites on the templates, forming primer-template hybrids), and extension (at medium temperature, a polymerase enzyme extends the hybrids into new double-stranded DNA). Each cycle approximately doubles the amount of DNA, producing exponential growth that eventually follows an S-curve as primers are depleted.
description.actors_and_components: The system has no concurrent actors. It models a single reaction vessel undergoing temperature cycling. The key molecular components tracked are: double-stranded DNA molecules, single-stranded template molecules, short primer molecules, and primer-template hybrid molecules.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five quantities: (1) the current temperature phase, which cycles through three levels representing extension temperature, denaturation temperature, and an intermediate cooling step; (2) the count of available primer molecules; (3) the count of double-stranded DNA molecules; (4) the count of single-stranded template molecules; (5) the count of primer-template hybrid molecules.
description.initial_state: The temperature is at the extension level. The primer count equals a constant representing the initial primer stock. The DNA count equals a constant representing the initial DNA stock. There are no templates and no hybrids, since all DNA starts in double-stranded form.
description.actions: Four actions model the PCR cycle: (1) Heating: raises temperature from extension level to denaturation level. All double-stranded DNA and hybrids are denatured into single-stranded templates. Primers from denatured hybrids are recovered. (2) Cooling: lowers temperature from denaturation level to extension level. No molecular changes occur. (3) Annealing: lowers temperature from extension level to the annealing level. A nondeterministically chosen number of primers bind to available templates, consuming both and producing that many hybrids. The number bound is between 1 and the minimum of available primers and templates. (4) Extension: raises temperature from annealing level to extension level. All hybrids are converted to double-stranded DNA.
description.safety_properties: Primer counts are always non-negative. Conservation of molecular material: the total count of templates plus primers plus twice the count of double-stranded DNA and hybrids remains constant throughout all transitions, equaling the initial primer stock plus twice the initial DNA stock.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED. A primer depletion property (eventually all primers are consumed) is defined but explicitly noted as not holding in general, because the system can stutter or cycle without consuming all primers.
description.model_bounds: The initial DNA count and initial primer count are declared as constants. For model checking, typical values are 5 for each.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification abstracts from many biological details: nucleotide supply is assumed unlimited, primer binding is nondeterministic (any number up to the available minimum may bind in a single annealing step), DNA re-annealing during cooling is neglected, and extension is assumed to complete for all available hybrids. Two types of primers are required in real PCR but the specification does not distinguish between them. No fairness assumptions are made on the temperature cycling, so the system may stutter indefinitely.

description.system_overview: This specification further refines the PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) model by distinguishing between different lengths of DNA molecules produced during amplification. In real PCR, the first few cycles produce DNA strands of varying lengths because polymerase extends primers to the end of the template. Only after several cycles does the target-length product (bounded by both primer sites) begin to accumulate exponentially. This specification tracks long, short, and target-length variants of templates, hybrids, and double-stranded DNA separately, providing a high-resolution view of PCR amplification dynamics.
description.actors_and_components: The system has no concurrent actors. It models a single PCR reaction vessel. The molecular components are classified by length: long templates (original-length single strands), short templates (one-primer-bounded), and target-length (tiny) templates (bounded by both primers), with corresponding hybrid and double-stranded categories. The desired product is the target-length double-stranded DNA.
description.state_variables: The system tracks fifteen quantities: (1) temperature phase; (2) stage indicator (initial, denatured, ready, annealed, extended); (3) cycle counter; (4) available primer count; (5-7) three categories of single-stranded templates: long, short, and target-length; (8-10) three categories of primer-template hybrids: long, short, and target-length; (11-14) four categories of double-stranded DNA: long-long (original), short-long, target-short, and target-target (the desired product).
description.initial_state: Temperature is at extension level. Stage is initial. Cycle counter is zero. Primer count equals the initial constant. The long-long double-stranded DNA count equals the initial DNA constant. All other molecular counts (all template types, all hybrid types, short-long doubles, target-short doubles, and product) are zero.
description.actions: Four actions model the PCR cycle with length-differentiated molecular tracking: (1) Heating: denatures all four double-strand categories and all three hybrid categories into their component single strands. Long-long doubles produce two long templates; short-long doubles produce one long and one short template; target-short doubles produce one short and one target-length template; product doubles produce two target-length templates. Primers are recovered from all denatured hybrids. (2) Cooling: lowers temperature from denaturation to ready. No molecular changes. (3) Annealing: primers bind to available templates. A nondeterministic total number of primers are consumed, distributed across the three template categories. Each template type produces the corresponding hybrid type. (4) Extension: each long hybrid becomes a short-long double-strand, each short hybrid becomes a target-short double-strand, and each target-length hybrid becomes a product molecule. The cycle counter increments.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: all molecular counts, temperature, stage, and cycle counter are within their expected domains. No target-length product is produced before the third cycle.
description.liveness_properties: Primer depletion: eventually all primers are consumed (inherited from the stages refinement via a refinement mapping).
description.model_bounds: Initial DNA and primer counts are declared as constants. For model checking, typical values are 5 for each. Deadlock checking is disabled.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on all four actions. This module refines the stages specification: a refinement mapping shows that the sum of all template types corresponds to the template count in the stages model, and similarly for hybrids and double-strands. The key insight modeled is that target-length product only begins to appear after two full cycles of amplification, as short templates must first be created from long templates before target-length strands can emerge.

description.system_overview: This specification refines the basic PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) model by adding a stage-tracking history variable and a cycle counter. In the basic model, temperature transitions could occur in any order; this refinement constrains them to follow the correct thermocycling sequence: denaturation, cooling, annealing, extension. The stage variable records the most recent completed phase, ensuring that each phase can only execute when the preceding phase has been completed. This enables counting the number of complete PCR cycles and proving that primers are eventually depleted.
description.actors_and_components: The system has no concurrent actors. It models a single PCR reaction vessel. The molecular components are the same as in the basic model: double-stranded DNA, single-stranded templates, primers, and primer-template hybrids.
description.state_variables: The system tracks seven quantities: (1) the current temperature phase (three levels as in the basic model); (2) the count of available primers; (3) the count of double-stranded DNA molecules; (4) the count of single-stranded templates; (5) the count of primer-template hybrids; (6) a stage indicator recording which phase was most recently completed, taking values from: initial, denatured, ready (cooled), annealed, or extended; (7) a cycle counter tracking how many complete PCR cycles have been executed.
description.initial_state: Temperature is at extension level. Primer and DNA counts equal their respective initial constants. Templates and hybrids are zero. The stage is set to the initial value. The cycle counter is zero.
description.actions: Four actions model the constrained PCR cycle: (1) Heating: enabled only when the stage is initial or extended. Raises temperature, denatures all DNA and hybrids into templates, recovers primers from hybrids. Sets stage to denatured. (2) Cooling: enabled only when the stage is denatured. Lowers temperature. No molecular changes. Sets stage to ready. (3) Annealing: enabled only when the stage is ready. A nondeterministic number of primers bind to templates, forming hybrids. Sets stage to annealed. (4) Extension: enabled only when the stage is annealed. All hybrids become double-stranded DNA. Increments the cycle counter. Sets stage to extended. The molecular transformations in each action are identical to the basic model.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: temperature, molecular counts, stage indicator, and cycle counter are all within their expected domains.
description.liveness_properties: Primer depletion: eventually all primers are consumed. This property holds in this refinement (unlike the basic model) because weak fairness on all four actions ensures continuous cycling, and each cycle consumes at least one primer.
description.model_bounds: Initial DNA and primer counts are declared as constants. For model checking, typical values are 5 for each. Deadlock checking is disabled because the system reaches a terminal state when primers are exhausted.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on all four temperature-cycling actions, ensuring that the system continuously progresses through PCR cycles and does not stutter indefinitely. This module refines the basic PCR specification: every behavior of this specification is also a behavior of the basic model.
