The stage variable acts as a history variable constraining the order of operations without changing the molecular dynamics.

description.system_overview: This specification models Lamport's distributed mutual-exclusion algorithm, which appeared as an example in the foundational paper 'Time, Clocks and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System' (Communications of the ACM, volume 21, number 7, pages 558-565, 1978). The algorithm allows a set of processes to coordinate access to a critical section using logical clocks and message passing over pairwise FIFO communication channels, without relying on shared memory.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a parameterized number of processes. Each process has its own local logical clock and communicates with every other process through dedicated point-to-point FIFO message channels. Three types of messages are exchanged: request messages (carrying the sender's clock value), acknowledgment messages, and release messages.
description.state_variables: The system tracks five pieces of state: (1) a local clock value for each process, (2) a table recording the clock value associated with each request that each process has received from every other process (zero if no pending request), (3) a set of acknowledgments each process has collected from other processes, (4) the message queues for every ordered pair of processes representing the pairwise FIFO network, and (5) the set of processes currently in the critical section.
description.initial_state: All process clocks start at one. No requests have been recorded (all entries are zero). No acknowledgments have been collected (all sets are empty). All message channels are empty. No process is in the critical section.
description.actions: A process can perform one of six actions: (1) Request access to the critical section by recording its own clock value and broadcasting a request to all other processes. (2) Receive a request from another process, record the request's clock value, update the local clock to be at least one more than the received clock, and send an acknowledgment back. (3) Receive an acknowledgment from another process and add that process to the acknowledgment set. (4) Enter the critical section, which requires having received acknowledgments from all processes and having a request with higher priority (lower clock, with process identifier as tiebreaker) than all other pending requests. (5) Exit the critical section by broadcasting a release message, clearing the process's own request, and resetting its acknowledgment set. (6) Receive a release message from another process and clear that process's request record.
description.safety_properties: The primary safety property is mutual exclusion: at most one process may be in the critical section at any given time. Additionally, a type correctness invariant ensures all variables remain within their expected domains, and a bounded network property states that no communication channel ever contains more than three messages.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The specification parameterizes the number of processes and includes a maximum clock bound used as a state constraint for finite-state model checking. Clock values must not exceed this bound during exploration.
description.additional_assumptions: Communication channels are pairwise FIFO: messages between any pair of processes are delivered in the order they were sent. The algorithm relies on Lamport's logical clock mechanism to establish a total ordering of events across the distributed system.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Non-Blocking Atomic Commitment (NBAC) protocol with crash failures, based on Raynal's 1997 case study of agreement problems in distributed systems. The protocol allows N processes to agree on committing or aborting a distributed transaction. Each process votes YES or NO, and the group must reach a consistent decision. The protocol uses an unreliable failure detector that may nondeterministically report whether some process has crashed.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes (numbered 1 through N) that communicate via message passing. Each process independently votes, sends its vote to all others, receives votes, and decides to commit or abort. A failure detector provides each process with a (potentially unreliable) indication of whether any process has crashed. Processes can crash at any point, after which they take no further steps.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) A program counter for each process, indicating its current phase: voting YES, voting NO, vote sent, decided to abort, decided to commit, or crashed. (2) A set of received messages for each process, where each message is a pair of a sender identifier and a vote value (YES or NO). (3) A global set of sent messages (pairs of sender and vote value) representing the messages available in the network. (4) A failure detector output for each process: a boolean indicating whether the process currently suspects some process has crashed.
description.initial_state: No messages have been sent (empty set). Each process starts with a nondeterministic initial vote of either YES or NO (its program counter is set to YES or NO accordingly). No process has received any messages (empty set for each). The failure detector output is nondeterministically initialized for each process.
description.actions: Each process can take one step per transition, consisting of receiving messages, updating the failure detector, and performing one of these actions: (1) Vote YES: If the process's current state is YES, it sends a YES message (adds the pair of its identifier and YES to the sent set) and moves to the sent state. (2) Vote NO: If the process's current state is NO, it sends a NO message and moves to the sent state. (3) Crash: A non-crashed process moves to the crashed state. No new messages are sent. (4) Decide after sending: If the process has sent its vote, it evaluates: (a) If the failure detector reports a suspected crash, the process aborts. (b) If any received message contains a NO vote, the process aborts. (c) If the failure detector reports no suspected crash AND the process has received YES votes from all N processes, the process commits. (5) Do nothing: The process does not change state (to avoid deadlock when no other action is enabled). Message reception is modeled as nondeterministically selecting a subset of sent messages that includes all previously received messages. The failure detector nondeterministically updates its output at each step.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: Sent messages are pairs of process identifiers and vote values. Program counters are in the valid state set. Received sets are subsets of valid message pairs. Failure detector outputs are booleans. Validity: If some process initially voted NO, then no process ever commits.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: N = 2 processes for model checking.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on the combined action of receiving messages plus voting (YES or NO) or deciding, ensuring that non-crashed processes eventually make progress. Crash transitions are not subject to fairness. The failure detector is completely nondeterministic in this specification -- it may switch between suspecting and not suspecting at each step. An alternative initial state where all processes vote YES is also defined but not used as the main specification.

description.system_overview: This specification models an asynchronous non-blocking atomic commitment algorithm with failure detectors, based on Guerraoui's 2001 paper on the hardness of failure-sensitive agreement problems. The protocol allows N processes to vote YES or NO and reach a consistent commit or abort decision. It uses a threshold-based counting abstraction rather than explicit message sets: instead of tracking individual messages, it counts how many YES and NO messages have been sent and received. Processes may crash, and a failure detector reports suspected crashes.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes (numbered 1 through N). Each process votes, sends its vote, receives vote counts, and decides to commit or abort. A failure detector provides each process with a boolean indicating whether it suspects some process has crashed. Crashed processes (marked with a special status) no longer participate but their unsent votes contribute to upper bounds on possible messages.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) The total count of NO messages sent by correct (non-crashed) processes. (2) The total count of YES messages sent by correct processes. (3) An upper bound on the number of NO messages that crashed processes might have sent (incremented when a process that voted NO crashes before sending). (4) An upper bound on the number of YES messages that crashed processes might have sent (incremented when a process that voted YES crashes before sending). (5) For each process, the count of YES messages it has received so far. (6) For each process, the count of NO messages it has received so far. (7) A failure detector output for each process (boolean). (8) A program counter for each process indicating its state: voting YES, voting NO, vote sent, decided abort, decided commit, or crashed.
description.initial_state: No messages have been sent or received (all counters are zero). Each process starts with a nondeterministic initial vote of YES or NO. The failure detector output is nondeterministically initialized for each process.
description.actions: Process actions: (1) Crash: A non-crashed process crashes. If it had not yet sent its vote, the upper bound for its vote type (YES or NO) is incremented, accounting for the possibility that it might have sent before crashing. (2) Receive: A process that has sent its vote can receive one message at a time. If its received YES count is below the sum of sent YES messages plus the upper bound from crashed processes, it can receive one more YES. Similarly for NO. If all available messages have been received, the process does nothing (to avoid deadlock). (3) Send YES: A process whose vote is YES and whose failure detector does not suspect a crash sends its vote (incrementing the sent YES count) and transitions to the sent state. (4) Send NO: Same as send YES but for NO votes. (5) Abort before sending: If a process's failure detector suspects a crash and the process has not yet sent its vote (still in YES or NO state), it immediately aborts. (6) Abort after sending: If a process has sent its vote and has received at least one NO message, it aborts. (7) Commit: If a process has sent its vote, has received zero NO messages, and has received at least N YES messages, it commits. (8) Do nothing: An unchanged-variables transition to prevent deadlock after deciding.
description.safety_properties: Agreement: No two correct processes decide differently -- it is impossible for one to commit while another aborts. Abort validity: If some process votes NO, then no process ever commits. Commit validity: If all processes vote YES and no failure is suspected, then no process crashes or aborts. Type invariant: All counters are in valid ranges (0 to N), received counts are bounded by sent counts plus upper bounds, program counters are in valid states, and failure detector outputs are booleans.
description.liveness_properties: Termination: If no process ever crashes and no process is ever suspected by the failure detector, then eventually every process reaches a decision (commit or abort).
description.model_bounds: N = 3 processes for model checking.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed on the combined receive, send, abort, and commit actions, ensuring non-crashed processes eventually make progress. Crash transitions and the do-nothing transition are not subject to fairness. The specification also defines two alternative initial conditions: one where all processes vote YES and one where all processes vote NO, each with its own specification formula. The failure detector satisfies two properties: every faulty process is permanently suspected, and no process is suspected unless it actually crashes. The counting abstraction makes the state space finite without requiring explicit message tracking.

description.system_overview: This specification models a distributed spanning tree construction algorithm. Starting from a designated root node, the algorithm builds a spanning tree over a network of processes connected by a given neighbor relation. Each non-root process that receives a message from a neighbor adopts that neighbor as its parent, thereby joining the tree. Processes propagate messages to their neighbors, and eventually every reachable process has a parent linking it back toward the root.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of processes connected by a static neighbor relation. One distinguished process serves as the root of the spanning tree. A special sentinel value represents the absence of a parent assignment. Processes communicate by sending messages (modeled as pairs of sender and receiver) through a shared message pool.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) a parent assignment for each process, initially set to a sentinel indicating no parent, (2) a report flag for each process indicating whether it has reported its parent assignment, and (3) a set of messages that have been sent between processes.
description.initial_state: All processes start with no parent assigned (set to the sentinel value). No process has reported. The message set is empty.
description.actions: There are three main actions: (1) Update: a non-root process that has no parent and receives a message from a neighbor adopts that neighbor as its parent. (2) Send: a process that is either the root or already has a parent sends a message to a neighbor it has not yet contacted. (3) Report (Parent): a process that has a parent and has not yet reported sets its report flag to true. At each step, a pair of processes is chosen, and if the first is a non-root with no parent that has a pending message from the second, an update occurs; otherwise one of the other actions or a stutter step is taken.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness ensures parent assignments respect the neighbor relation, report flags are boolean, and messages are pairs of processes. Once a process has a parent, it keeps that same parent forever (one-parent stability). A sent-message property ensures that processes without parents do not appear as senders in the message set.
description.liveness_properties: Under weak fairness, the algorithm terminates: eventually every non-root process has a parent that is a valid neighbor.
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.additional_assumptions: The neighbor relation is given as a static set of ordered pairs of processes. The algorithm assumes the network is connected from the root through the neighbor relation so that all processes are reachable.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the TCP connection state machine specification. It extends the TCP specification and provides a restricted initial state and action constraints that make the state space finite and amenable to exhaustive model checking. Instead of starting from the CLOSED state, one peer begins in SYN-SENT (having already performed an active open) and the other begins in LISTEN (having already performed a passive open), with the corresponding SYN segment already in flight.
description.actors_and_components: Same as the TCP specification: exactly two peers communicating over ordered network queues. This module names the two peers as specific constants and defines a symmetry set for them.
description.state_variables: Inherits all state variables from the TCP specification. No additional state variables are introduced.
description.initial_state: One peer starts in SYN-SENT and the other in LISTEN, both with their transmission control blocks created. The listening peer's network queue contains a single SYN segment (the one sent by the active opener). The active opener's queue is empty. This models a scenario where one active open and one passive open have already occurred.
description.actions: Inherits all actions from the TCP specification, with two additional constraints: (1) A no-retransmission constraint prevents consecutive identical messages in any peer's network queue. (2) A single-active-open constraint prevents any further active open, passive open, or send user commands, since the initial open is already accounted for in the initial state. These constraints bound the state space to make model checking feasible.
description.safety_properties: Inherits from the TCP specification: connection state consistency (when no messages are in flight and one peer is established, the other must also be established) and type correctness.
description.liveness_properties: Inherits from the TCP specification: a peer in SYN-SENT eventually reaches ESTABLISHED, LISTEN, or CLOSED.
description.model_bounds: The two peers are instantiated as specific named constants. Symmetry reduction over the two peers is defined but commented out (must be disabled for liveness checking). The initial state constrains one peer to SYN-SENT and the other to LISTEN. Action constraints prevent additional connection opens and message retransmission to keep the state space finite.
description.additional_assumptions: This module is designed for model checking only. It assumes exactly one connection lifecycle starting from a specific point (one active open already completed). The no-retransmission constraint and single-active-open constraint are modeling simplifications to ensure finite state exploration. Symmetry reduction is available but must be disabled when checking liveness properties.

description.system_overview: This specification models the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection state machine as defined in RFC 9293. It abstracts from low-level details such as sequence numbers and focuses on the state transitions of two communicating peers. The model captures the full lifecycle of a TCP connection: establishment via the three-way handshake (both active and passive open), data transfer in the established state, and connection teardown via FIN exchange, as well as reset handling.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of exactly two peers that communicate over a network. Each peer maintains its own connection state and a transmission control block (a boolean indicating whether the connection context exists). The network is modeled as a pair of ordered message queues, one per peer, carrying protocol segments. User commands (active open, passive open, close, send) drive the peers, while the system responds to incoming segments.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) a boolean per peer indicating whether the transmission control block (connection context) exists; (2) a connection state per peer, drawn from the eleven TCP states: CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSING, CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK, and TIME-WAIT; (3) an ordered sequence of in-flight messages per peer, where each message is one of: SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK, RST, FIN, or ACK-of-FIN.
description.initial_state: Both peers start in the CLOSED state. Neither peer has a transmission control block. Both network queues are empty.
description.actions: User commands: (a) Passive open: a closed peer creates a transmission control block and moves to the LISTEN state. (b) Active open: a closed peer creates a transmission control block, sends a SYN segment to the remote peer, and moves to SYN-SENT. (c) Send: a listening peer sends a SYN and moves to SYN-SENT. (d) Close: depending on current state, a peer either deletes its control block (from LISTEN or SYN-SENT), sends a FIN (from SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, or CLOSE-WAIT), and transitions accordingly. System responses: (a) A peer in SYN-SENT that receives a SYN responds with SYN+ACK and moves to SYN-RECEIVED; if it receives SYN+ACK it responds with ACK and moves to ESTABLISHED. (b) A peer in SYN-RECEIVED that receives RST returns to LISTEN; receiving ACK moves it to ESTABLISHED. (c) A listening peer that receives SYN responds with SYN+ACK and moves to SYN-RECEIVED. (d) An established peer that receives FIN sends ACK-of-FIN and moves to CLOSE-WAIT. (e) Connection teardown proceeds through FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, and TIME-WAIT states with appropriate FIN and ACK-of-FIN exchanges. (f) Reset handling: any peer with a control block can send RST and move to TIME-WAIT; any peer receiving RST transitions to either LISTEN or CLOSED. (g) A combined transition handles receiving both FIN and ACK-of-FIN simultaneously, skipping the CLOSING state and going directly to TIME-WAIT.
description.safety_properties: Connection state consistency: when both network queues are empty and one peer is in the established state, the other peer must also be in the established state. Type correctness: control blocks are boolean, connection states are valid TCP states, and network queues contain only valid segment types.
description.liveness_properties: Progress: if a peer enters the SYN-SENT state, it eventually reaches either ESTABLISHED, LISTEN, or CLOSED.
description.model_bounds: The number of peers is fixed at exactly two. The set of segment types is fixed. For model checking, peers are instantiated as two specific constants.
description.additional_assumptions: The model abstracts from sequence numbers, window management, retransmission timers, and data transfer. Weak fairness is assumed on system transitions and on the close-from-SYN-SENT user command (to prevent a peer from being stuck in SYN-SENT indefinitely). The TIME-WAIT to CLOSED transition abstracts the 2*MSL timeout. Messages are delivered in order (FIFO queues) but the model does not include message loss or reordering.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Tower of Hanoi puzzle using sequences of integers to represent each tower. The Tower of Hanoi is a mathematical puzzle with three rods and a number of disks of different sizes. All disks start stacked in ascending order of size on one rod (smallest at top). The objective is to move the entire stack to the third rod, moving only one disk at a time and never placing a larger disk on top of a smaller one. The minimum number of moves for n disks is 2^n - 1.
description.actors_and_components: There are no concurrent actors. The system is a single-player puzzle with exactly three towers (positions) where disks can be placed.
description.state_variables: The system maintains a tuple of three sequences, one per tower. Each sequence represents a stack of disks on that tower, ordered from top to bottom (the first element is the topmost, smallest disk). Each disk is represented by a natural number indicating its size. The total number of disks across all three towers remains constant throughout execution.
description.initial_state: The three towers are initialized with configurable starting sequences. The typical configuration places all disks on the first tower in ascending size order (e.g., the sequence 1,2,3 for three disks) with the other two towers empty.
description.actions: A single move action selects a source tower and a destination tower (which must be different). The move is valid if the source tower is not empty and either the destination tower is empty or the top disk of the source tower is smaller than the top disk of the destination tower. When a move occurs, the top disk is removed from the source tower and placed on top of the destination tower.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: the system always has exactly three towers, each being a sequence of natural numbers. Element conservation: the set of disk sizes present across all towers equals the original set of disk sizes. Total count conservation: the total number of disks across all towers remains constant.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED. The specification does not assert liveness. The puzzle is solved by checking whether the negation of the solved state is an invariant; a counterexample trace shows the solution. The solved state is when the first two towers are empty and the third tower contains all disks in ascending order.
description.model_bounds: The initial tower configurations are declared as constants (three sequences). For model checking, typical values are a sequence of 1 through n on the first tower and empty sequences for the other two.
description.additional_assumptions: Unlike the bitwise variant of this puzzle, this specification represents disks explicitly as integer sizes in sequences, making the ordering constraint straightforward to check. The specification models exactly three towers (not configurable). All legal moves are explored nondeterministically; no solving strategy is imposed.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Tower of Hanoi puzzle using a bitwise representation of disk positions. The Tower of Hanoi is a mathematical puzzle consisting of a configurable number of disks of distinct sizes and a configurable number of towers (pegs). All disks start stacked on the first tower in order of size (largest at the bottom). The objective is to move all disks to the last tower, subject to the constraint that only one disk may be moved at a time and no disk may be placed on top of a smaller disk. The minimum number of moves to solve an n-disk puzzle is 2^n - 1.
description.actors_and_components: There are no concurrent actors. The system is a single-player puzzle. The components are D disks of sizes that are powers of two (1, 2, 4, ..., 2^(D-1)) and N towers.
description.state_variables: The system maintains an array of N tower values, one per tower. Each tower's value is a natural number whose binary representation encodes which disks are on that tower: bit position k is set if the disk of size 2^k is present on that tower. A tower value of zero means the tower is empty. The sum of all tower values always equals 2^D - 1 (all disks are accounted for).
description.initial_state: All disks are on the first tower (its value is 2^D - 1, meaning all bits are set). All other towers are empty (value zero).
description.actions: A single move action selects a disk (which must be a power of two), a source tower, and a destination tower. The move is valid if: (1) the disk is on the source tower (the corresponding bit is set), (2) the disk is the smallest disk on the source tower (all lower-order bits are zero), and (3) the destination tower has no disk smaller than the one being moved (all lower-order bits are zero) or is empty. When a move occurs, the disk's value is subtracted from the source tower and added to the destination tower.
description.safety_properties: Conservation: the sum of all tower values equals 2^D - 1 at all times (no disks are created or destroyed). Type correctness: all tower values are natural numbers less than 2^D.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED. The specification does not assert liveness. Instead, the puzzle is solved by checking whether the negation of the goal state (all disks on the last tower) is an invariant; a counterexample trace produced by the model checker demonstrates the solution.
description.model_bounds: D (number of disks) and N (number of towers) are declared as constants. For model checking, typical values are D=3 and N=3, which requires 7 moves to solve.
description.additional_assumptions: Disks are represented as powers of two, and tower state is encoded as the sum of present disk values. Bitwise AND is used to test disk presence and ordering constraints; this requires a custom operator module that implements bitwise AND either in pure arithmetic or via a Java override class. The specification does not enforce a strategy; all legal moves are explored nondeterministically.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Transaction Commit protocol, which defines the requirements for a set of resource managers participating in a distributed transaction to reach agreement on whether to commit or abort. It captures the fundamental safety properties that any transaction commit implementation (such as two-phase commit or Paxos commit) must satisfy.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of resource managers (RMs), each of which independently decides whether to prepare (vote to commit) or abort. There is no explicit coordinator; the specification describes the allowed behaviors of the resource managers themselves.
description.state_variables: The system tracks a single mapping from each resource manager to its current state, which can be one of four values: working (initial, has not yet voted), prepared (voted to commit), committed (final commit decision), or aborted (final abort decision).
description.initial_state: Every resource manager starts in the working state.
description.actions: Two types of actions can occur for each resource manager: (1) Prepare: A resource manager that is currently working transitions to the prepared state, indicating it votes to commit. (2) Decide: A resource manager makes a final decision. It may commit if it is prepared and every resource manager in the system is either prepared or already committed. It may abort if it is working or prepared and no resource manager has yet committed. These conditions ensure that a commit decision is only possible when all participants have prepared, and an abort is only possible before any participant has committed.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: every resource manager is always in one of the four valid states. Consistency: it is impossible for one resource manager to be in the aborted state while another is in the committed state. Together these guarantee that all resource managers that reach a final decision agree on the outcome.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The set of resource managers is declared as a constant. For model checking, it is typically instantiated with a small finite set such as three resource managers.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification describes only safety properties. It does not require that any action eventually be taken (no fairness conditions). The specification serves as a correctness criterion: more detailed protocols such as two-phase commit are shown to implement this specification via refinement.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Two-Phase Commit protocol, in which a transaction manager (TM) coordinates a set of resource managers (RMs) to reach agreement on whether to commit or abort a distributed transaction. The protocol implements the abstract transaction commit specification by adding an explicit coordinator and message-passing communication. Only safety properties are specified; liveness (progress) is not modeled.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a transaction manager and a finite set of resource managers that communicate by message passing. The transaction manager collects preparation votes from RMs, makes a global commit-or-abort decision, and broadcasts the result. Resource managers independently prepare (vote to commit) or choose to abort, and act on the transaction manager's decision when it arrives.
description.state_variables: The system tracks four pieces of state: (1) A mapping from each resource manager to its current state (working, prepared, committed, or aborted). (2) The transaction manager's state (initial, committed, or aborted). (3) The set of resource managers from which the transaction manager has received preparation messages. (4) The set of all messages that have ever been sent, which grows monotonically and is never reduced. Messages are of three types: a preparation message identifying a specific resource manager, a commit broadcast, or an abort broadcast.
description.initial_state: All resource managers are in the working state. The transaction manager is in its initial state. No resource managers have been recorded as prepared by the transaction manager. No messages have been sent.
description.actions: The transaction manager has three actions: (1) Receive prepared: while in its initial state, record that a specific RM has sent a preparation message. (2) Commit: if the TM is in its initial state and has received preparation messages from every RM, transition to committed and broadcast a commit message. (3) Abort: if the TM is in its initial state, transition to aborted and broadcast an abort message. Each resource manager has four actions: (1) Prepare: a working RM transitions to prepared and sends a preparation message to the TM. (2) Choose to abort: a working RM spontaneously transitions to aborted without sending any message. (3) Receive commit: upon seeing a commit broadcast, an RM transitions to committed. (4) Receive abort: upon seeing an abort broadcast, an RM transitions to aborted.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: all state variables remain within their declared types at all times. The protocol implements the abstract transaction commit specification, meaning the consistency invariant holds: no resource manager is aborted while another is committed.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The set of resource managers is a constant. For model checking, it is typically instantiated with three resource managers.
description.additional_assumptions: Messages are modeled as a set that only grows; messages are never removed or lost. An action that in a real implementation would be triggered by receiving a message is here enabled by the existence of that message in the sent set. This simplification is valid because only safety properties are specified: there is no requirement that messages be received, so message loss and non-receipt are indistinguishable. The specification imports the abstract transaction commit module and asserts refinement: the two-phase commit protocol implements the abstract specification. Abort messages from RMs to the TM are omitted for simplicity; the TM's spontaneous abort action represents this.

description.system_overview: This specification models a modified Two-Phase Commit protocol with a Backup Transaction Manager (BTM). When the primary transaction manager fails after making a decision, the BTM can take over and finalize the transaction, preventing the blocking problem inherent in standard two-phase commit. The specification is written in PlusCal and translated to TLA+, modeling both resource manager and transaction manager failures.
description.actors_and_components: The system has three types of processes: (1) A set of resource managers that prepare, commit, abort, or fail. (2) A primary transaction manager that decides to commit or abort the transaction, and may fail after deciding. (3) A backup transaction manager that activates when the primary TM has failed and takes over the decision-making role using the same commit/abort logic.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) A mapping from each resource manager to its current state, which can be working, prepared, committed, aborted, or failed. (2) The transaction manager's state, which can be initial, commit, abort, or hidden (representing failure after a decision). (3) A program counter for each process tracking its current control location.
description.initial_state: All resource managers are in the working state. The transaction manager is in its initial state. All process program counters are at their starting labels.
description.actions: Resource managers loop while working or prepared, and in each iteration nondeterministically choose one of three actions: (1) Prepare: transition from working to prepared. (2) Decide: if the TM has decided to commit, transition to committed; or if still working or the TM has decided to abort, transition to aborted. (3) Fail: if RM failure is enabled and no other RM has already failed, transition to failed. The primary TM nondeterministically chooses to commit or abort: it commits if all RMs are prepared (or any RM is already committed), and aborts if any RM is aborted or failed and no RM has committed. After deciding, if TM failure is enabled, the TM transitions to the hidden state (simulating a crash). The backup TM activates only when the primary TM is in the hidden state: it then makes the same commit or abort decision using identical logic and sets the TM state accordingly.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: each RM is always in one of the five valid states and the TM is always in one of the four valid states. Consistency: no two resource managers may be in conflicting final states (one committed and another aborted).
description.liveness_properties: Termination: all processes eventually reach a terminal state. This is guaranteed by weak fairness on all processes, including the BTM which ensures progress when the primary TM fails.
description.model_bounds: The set of resource managers is a constant, typically three. Two boolean constants control whether RM failure and TM failure are enabled.
description.additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for all processes (resource managers, primary TM, and backup TM). The model assumes clean crash failures, not Byzantine behavior. The BTM does not fail. At most one RM may fail at a time. The specification uses PlusCal with explicit program counter labels for each step. The commit condition accounts for the case where the primary TM committed and an RM learned the decision before the TM failed, allowing the BTM to also commit. Stuttering is allowed when all processes have terminated to prevent false deadlock detection.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Paxos Commit algorithm, which achieves fault-tolerant distributed transaction commit by running a separate Paxos consensus instance for each resource manager's prepare-or-abort decision. It replaces the single coordinator of two-phase commit with a set of acceptors and a leader, tolerating F failures among 2F+1 acceptors. The classic two-phase commit protocol is obtained as the special case with a single acceptor (F=0). Only safety properties are specified.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of three types of participants: (1) Resource managers that prepare or abort, and act on the global commit/abort decision. (2) Acceptors that participate in multiple Paxos consensus instances (one per RM) by processing phase 1 and phase 2 messages. (3) Leaders that coordinate ballot rounds by sending phase 1a and phase 2a messages and deciding the transaction outcome when sufficient votes are collected. Leader selection is not modeled; any process may act as leader.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) A mapping from each resource manager to its current state (working, prepared, committed, or aborted). (2) For each RM-acceptor pair, the acceptor's state in that RM's consensus instance, consisting of the highest ballot number the acceptor has responded to, the ballot number and value of its most recent vote (or sentinel values if it has not voted). (3) The set of all messages ever sent, which grows monotonically. Message types include: phase 1a (ballot initiation from leader), phase 1b (acceptor response with vote history), phase 2a (leader proposal with value), phase 2b (acceptor vote), and commit/abort announcements.
description.initial_state: All resource managers are in the working state. Every acceptor's state for every RM instance has its highest-responded ballot set to the initial ballot, no previous vote recorded, and no value voted for. No messages have been sent.
description.actions: Resource manager actions: (1) Prepare: a working RM transitions to prepared and sends a phase 2a message for ballot zero with value prepared. (2) Choose to abort: a working RM transitions to aborted and sends a phase 2a message for ballot zero with value aborted. (3) Receive commit: an RM seeing a commit announcement transitions to committed. (4) Receive abort: an RM seeing an abort announcement transitions to aborted. Leader actions: (5) Phase 1a: a leader initiates a new ballot for a specific RM instance by sending a phase 1a message. (6) Phase 2a: when the leader has received phase 1b messages from a majority of acceptors for a given ballot in a given RM instance, it determines a safe value and sends a phase 2a message. If all responding acceptors reported no previous vote, the leader chooses aborted; otherwise it uses the value from the highest-numbered previous vote. (7) Decide: when all RM instances have a value chosen by a majority (all prepared means commit; any aborted means abort), the leader announces the result. Acceptor actions: (8) Phase 1b: an acceptor responds to a phase 1a message if the ballot number exceeds its current highest ballot, updating that ballot and reporting its vote history. (9) Phase 2b: an acceptor votes for the value in a phase 2a message if the ballot number is at least its current highest ballot, updating its ballot and vote records.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: all state variables remain within their declared types. The specification implements the abstract transaction commit specification, ensuring consistency: no resource manager is committed while another is aborted.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: Constants include the set of resource managers, the set of acceptors, the set of majorities (each being a subset of acceptors such that any two majorities overlap), and the set of ballot numbers (which must include zero and be a subset of natural numbers). For model checking, typical values are two resource managers, three acceptors, three majority sets of size two, and ballot numbers zero and one.
description.additional_assumptions: Messages are modeled as a set that only grows; no message loss or duplication is modeled explicitly since only safety is specified. The initial ballot (ballot zero) is used by RMs to directly propose their prepared/aborted decisions, bypassing phase 1 for that ballot. A helper function computes the maximum of a set of numbers, returning negative one for the empty set. The specification imports the abstract transaction commit module and asserts that Paxos Commit implements it via refinement. Any two declared majorities must have a non-empty intersection.

description.system_overview: This specification models a system that alternately performs two actions, referred to as the zeroth and first actions. A control variable alternates between zero and one, triggering the corresponding action on each transition. This captures the fundamental pattern of two processes taking turns, abstracted away from any particular implementation.
description.actors_and_components: The system is parameterized by two constant operators: one describing valid initial states for the data component, and one describing valid transitions for each of the two alternating actions. The actors are implicit: the zeroth action corresponds to one party (e.g., a producer) and the first action to the other party (e.g., a consumer).
description.state_variables: The system tracks two pieces of state: (1) A control variable that alternates between zero and one, indicating which action should occur next. (2) A data variable representing the application-specific state that is modified by each action.
description.initial_state: The control variable starts at zero. The data variable satisfies the initial-state predicate provided as a constant parameter.
description.actions: A single next-state relation: the control variable advances from its current value to the next (cycling between zero and one using modular arithmetic), and the data variable is updated according to the action predicate corresponding to the current control value. The zeroth action fires when the control is zero, and the first action fires when the control is one.
description.safety_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses higher-order constant operators: a unary predicate for initial data states and a ternary predicate relating the action index, current data value, and next data value. A note observes that a philosophically complete specification would hide the control variable using existential quantification, but this is omitted for practical engineering reasons.

description.system_overview: This specification models the two-phase handshake, a fundamental hardware synchronization protocol in which a Producer and a Consumer alternately perform actions, with the Producer going first. Two control signals are used to coordinate the alternation. The specification proves that this protocol implements the abstract alternating specification under a refinement mapping.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of two processes: a Producer and a Consumer. They communicate through two binary control signals. The Producer acts when both signals agree, and the Consumer acts when they disagree. The system is parameterized by constant operators describing valid initial data states and valid action transitions.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) The producer's control signal, a binary value (zero or one). (2) The consumer's control signal, a binary value (zero or one). (3) A data variable representing the application-specific state modified by each action.
description.initial_state: Both control signals start at zero. The data variable satisfies the initial-state predicate provided as a constant parameter.
description.actions: Two actions can occur: (1) Producer step: enabled when both control signals have the same value. The producer performs the zeroth action (updating the data), then toggles its control signal (advancing it by one modulo two). The consumer's signal is unchanged. (2) Consumer step: enabled when the control signals differ. The consumer performs the first action (updating the data), then toggles its control signal (advancing it by one modulo two). The producer's signal is unchanged.
description.safety_properties: An invariant states that both control signals are always in the set containing zero and one. The specification proves that the two-phase handshake implements the abstract alternating specification: the sum of the two control signals modulo two serves as the refinement mapping for the abstract control variable.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.additional_assumptions: The specification includes a formal machine-checked proof (using the TLAPS proof system) that the two-phase handshake implements the alternating specification. The proof establishes the invariant on both signals and shows that every step of the handshake protocol corresponds to a valid step of the abstract specification under the refinement mapping. The data operations are parameterized by higher-order constant operators for initial states and transitions.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the two-phase handshake specification. It instantiates the abstract constant operators with concrete definitions to make the specification amenable to finite model checking by TLC.
description.actors_and_components: Same as the TwoPhase handshake specification: a Producer and Consumer alternating via two binary control signals. This module provides concrete implementations of the parameterized data operations.
description.state_variables: Inherits all state variables from the TwoPhase specification: two binary control signals and a data variable.
description.initial_state: Both control signals start at zero. The data variable is initialized to zero (the concrete initial-state predicate requires the data to equal zero).
description.actions: Inherits all actions from the TwoPhase specification. The concrete action predicate for both the zeroth and first actions is the identity: the data value is left unchanged (the next data value equals the current data value).
description.safety_properties: Inherits the invariant from TwoPhase ensuring both control signals are binary. The implementation refinement theorem from TwoPhase also applies.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The data variable and control signals are bounded to small finite values. The identity action and zero-initialized data ensure the state space is minimal.
description.additional_assumptions: This module uses the TLA+ INSTANCE mechanism to import the TwoPhase specification with its constant parameters replaced by concrete operators. The data initial predicate requires data to equal zero. The data action predicate is the identity function (no change), making the specification trivial in the data dimension so the model checker can focus on the control protocol behavior.

description.system_overview: This specification models the original protocol used by the Nano cryptocurrency blockchain, which uses a block-lattice data structure where every account has its own blockchain (account chain). The specification focuses on modeling hash functions and cryptographic signatures, and demonstrates the challenges of using finite model checking to analyze blockchain-like data structures that record action history in an ordered way.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of: (1) Network nodes, each owning a private key and maintaining a local copy of the distributed ledger. (2) Accounts identified by public keys, each with its own chain of blocks. (3) A genesis account that holds the initial total coin supply. The protocol uses Ed25519-style key pairs for signing and Blake2b-style hashing for block identification.
description.state_variables: The system tracks three pieces of state: (1) The last calculated block hash, used for ordering block creation. (2) A distributed ledger replicated across all nodes, mapping block hashes to signed blocks (or an empty sentinel). Each node maintains its own copy. (3) A set of received-but-not-yet-validated blocks for each node, representing blocks in transit awaiting confirmation.
description.initial_state: The last hash is set to a sentinel value indicating no blocks exist. Every node's ledger maps all hashes to the empty sentinel (no blocks recorded). Every node's received set is empty.
description.actions: The system supports several block creation and processing actions: (1) Create genesis block: a private key holder creates the initial block containing the entire coin supply, signed with their key and added to all nodes' ledgers simultaneously. Can only happen once. (2) Create send block: a node creates a block that reduces its account balance and designates a recipient. The block references the previous block in the sender's chain and must not send more than the available balance. (3) Create open block: a node opens a new account by referencing a send block directed to its public key, establishing the account's first block. (4) Create receive block: a node creates a block referencing both its previous block and a send block directed to it, adding the sent amount to its balance. (5) Create change representative block: a node changes its voting representative by creating a block referencing its previous block. Each created block is broadcast to all nodes' received sets. Processing actions validate received blocks against the node's local ledger copy and add them to the ledger. Validation includes checking cryptographic signatures against the account's public key, verifying referenced blocks exist, and checking block-type-specific rules (e.g., send blocks cannot overdraw, open blocks must reference an unreceived send, receive blocks must reference an unclaimed send).
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: the last hash, distributed ledger, and received sets maintain their declared types. Cryptographic invariant: every block in every node's ledger has a valid signature that matches the public key of the account that owns the chain containing that block.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: Constants include the set of block hashes, a hash calculation operator (modeled externally), the set of private and public keys, a mapping from private to public keys, the set of network nodes, the total genesis balance (a natural number), and a mapping from nodes to their owned private keys.
description.additional_assumptions: The hash calculation is modeled as an abstract constant operator that maps block data and the previous hash to a new hash, enabling different implementations for specification versus model checking. Balance tracking uses recursive functions to walk the account chain. A balance invariant asserts that the sum of all account balances never exceeds the genesis balance, though this is defined separately from the main safety invariant. The specification notes that blockchains have super-exponential state space scaling because action order is recorded in the chain itself, making finite model checking of limited effectiveness for these structures.

description.system_overview: This is a model-checking configuration module for the Nano blockchain specification. It makes the abstract Nano specification amenable to finite model checking by providing a concrete hash function implementation, handling hash depletion gracefully, and defining a state view that removes hash ordering from state comparison. The module works around TLC's level-checking restrictions by overriding the hash calculation constant in the model configuration rather than directly in the module.
description.actors_and_components: Same as the Nano specification: network nodes with private keys maintaining distributed ledgers. This module adds a hash function mapping that tracks which block is stored at each hash, enabling a concrete implementation of hash calculation.
description.state_variables: Inherits all state variables from the Nano specification (last hash, distributed ledger, received blocks) and adds one additional variable: a hash function mapping from hashes to blocks (or the empty sentinel), which tracks the assignment of hashes to blocks as they are created.
description.initial_state: The hash function maps every hash to the empty sentinel (no blocks assigned). All inherited state from the Nano specification is initialized as in that specification.
description.actions: Inherits all actions from the Nano specification (genesis block creation, send, open, receive, and change representative block creation and processing). Adds a check before each step: if there are no undefined (unused) hashes remaining, the system stutters (takes no action) rather than failing. The hash calculation implementation finds an unused hash for each new block and updates the hash function mapping.
description.safety_properties: Type invariant: the hash function mapping maintains its declared type, and all Nano type invariants hold. Safety invariant: all Nano cryptographic invariants hold.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: The hash set size controls the maximum number of blocks that can be created. Three configurations exist with increasing hash set sizes (three, four, and five hashes). All configurations use two private keys, two public keys, two nodes, and a genesis balance of three. The state view for model checking excludes the hash function and last hash variables, so states that differ only in hash assignment order are considered equivalent.
description.additional_assumptions: The hash function implementation assigns hashes to blocks on a first-available basis: when a new block needs a hash, it picks any hash currently mapped to the empty sentinel. If an existing block is rehashed, the same hash is returned. The key pair and node ownership mappings are chosen deterministically using bijective mappings between private keys and public keys, and between nodes and private keys. The set of private keys and public keys must have equal cardinality, and the number of private keys must not exceed the number of nodes. The module uses TLC's constant override mechanism to work around level-checking restrictions on variable-level hash functions.

description.system_overview: This specification defines the consensus problem: a set of processes must choose a single value from a set of possible values. It provides a trivial high-level specification that describes the allowed behaviors of a consensus algorithm, serving as the correctness criterion that more detailed algorithms (such as Paxos) must implement via refinement. The specification includes both safety and liveness properties with formal machine-checked proofs.
description.actors_and_components: The system is parameterized by a set of choosable values. There are no explicit process identifiers; the specification abstracts away the mechanism of choosing and focuses on what it means for a value to be chosen. In practice, propose and learn actions would be added by a real consensus algorithm.
description.state_variables: The system tracks a single piece of state: the set of chosen values, which starts empty and may transition to a singleton set containing one chosen value.
description.initial_state: The set of chosen values is empty (no value has been chosen).
description.actions: A single action: when no value has been chosen yet (the chosen set is empty), one value is nondeterministically selected from the set of possible values and the chosen set becomes the singleton containing that value. This action can occur at most once, after which no further state changes are possible.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness: the chosen set is always a subset of the value set and is always finite. At most one value is ever chosen: the cardinality of the chosen set never exceeds one. These properties are proved as invariants using formal proofs.
description.liveness_properties: Under a liveness specification that adds weak fairness to the next-state action, eventually some value is chosen (the chosen set becomes non-empty). This requires the assumption that the set of possible values is non-empty.
description.model_bounds: The set of possible values is a constant. For model checking, it is typically instantiated with a small finite set such as three values.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses PlusCal for the algorithm description, translated to TLA+. The liveness specification is defined separately from the safety specification by conjoining weak fairness of the next-state action. A formal proof establishes that the safety invariant is inductive, and a separate liveness proof shows that fairness guarantees eventual value selection. A theorem establishes an equivalent formulation of the live specification useful for refinement proofs. The set of values must be non-empty for the liveness property to hold.

description.system_overview: This specification models a high-level consensus algorithm based on voting with ballots. A set of acceptors cooperatively choose a value by casting votes in numbered ballot rounds. A value is chosen when a quorum of acceptors all vote for the same value in the same ballot. The algorithm refines the abstract consensus specification and serves as the foundation for more concrete Paxos variants.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of acceptors that cast votes in ballots. A quorum is defined as any set of acceptors such that any two quorums have a non-empty intersection. There are no explicit leader or proposer processes; the algorithm specifies only what actions acceptors may take.
description.state_variables: The system tracks two arrays indexed by acceptor: (1) The set of votes cast by each acceptor, where each vote is a pair of a ballot number and a value. (2) The highest ballot number in which each acceptor has participated (or negative one if it has not yet participated). An acceptor cannot vote in any ballot lower than its recorded maximum.
description.initial_state: Every acceptor has cast no votes (empty vote set). Every acceptor's maximum ballot is negative one (has not participated in any ballot).
description.actions: Each acceptor can perform two actions in each step, nondeterministically choosing a ballot number: (1) Increase maximum ballot: if the chosen ballot exceeds the acceptor's current maximum ballot, update the maximum to the chosen ballot. This prevents the acceptor from voting in lower-numbered ballots. (2) Vote for a value: if the chosen ballot is at least the acceptor's current maximum ballot, the acceptor has not already voted in that ballot, all other acceptors that voted in that ballot voted for the same value, and the value is safe at that ballot number, then the acceptor casts a vote for that value and updates its maximum ballot. Safety at a ballot is defined recursively: a value is safe at ballot zero unconditionally; at higher ballots, it is safe if there exists a quorum where all members have participated at or above that ballot, and either no member voted in any ballot between some cutoff and the current ballot, or the value was itself safe at the cutoff ballot and all votes at the cutoff were for the same value.
description.safety_properties: Four invariants are maintained: (1) Type correctness for votes and maximum ballots. (2) An acceptor's maximum ballot is at least as large as the ballot of any vote it has cast. (3) If an acceptor has voted in a ballot, it has not voted in any ballot between that vote's ballot and its maximum ballot. (4) Every vote cast is for a value that is safe at the vote's ballot number. Together these ensure the key safety property: the set of chosen values always has cardinality at most one. The specification formally refines the abstract consensus specification.
description.liveness_properties: A liveness specification adds fairness conditions ensuring that if a quorum of acceptors are responsive and a ballot is sufficiently stable, then eventually some value is chosen.
description.model_bounds: Constants include the set of choosable values, the set of acceptors, and the set of quorums. Ballot numbers are natural numbers. For model checking, typical values are two values, three acceptors, and all subsets of size two or more as quorums, with ballots restricted to zero through two.
description.additional_assumptions: The specification uses PlusCal for the algorithm, translated to TLA+. It imports the abstract consensus specification and proves refinement: the set of values for which a quorum has unanimously voted in some ballot equals the chosen set of the consensus specification. The recursive safety definition uses a function definition rather than recursive operator definition because the TLAPS proof system does not support the latter. The specification includes formal proofs of all invariants and the refinement theorem, checked by TLAPS. Quorums must satisfy the intersection property: any two quorums share at least one acceptor.

description.system_overview: This specification models PCon, a variant of the classic Paxos consensus algorithm that introduces phase 1c messages to separate the safety-assertion and voting functions of phase 2a messages. In classic Paxos, a phase 2a message both asserts that a value is safe and instructs acceptors to vote for it. In PCon, a phase 1c message asserts safety, and phase 2a is sent only after a corresponding 1c message exists. This variant is useful for reconfiguration scenarios where different sets of acceptors handle different ballots, as the 1c messages propagate safety knowledge and remove dependency on earlier ballot acceptors.
description.actors_and_components: The system has two types of processes: (1) Acceptors that respond to ballot messages by reporting their vote history (phase 1b) and casting votes (phase 2b). (2) Leaders, one per ballot, that initiate ballots (phase 1a), determine which values are safe (phase 1c), and propose values for voting (phase 2a). Multiple leaders may be active concurrently, and leader selection is not assumed to be reliable.
description.state_variables: The system tracks four arrays and a message set: (1) For each acceptor, the highest ballot number it has participated in. (2) For each acceptor, the highest ballot number in which it voted (or negative one if never voted). (3) For each acceptor, the value it voted for in its highest voting ballot (or a sentinel if never voted). (4) The set of all messages ever sent, growing monotonically. Messages include five types: 1a (ballot initiation), 1b (acceptor response with vote history), 1c (leader assertion that a value is safe), 2a (leader proposal), and 2b (acceptor vote).
description.initial_state: All acceptors have maximum ballot negative one, maximum voting ballot negative one, and maximum voting value set to the sentinel. No messages have been sent.
description.actions: Leader actions: (1) Phase 1a: send a ballot initiation message. (2) Phase 1c: after receiving phase 1b responses from a quorum for a given ballot, determine which values are safe at that ballot (using the ShowsSafeAt predicate that checks quorum responses) and send 1c messages for those values. (3) Phase 2a: if no phase 2a has been sent for this ballot and a 1c message exists for a value at this ballot, send a 2a message proposing that value. Acceptor actions: (4) Phase 1b: if a 1a message exists for a ballot exceeding the acceptor's maximum, update the maximum ballot and respond with current vote history. (5) Phase 2b: if a 2a message exists for a ballot at least equal to the acceptor's maximum, cast a vote for the proposed value, updating all acceptor state accordingly.
description.safety_properties: Type correctness for all variables and messages. An inductive invariant consisting of five conjuncts: (1) Acceptor state consistency: maximum ballot is at least maximum voting ballot, and the acceptor did not vote in ballots between the two. (2) Phase 1b message accuracy: messages correctly reflect acceptor state at time of sending. (3) Phase 1c correctness: every 1c message asserts a value that is indeed safe at that ballot (per the voting algorithm's safety definition). (4) Phase 2a provenance: every 2a message has a corresponding 1c message. (5) Type correctness. Together these ensure the specification implements the voting algorithm, which in turn implements consensus.
description.liveness_properties: If there exists a ballot and quorum such that: no higher ballot's phase 1a has been or will be sent, the leader eventually sends a phase 1a for this ballot, each acceptor in the quorum eventually responds to ballot messages, and the leader eventually executes phase 2a if enabled, then eventually some value is chosen.
description.model_bounds: Constants include the set of choosable values, the set of acceptors, and the set of quorums. Ballots are natural numbers. For model checking, typical values are two values, three acceptors, three quorums of size two, and ballots zero through two.
description.additional_assumptions: Ballots and acceptors are assumed to be disjoint sets so they can be used as process identifiers simultaneously. The specification uses PlusCal, translated to TLA+. It imports the voting specification and proves refinement: the votes derived from phase 2b messages implement the voting algorithm's vote tracking, and the maximum ballot array directly maps. The ShowsSafeAt predicate checks whether a quorum's phase 1b responses demonstrate safety, potentially using 1c messages from earlier ballots to establish safety of values. Omission faults (message loss, process crashes) are handled implicitly: the safety specification never requires any action to occur.

description.system_overview: This specification models a Byzantine Paxos consensus algorithm (BPCon), extending the PCon variant of Paxos to tolerate Byzantine (arbitrary/malicious) failures among acceptors and leaders. It abstracts and generalizes the consensus algorithm from Castro and Liskov's Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT). Good acceptors execute the Paxos protocol faithfully, while faulty acceptors may send arbitrary messages. Safety is guaranteed as long as any two Byzantine quorums share at least one good acceptor.
description.actors_and_components: The system has three categories of participants: (1) Good (non-faulty) acceptors that follow the protocol faithfully. (2) Fake (possibly malicious) acceptors that may send arbitrary syntactically correct messages. (3) Leaders, one per ballot, that may be faulty (any leader can send any syntactically correct message). A Byzantine quorum is a set of acceptors (real and fake) that includes a quorum of good ones. A weak quorum is a set containing at least one good acceptor.
description.state_variables: The system tracks four arrays indexed by good acceptor and a message set: (1) For each good acceptor, the highest ballot participated in. (2) For each good acceptor, the highest ballot in which it voted (or negative one if never voted). (3) For each good acceptor, the value voted for at the highest voting ballot (or sentinel if never voted). (4) The set of all messages ever sent. Message types include: 1a (ballot initiation), 1b (acceptor response with vote history), 1c (safety assertion), 2a (leader proposal), 2b (acceptor vote), and a special fake type that allows faulty acceptors to inject arbitrary 1b and 2b messages.
description.initial_state: All good acceptors have maximum ballot negative one, maximum voting ballot negative one, and sentinel voting value. No messages have been sent.
description.actions: Good acceptor actions mirror the non-Byzantine protocol: (1) Phase 1b: respond to a 1a message for a higher ballot with current vote state. (2) Phase 2b: vote for a value proposed in a 2a message for a ballot at least equal to the acceptor's maximum ballot. Leader actions are unrestricted since leaders may be Byzantine: (3) Phase 1a: any leader may send any 1a message at any time. (4) Phase 1c: a leader may send a 1c message for any value shown safe by a Byzantine quorum's 1b responses. (5) Phase 2a: a leader may propose any value for which a 1c message exists in the current ballot and no 2a has been sent yet. Faulty acceptor action: (6) A fake acceptor may inject any syntactically correct 1b or 2b message at any time, potentially lying about its vote history or votes.
description.safety_properties: An inductive invariant ensures: (1) Good acceptors maintain consistent state (maximum ballot at least equals maximum voting ballot, no votes in gaps). (2) Phase 1b messages from good acceptors accurately reflect their state. (3) Phase 1c messages correctly assert value safety (accounting for Byzantine behavior). (4) Phase 2a messages have corresponding 1c messages. (5) Good acceptors' 2b votes are consistent with their state. The key safety guarantee is that the algorithm implements the non-Byzantine PCon specification when restricted to good acceptors, which in turn implements consensus: at most one value is ever chosen.
description.liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED
description.model_bounds: Constants include the set of values, good acceptors, fake acceptors, Byzantine quorums, and weak quorums. For model checking, typical values are two values, three good acceptors, one fake acceptor, Byzantine quorums are all sets of three or more from the four total acceptors, and weak quorums are all sets of two or more. Ballots are restricted to zero through two.
description.additional_assumptions: Good and fake acceptor sets must be disjoint. Any two Byzantine quorums must share at least one good acceptor (the fundamental Byzantine quorum intersection property). Every weak quorum must contain at least one good acceptor. The specification uses a prophecy-constant approach: which acceptors are good versus fake is declared in advance, but good acceptors' actions do not depend on this knowledge. The ShowsSafeAt predicate for the Byzantine case requires checking that a weak quorum of 2b senders for an earlier ballot all agreed on a value, providing resilience against forged messages. The specification imports the non-Byzantine PCon module and proves refinement, with votes and maximum ballots of good acceptors serving as the refinement mapping.

description.system_overview: This specification models the Dijkstra-Scholten algorithm for detecting termination of diffusing computations in a distributed system. The algorithm was published by E.W. Dijkstra and C.S. Scholten in 'Termination detection for diffusing computations' (Information Processing Letters, 11(1):1-4, 1980). The algorithm detects when a distributed computation initiated by a single leader process has terminated, meaning all processes are idle and no messages are in transit. The key insight is constructing a dynamic overlay tree over an arbitrary network topology, where non-neutral processes form a tree rooted at the leader.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of processes connected by a directed graph (network). One distinguished process is the leader, which initiates the computation. The leader has only outgoing edges and cannot receive computation messages. Each process can be either busy (computing) or idle. Busy processes can send computation messages along outgoing edges. The algorithm introduces control messages called acknowledgments (acks) that flow in the reverse direction of computation messages. An overlay tree is dynamically maintained, where each non-neutral process has a parent in the tree.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) whether each process is currently active (busy) or idle, (2) for each directed edge, the count of messages sent along that edge that have not yet been acknowledged, (3) for each directed edge, the count of messages received along that edge that have not yet been acknowledged by the receiver, (4) for each non-leader process, which edge connects it to its parent in the overlay tree (or a sentinel value indicating the process has no parent), (5) for each edge, the number of computation messages currently in transit, and (6) for each edge, the number of acknowledgment (control) messages currently in transit.
description.initial_state: Initially, only the leader is active (busy); all other processes are idle. No computation messages have been sent, so all message and acknowledgment counters on all edges are zero. No non-leader process has a parent in the overlay tree.
description.actions: The algorithm defines five types of actions: (1) Send message: an active process sends a computation message along one of its outgoing edges, incrementing the sent-unacknowledged counter and the in-transit message count for that edge. (2) Receive acknowledgment: a process receives an acknowledgment on one of its outgoing edges, decrementing both the ack-in-transit counter and the sent-unacknowledged counter. (3) Send acknowledgment: a process sends an acknowledgment back along an incoming edge, subject to constraints that prevent the process from sending its last ack to its parent until the process is neutral (idle, with all messages acknowledged in both directions). When a process becomes neutral after sending an ack, it removes itself from the overlay tree. (4) Receive message: a process receives a computation message on an incoming edge, becoming active. If the process was neutral before receiving, the sender becomes the process's parent in the overlay tree. (5) Idle: an active process may become idle at any time.
description.safety_properties: The main safety property is that if the leader is neutral (idle, with all sent messages acknowledged and all received messages acknowledged), then every other process is also neutral. This ensures the leader detects termination only when the computation has truly terminated. Additionally, the overlay tree of non-neutral processes always forms a valid tree rooted at the leader (when non-empty), and the message counters remain consistent: for any edge, the sent-unacknowledged count equals the sum of received-unacknowledged count, in-transit acks, and in-transit messages.
description.liveness_properties: If the computation terminates (all processes become idle and there are no messages in transit), then the leader eventually becomes neutral, thereby detecting termination.
description.model_bounds: The set of processes and the network topology (directed edge set) are declared as constants. For model checking, these must be instantiated with specific finite sets. Message and acknowledgment counters may need explicit bounds to keep the state space finite.
description.additional_assumptions: Messages are never lost (both computation and control messages are delivered reliably). Message ordering does not matter for correctness. Self-loops are not allowed in the network graph. Non-Byzantine process failures cannot cause the leader to falsely believe a non-terminated computation has terminated, but may prevent termination from being detected. Weak fairness is assumed for the next-state action.

description.system_overview: This specification is a PlusCal representation of the Dijkstra-Scholten algorithm for detecting termination of a distributed computation initiated by a designated root node. Published by E.W. Dijkstra and C.S. Scholten in 'Termination detection for diffusing computations' (Information Processing Letters, 11(1):1-4, 1980). The algorithm maintains a spanning tree that contains all active nodes. Inactive leaf nodes detach themselves from the tree, but may later be reactivated by receiving a message and reattach. When the root node has no more children and becomes inactive, it declares termination.
description.actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of nodes, one of which is designated as the initiator (root). Each node operates as an independent process that can send base messages to other nodes, receive messages, terminate (become inactive), receive acknowledgments, and detach from the spanning tree or declare termination. A shared network provides message-passing infrastructure with per-sender message queues and acknowledgment counters for each node.
description.state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a global termination detection flag indicating whether termination has been declared, (2) a network structure that for each node maintains a count of pending base messages from each sending node and a count of pending acknowledgment messages, (3) per-node activity status (active or inactive), (4) per-node parent pointer indicating the node's parent in the spanning tree or a sentinel value if the node has no parent, and (5) per-node count of active children (sons) in the spanning tree.
description.initial_state: Termination has not been detected. The network has no pending messages or acknowledgments. Only the initiator is active; all other nodes are inactive. The initiator's parent is itself; all other nodes have no parent. All nodes start with zero active children.
description.actions: Each node process runs in an infinite loop choosing nondeterministically among five operations: (1) Send message: an active node sends a base message to some other node, incrementing its active children count.
